The Eleventh Chapter: The Śākta Kāmarāja-vidyā, the Exposition of the Lopāmudrā-bheda, and the Exposition of the Śākta Pañcamī-bheda (Recalling the previously mentioned defects of mantras).
In this tenth chapter, concerning the Śrīvidyā, I have indeed written down the cause for the curse upon the mantra. (1)

(Now, the promise to describe the unfastened Vidyā) Now, therefore, [I shall describe] the unfastened Vidyā belonging to Śakti, which is extremely difficult to obtain and was proclaimed by Śiva in the Great Tantra of the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya).
By the grace of the glorious Guru, I shall explain the supreme [reality] through symbolic terminology.
(The Śāktakāmarājavidyā, therein the Vāgbhava-kūṭa: Vāmākṣī, the syllable Bhaga, Kāma, Indra, and Maheśvarī.
(In the Kāmarāja-śakti-kūṭa:)
As before, the two syllables known as Kāma and Śakti are of the nature of being unfastened.

1–2 | Having previously established in the tenth chapter, by means of the narrative of Kamalākara, that the Śāmbhava Kāmarāja mantra acts as an obstacle to spiritual attainment (*siddhi*) when under a curse, he recalls that point in this chapter with the words beginning "In the chapter... and so forth. That is the Śāmbhava Kāmarāja Vidyā.
Without following the procedure for removing the defect of being "pinned" (kīlita), the unpropitiated [Vidyā] obstructs success.

However, the Śākta-Kāmarāja-Vidyā to be described hereafter is to be especially adopted by practitioners because it is free from defects such as being pinned; this is what he states with the words beginning "atha ataḥ."
3. Now, he describes that unfastened *Śāktakāmarāja* vidyā according to the *Ūrdhvāmnāya Tantra*, beginning with the words "vāmākṣī" and so forth.
*Vāmākṣī* is the letter *ī*; *bhagavarṇa* is the letter *e*; *kāma* is the letter *ka*; and *indra* is the letter *la*.
(The state of being unfastened and its excellence [belong] to this [vidyā]).
The unbarred Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), belonging to Śakti, bestows the accomplishment of all aims;
endowed with potency, she is eternal, grants liberation, and brings the three worlds under her control. || 4 ||
(Its conformity with a specific tradition:
This Great Vidyā of the Eastern Tradition must be guarded with great effort.
(The promise to describe Lopāmudrā as conforming to the Western Tradition:)
I shall now describe Lopāmudrā, who is conjoined with the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya).
Ha-sau are Kāma and Śakra; O Śivā, Soma, Sūrya, Madanadahanah, Śakra, and Girijā, you who are devoted to destroying the fear of the world!
Vidhu, Brahmā, Bhūmi, and she who is joined with the seed that generates the worlds—these fortunate ones are skilled in the knowledge of the supreme state. || 7 ||

*Maheśvarī* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, it results in *ī e ka la hrīṃ*, which is the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. Regarding the phrase "as before," the intended meaning here is as follows: previously, in the *Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja-vidyā*, that [mantra] was secured by the very inclusion of the aforementioned *vāgbhava-kūṭa*, namely *ka e ī la hrīṃ*; therefore, by abandoning that *vāgbhava-kūṭa*...

If the other two *kūṭas*, namely *ī e ka la hrīm*, were joined with the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* mentioned in this mantra, then there would be no fault of being "bolted" (*kīlita*). To indicate this very point, having here stated only the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* which is distinct from that [previous one], [the text] proceeds as before with the words "called Kāma and Śakti," etc., regarding these two: *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* and *sa ka la hrīm*.
The essential point is that the inclusion of both *kāmarāja* and *śakti* clusters signifies the extraction of the mantra as a whole and its state of being "unbolted" (*niṣkīlita*).
Having first divided the three clusters, the complete mantra is now demonstrated:
7. Regarding the mantra *hasau*, he describes *śāmbhavī*, *lopāmudrā*, and that which is joined with the fault of *saṃhāra* (retraction) by means of the words beginning with "hasau. *Hasau*... [etc.]
(The nature of the three peaks according to etymology: The white *vāgbhava*, the primordial seed-syllable, is proclaimed in the scriptures as bestowing intelligence;
the red *kāma*, the supreme sovereign of desire, resembles ten million rays of light other than white.

That which is celebrated by practitioners as the Śākta, the Gaura, the seed-syllable that pacifies infinite suffering, and which is auspicious, is the source of the world— including all things moving and stationary— and is under its control.
(The excellence of this [vidyā]):
The Goddess Tripurasundarī herself consists of Śiva and Śakti;
she is the supreme vidyā, difficult to attain, and endowed with the quality of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
That is designated as Śāmbhavī; therein [is] the Vāgbhava-kūṭa of Śāktalopāmudrā.
Now I shall describe the Śākta [kūṭas]. || 9 ||

The letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, desire (*kāma*) which is the letter *ka*, Śakra who is the letter *la*, and *hrīṃ*—the one intent on destroying the fear of the world. Thus, *ha sa ka la hrīṃ* is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa. Regarding "Śiva": Śiva is the letter *a*, Soma is the letter *sa*, Sūrya is the letter *ka*, the burner of Madana is the letter *ha*, Śakra is the letter *la*, and Girijā is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*.

The *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja. Regarding "Vidhu": *vidhu* is the letter *sa*; *brahmā* is the letter *ka*; *bhūmi* is the letter *la*; and the seed-syllable of the mother of the worlds (*bhuvanajanī*) is *hrīṃ*. It is composed of these. Thus, *sa ka la hrīṃ* is the *kūṭa* of Śakti. And so, the mantra formed by the combination of these is shown according to its division into *kūṭas*: [The resulting mantra is: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsphreṃ hsauḥ oṃ namo bhagavati annapūrṇe svāhā*. [This is followed by the *kūṭas*: 1. *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsphreṃ hsauḥ oṃ namo bhagavati annapūrṇe svāhā* (the *kūṭa* of Vidyā). 2. *sa ka la hrīṃ* (the *kūṭa* of Śakti). 3. *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsphreṃ hsauḥ oṃ namo bhagavati annapūrṇe svāhā* (the *kūṭa* of Vidyā again). Thus, the mantra is presented through the distinction of its *kūṭas*.
(Śāmbhavī is the first; Lopāmudrā is endowed with the fault of withdrawal. The Vāgbhava-kūṭa and the Kāmarāja-kūṭa.
The peak of power:
*ha ha*
sa sa sa
Ka ka ka
la la ha (lalaha)
Hrīṃ hrīṃ la.

Hrīṃ 8. He explains the nature of the three *kūṭas*, beginning with the *vāgbhava*, which constitute the component parts of the *nirukta* mantra, by means of the passage beginning with "white" (*śuklam*). "Śākta" means the *kūṭa* of Śakti.
9–10 | Having thus described the Śāmbhava Lopāmudrā, he states the fifteen-syllable Śākta Lopāmudrā: Jhiṇṭīśa, Bhaga, Kāma, Devarāja, and Maheśvarī.
In the *kāmarāja-śakti-kūṭa*, as before, the two syllables known as *kāma* and *śakti* are of the nature of being unfastened (*niṣkīlita*). || 10 ||
(The seventeen-syllable Śāktalopāmudrā): This is the venerable Mahātripurasundarī conjoined with the vital breaths.
(Her excellence:)
This knowledge is to be known, supreme, secret, and free from the defect of dissolution;
it was previously described as the power of withdrawal, and being devoid of bestowal, it does not grant enjoyment.

By the words "Jhiṇṭīśa," and so forth: Jhiṇṭīśa is the vowel *e*; Bhaga here is the vowel *ī*; Kāma is the letter *ka*; Devarāja is the letter *la*; Maheśvarī is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *e ī ka la hrīṃ* is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa. "As before" means that the Kāmarāja-kūṭa and the Śakti-kūṭa are as previously described, namely like the Śāmbhava and Lopāmudrā [kūṭas]. This is the essential nature of the mantra composed of these three kūṭas.
It is demonstrated by the arrangement of lines:
(the fifteen-syllabled Śāktalopāmudrā) is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
The peak-syllable of desire-passion and the peak-syllable of power.
Ha sa sa.
ka ka ka
la la ha (lalaha)
hrīṃ hrīṃ la
Hrīṃ (this seventeen-syllable mantra is) the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
The peak-syllable of Kāmarāja and the peak-syllable of Śakti.
Ha sa sa.
ka ka ka
Lālahā
Hrīṃ hrīṃ la.
Haṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ

11. He states another mantra: "This," etc. The previously mentioned fifteen-syllabled *Śrī* is indeed *Śrīvidyā*; if it is conjoined with *prāṇa*, meaning with the two syllables of the *haṃsa*-seed-mantra (*haṃsa*), then it becomes the seventeen-syllabled *Mahātripurasundarī*. This is stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
At the end of *trikūṭa* is the seed-syllable *haṃsa*, adorned with the *bindu* and the *sarga*;
this is Śrī, conjoined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which liberates one from the suffering of poverty.
Thus, the nature of this mantra is demonstrated: (p.
329) When, at the beginning and at the end, there is the *trimūrtikā* and the *jyotsnā*, and likewise thereafter;
For at that time, having been applied to the mantra, the seed-syllable proceeds as a specific phoneme in due order. || 12 ||
This essence (another mantra of seventeen syllables) has been told; now I shall speak of the supreme one as well.
(Regarding the distinction between the Vāgbhava and Kāmarāja clusters:
If Śakti were to be the first [syllable] in both the Vāgbhava and the Kāmarāja, [then... 13.
This vidyā bestows all accomplishments, grants liberation, and bestows enjoyment;
thereafter, one should join the Śakti-kūṭa as before.

12. He states another mantra: "In the east," etc. When, at the beginning of the previously mentioned Vāgbhava-kūṭa of the Kāmarāja-vidyā, there is the Trimūrtikā—the long *īkāra*—and likewise the Jyotsnā—the *ekāra*—then it should be understood that the Vāgbhava-kūṭa becomes: *ī e ka la hrīṃ*. At that time, in the mantra...

The meaning is: in the previously mentioned Kāmarāja-vidyā beginning with the letter *ī*; having applied the seed-syllable *haṃsa*, [it is placed] at the end of the three peaks (*trikūṭa*), as is seen in the mantra to be described later.
The meaning is that by this sequential application of the specific syllables, it becomes a distinguished mantra. This mantra is demonstrated by the following layout of lines:
[Layout follows] This mantra is thus shown by the falling of the lines.
13–15 | Now, he promises to state another seventeen-syllable mantra with the words "And the supreme," etc.

Since this mantra also consists of three peaks (*kūṭa*), he first explains the arrangement of the *vāgbhava* and *kāmarāja* peaks with the words "The *vāgbhava*," etc. If, in the *vāgbhava* peak of the aforementioned seventeen-syllable mantra itself, Śakti were to be the first [syllable]...
The meaning is that one should join the letter *e*, which was previously situated below the letter *a*, before the letter *ī*. Likewise, in the *Kāmarāja* peak (*kūṭa*),
if there is *Śakti* at the end of the three peaks, it is the seed-syllable *Haṃsa* endowed with the *bindu* and the *sarga*.
Then the seventeenth Vidyā destroys suffering and poverty. || 15 ||
The syllable *aiṃ* is in the first peak (*kūṭa*), the syllable *klīṃ* in the Kāmarāja peak, and the syllable *sauḥ* in the Śakti peak; this is the eighteen-syllable Vidyā. (16)
The letter *sa* should be at the beginning; the meaning is that if one places the letter *sa*, which is situated below the letter *ha*, before the letter *ha*.
By this, it is stated that "e ī ka la hrīṃ" is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, and "sa ha ka ha la hrīṃ" is the Kāmarāja-kūṭa.
He describes the fruit of reciting these two kūṭas with the words beginning with "sarvasiddhikarī. Regarding the Śakti-kūṭa, he says "as before"; [this refers to] of this mantra.

Since it is based on the fifteen-syllable Śāktalopāmudrā mantra, as before, by the term "Śaktikūṭa," one should understand that it is precisely the Śāktakāmarāja-Śaktikūṭa: *sa ka la hrīṃ*. The meaning is that at the end of that Śaktikūṭa, one should join the two syllables of the Haṃsabīja (*haṃ saḥ*), endowed with the Bindu and Visarga. Otherwise, [the purpose] would have been fulfilled by the Haṃsabīja alone mentioned previously.

It should be understood that [otherwise] the statement beginning with "at the end of Trikūṭa from the gain" would be redundant. The configuration of this [mantra] is demonstrated by the drawing of lines—
(the seventeen-syllabled mantra).
The Vāgbhava peak, the Kāmarāja peak, and the Śakti peak.
And so it is,
and so it is.
Ha ka ka.
Kala kala!
ha hrīṃ hrīṃ
la haṃ hrīṃ
That [eighteen-syllable mantra] is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
The peak-syllable of desire-passion is the peak-syllable of power:
Ai.
klīṃ sauḥ e
Ha sa sa.
Ka ka ka.
Lālahā (la la ha)
hrīṃ hrīṃ la

Hrīṃ (16). He now states the eighteen-syllable Vidyā composed of three *kūṭas* (sections), beginning with the syllable *ai*. Regarding the aforementioned mantra, which is devoid of the two syllables in the form of *haṃsa*, at the beginning of the first of the three *kūṭas*, namely the *Vāgbhava-kūṭa*:

If one should append the syllable *ai* to the remainder, the syllable *klīṃ* at the beginning of the second *Kāmarāja-kūṭa*, and the syllable *sauḥ* at the beginning of the third *Śakti-kūṭa*, then the previously mentioned fifteen-syllabled *vidyā* itself—namely *ai klīṃ sauḥ*—becomes eighteen-syllabled through the addition of these three syllables; this is the established meaning. Its arrangement is now demonstrated:
(p. 331) (The twenty-syllable mantra): When joined with *haṃsa* at the very end, it then becomes a twenty-syllable [mantra].
(In this matter, there is the definitive conclusion of the authoritative tantras.)
Having understood the doctrine of the Mantranirṇaya-tantra, it is thus proclaimed. || 17 ||
(The Praise of the Śāktavāmakeśī-vidyā) The Vidyā known as Vāmakeśī, which has been proclaimed in the Pūrvāmnāya—
that Śākta [Vidyā], endowed with potency and bestowing accomplishment, is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (18)
(The Nature of the Vidyā) First is the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable; now I shall speak of the different seed-syllables (*bīja*).
One should then recite Maheśa, Śakti, Kāma, and the seed-syllable of Śakra.

17. He speaks of the twenty-syllable [vidyā] with the words "at the end of all. This means at the very end of this eighteen-syllable vidyā, that is, at the end of the *śakti*-kūṭa. By the insertion of the two syllables "haṃsa," the vidyā becomes twenty-syllabled;
such is the sequence agreed upon in the *Mantranirṇaya-tantra*. Its arrangement is as follows:
(The twenty-syllable Vidyā):
the Vāgbhava peak and the Kāmarāja peak.
The Śakti-kūṭa is ai/ klīṃ.
sauḥ e ha
He is he.
Ka ka la.
la ha hrīṃ
Hrīṃ La Haṃ
Hrīṃ Saḥ 18. Previously, in the tenth chapter, [it was stated]: "Kandarpa, joined with Viṣṇu, together with Adharamukha," and so forth.

That very [power] which is designated as the *Śāmbhava*, *Kāmarāja*, and *Vidyā* is called *Śāmbhavī*; it is stated in that very same [text]: "She is *Vāmakeśī*, she is *Śāmbhavī*, and she is proclaimed by the *Pūrvāmnāyas*," and so forth. Furthermore, she is "bolted" (*kīlitā*) and acts as an obstacle to spiritual attainment (*siddhi*). However, the *Śākta* [form], *Vāmakeśī*, is powerful and bestows attainment; this is what the *Pūrvāmnāya* and other texts state.

19. Regarding what the essential nature of that Śāktavāmakeśī is, he says: "The first," and so forth. First is Mahāmāyā; after that, [the seed-syllable] accompanied by the *kīla* and endowed with the *vāgbhava*. 19.
(Another method:
If this Vāgbhava and Śakti were joined together from the very beginning, then this most secret Vidyā would not have been proclaimed in the scriptures. (20)
Śiva, Śakti, then Brahmā, Śiva, and thereafter Śakra;
after that, Mahāmāyā, and immediately following that, the seed-syllable of Brahmā.
The connection is as follows: "I shall speak of the division of the seeds regarding the Vāgbhava-kūṭa which has been obtained. And thus:
It should be understood that its differentiation occurs solely through the division of the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), whereas the *kāmarāja* and *śakti* peaks remain exactly as before.
Now, he states the *vāgbhava* peak with the words beginning "Maheśa" and so forth: *maheśa* is the letter *ha*; *śakti* is the letter *sa*; *kāma* is the letter *ka*;
*śakrabīja* is the letter *la*; and *mahāmāyā* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha sa ka la hrīṃ* is the *vāgbhava* peak.

He states the nature of the combined mantra with the words "sakīlam" (with the *kīla*). This means that one should recite that which is endowed with the *vāgbhava* [syllable], distinguished by the *vāgbhava*-peak (*kūṭa*), together with the *kīla*—that is, the *kāmarāja* [syllable] fixed within the *śāmbhava*, along with that *kāmarāja*-peak and the *śakti*-peak.
Its essential form is demonstrated by the drawing of the lines as follows:

20–21 | He states another method with the words beginning "yadi" (if). The connection is as follows: "If, having written this Vāgbhava-kūṭa, the Śakti—the letter *sa*—were first joined there, prior to the letter *ha*.
And thus, when the letter *sa* is joined before the letter *ha* in the previously mentioned Vāgbhava, the Vāgbhava-kūṭa becomes: *sa ha ka la hrīṃ*.

Regarding this *kāmarājakūṭa*, Śiva states the specific details with the words beginning with "Śiva" and so forth. "Śiva" is the letter *ha*; "Śakti" is the letter *sa*; "Brahmā" is the letter *ka*; again "Śiva" is the letter *ha*; "Śakra" is the letter *la*; "Mahāmāyā" is *hrīṃ*; and near that is the seed-syllable of Brahmā (*brahmabīja*), which is the seed-syllable of Kāma, *klīṃ*. Thus, the *kāmarājakūṭa* is: *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ klīṃ*. He now states the *śaktikūṭa*:
"As before" means that by this, *sa ka la hrīm* is established as the *śaktikūṭa*. This mantra is demonstrated by the drawing of lines;
as before, the *śaktibīja* is [the Śākta Lopāmudrā as accepted in the Western Tradition].
Now listen as I speak of the Śākta [system]. || 21 ||
(Therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
Śakti, Maheśa, Kāma, and the seed-syllable of Śakra, O Supreme Goddess. (In the Kāmarāja-śakti-kūṭa:)
As before, the two phonemes known as Kāma and Śakti are of the nature of being unfastened (niṣkīlita). || 22 ||
(The division of Śāktakāmarāja:
the Vāgbhava-kūṭa and the Kāmarāja-kūṭa.
The peak of power is *sa* and *ha*.
He indeed is he.
Ka ka ka
la la ha
Hrīṃ hrīṃ la.
Hrīṃ Klīṃ 21–22. He states the Śākta Lopāmudrā with the words "Listen to the Śākta," etc.; this also is as before.

It consists of three peaks (*kūṭa*). Therein, he first defines the *vāgbhava* peak with the words beginning "Śakti" and so forth: *Śakti* is the letter *sa*; *Maheśa* is the letter *ha*; *Kāma* is the letter *ka*; the seed-syllable of Śakra (*śakrabīja*) is the letter *la*; and *Pareśvarī* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *sa ha ka la hrīṃ* is the *vāgbhava* peak. He then defines the second, the *kāmarāja* peak, and the third, the *śakti* peak:

By the phrase "as before," etc., the meaning is that the *kāmarāja-kūṭa* and the *śakti-kūṭa* consist of the forms *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* and *sa ka la hrīṃ*, respectively. However, in the *Āgamatattvavilāsa*, the *kāmarāja-kūṭa* is shown as *ha sa ka la hrīṃ*. (p.
34) Based on this, the determination of the *āgama* [is established].
Thus is the Śākta Mahāvidyā conjoined with the Western Tradition.
(This is the determination of the presiding deities of these three syllables.
Vāgīśvarī, the power of knowledge, bestows liberation within the Vāgbhava [syllable]. || 23 ||
In Kāmarāja, she is Kāmakalā, who awakens the Great Principle;
in Śaktibīja, she is Mahāmāyā, whose very nature is the union of Śiva and Śakti.
Thus is that three-syllabled vidyā, Mahātripurasundarī.
(Another method: Listen also to the supreme power within the Vāmakeśī Vidyā;
when it resides in the seed-syllable of the Bhaga, there is nothing superior to this in the three worlds. (26)
The other [powers], beginning with Prakāśā, are certainly Māyā by virtue of their state of union;
that alone is designated as the letter E (ekāra), and no other is called Ekāra.
From the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) down to the shell of the universe, the world exists even today. || 27 ||
(The Śākta Kāmarāja-vidyā, wherein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
This is Bhaga; then Māyā, Brahmā, Śakra, and the beloved of Hara.
(The Kāmarāja-kūṭa.)
Śiva, Śakti, Vidhi, Śūnya, Vajradhṛk, and Parameśvarī. || 28 ||
(Śaktikūṭa:
Hādyam, Mādana, and Śakra, followed by Mahāmāyā;
(its threefold division).
Then the practitioner should impart the seed-syllable of Brahmā at the end of the three peaks.
23–25 | "Joined with the Western Tradition" means it is propounded within the Western Tradition.

He describes the presiding deities of these three *kūṭas* by way of defining their fruits, beginning with the words "Vāgīśvarī" and so forth. "The three-syllabled one" means the one consisting of three *kūṭas*.
28–30 | Again, he states the internal *vidyā* of Śaktikāmarāja with the words beginning "etad" and so forth. *Bhaga* is the letter *e*; *māyā* is the letter *ī*;

*brahmā* is the letter *ka*; *śakra* is the letter *la*; and *harapriyā* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *e ī ka la hrīṃ* constitutes the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. He clearly explains its status as the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* in the *Śrīkrama*, as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
The first is the Vidyā Sundarī; the second is Brahmasundarī.
Within the Śaktikūṭa, Mahāmāyā is considered to be Anantasundarī.
Then, from that [syllable], one takes the portion *bhagaṃ*, followed by *māyā* (the letter *ī*), *brahmā* (the letter *a*), *śakra* (the letter *a*), and *hara* (the letter *ha*).
This is joined with the left eye (the letter *u*) and adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*.
This is declared to be the origin of speech (*vāgabhava*), possessing the power of desire (*kāmaśaktika*) as before. Thus it is said.

He states the *kāmarāja-kūṭa* with the words beginning "Śiva," and so forth. Śiva is the letter *ha*; Śakti is the letter *sa*; Vidhi is the letter *ka*; Śūnya is the letter *ha*; Vajradhṛk is the letter *la*; and Parameśvarī is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* is the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*. He states the *śakti-kūṭa* with the words "the first of *ha*," and so forth. "The first of *ha*" (*hādya*) is the letter *sa*; Mādana is...

The letter *ka*, *śakra* (the letter *śa*), and *mahāmāyā* (*hrīṃ*). Thus, *ka-la-hrīṃ* is the Śakti-kūṭa. Regarding the term "Brahma-bīja": according to the reading "at the end of the three kūṭas," it means that one should place the Brahma-bīja—the Praṇava—at the end of the three kūṭas, namely the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti-kūṭas which constitute the aforementioned mantra. [Thus: *e ī ka la hrīṃ oṃ*. *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*.

Oṃ. Thus, the nature of the mantra is established as *sa ka la hrīṃ oṃ*. However, in the *Pādaṭīkā* on manuscript B, the reading *trikūṭeṣu* is observed where [the text] says *trikūṭānte*; furthermore, in the *Tantrasāra*, there is the statement: "O Supreme Goddess, when one should give the seed-syllable of Brahmā (*brahmabīja*) at the end of the three peaks (*trikūṭe*)," which indicates that there is no fixed rule regarding the mantra ending with the *praṇava* (Oṃ). In the *Āgamatattvavilāsa*, it is stated: "The seed-syllable of Brahmā is the *praṇava* (*oṃ*). It...

If [the syllable] is at the beginning of the first *kūṭa*, she is Sundarī; if at the beginning of the second *kūṭa*, she is Brahmasundarī; and if at the beginning of the third *kūṭa*, she is Anantasundarī.

This is because the status of being preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) is specifically established through such statements, and because the sequence for extracting the mantra consisting of three *kūṭas* preceded by the *praṇava* is observed in the *Pāda-ṭīkā* on manuscript B; thus, in the phrase "at the end of the three *kūṭas*," the locative plural *trikūṭeṣu* is intended.
The reading appears correct. He states this triad of vidyās concerning this mantra, beginning with "the first is the Sundarī vidyā," and so forth.

Here, this should be noted: as for the application of the *praṇava* (syllable Om) to the three peaks (*trikūṭa*) mentioned in the preceding statement, that applies specifically to the different vidyās such as Sundarī and others, but not universally. For instance, in the previously mentioned fifteen-syllable mantra consisting of three peaks:

By joining the *praṇava* (Oṃ) to the first *kūṭa* alone, the *Sundarī-vidyā* arises. By joining the *praṇava* to the second *kūṭa*, excluding the first and third *kūṭas*, the *Brahma-sundarī* arises; by joining it to the third *kūṭa*, excluding the first and second, the *Ananta-sundarī* arises. Thus, through the addition of a single *praṇava* to each [part] of the fifteen-syllable mantra, its sixteen-syllable nature is established. It is precisely with this intention that—
It has been stated that "this is indeed the sixteen-fold Vidyā," and so forth. These three mantras are clearly demonstrated by means of a line-diagram for the sake of easy understanding:
(The Eighteen-Syllable Sundarī [the Sixteen-fold]).
The Vāgbhava-kūṭa, the Kāmarāja-kūṭa, and the Śakti-kūṭa.
Oṃ ha sa.
And that is it.
Kalaka (The Black One)
ha hrīṃ la
la hrīṃ hrīṃ
This sixteenth Vidyā has been shown according to its various manifestations. (Its excellence: This Vidyā is to be known as supreme, secret, and devoid of the form of withdrawal. || 31 ||
(Another mantra:
This is Śrī, conjoined with the vital breaths, the destroyer of suffering and poverty. || 32 ||
(Another mantra) Now I shall declare that Vidyā which is captivating through the King of Desire.
(The Vāgbhava peak-syllable)
The seed-syllable of Śiva, Śakti, Soma, Mādana, and Purandara. || 33 ||
(Brahmasundarī Ṣoḍaśī) is the peak-syllable of Vāgbhava and the peak-syllable of Kāmarāja.
The peak of power:
E Oṃ.
He indeed said:
"Ka."
Ka-sa-la (Kashmir)
la ka hrīṃ
Hrīṃ Ha La
Hrīṃ (Anantasundarī [Ṣoḍaśī]) is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
The peak-syllable of desire-passion and the peak-syllable of power.
Ha Oṃ Sa.
He is Ka-Ka.
Kalaha (Quarrel)
la hrīṃ la
hrīṃ hrīṃ (the Vidyā of Kāmarāja)
The Vāgbhava peak, the Kāmarāja peak, and the Śakti peak.
And he is that.
He is Ka-Ka.
Kala kala!
ha hrīṃ hrīṃ
la haṃ hrīṃ

He is [number] 32. He states another mantra with the words "this" (eṣā) and so forth. The meaning is that this previously mentioned Śrī Sundarī Vidyā is conjoined with the *prāṇa* seed-syllable, namely *haṃsaḥ*. Although no specific detail is mentioned here, it should be understood that the conjunction with the *haṃsa* seed-syllable occurs at the end of the *śakti-kūṭa*.

"Within the end of the three peaks (*trikūṭa*) is the seed-syllable *haṃsa*, adorned with the *bindu* and the *sarga* [visarga]," according to the observation of the statement from the *Tantrasāra*. "Within the end of the three peaks" means at the end of the third peak. (33–34) He states another form of Śāktalopāmudrā with the passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and ending with "the Great Knowledge" (*mahāvidyā*). Kāma—
In Mahāmāyā (the peak-syllable of Kāmarāja-śakti),
one should extract Kāma and Śakti as before.
Thus is this Great Vidyā (now the nine-syllabled one); listen now to another as well.
(Therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
O Bhuvaneśī, Śiva and Śakti are the supreme Vāgbhava seed-syllable.
(The Kāmarāja-kūṭa:)
Then, beyond that, [he saw] the king of birds, five-faced Mahāmāyā.

"Rājamanoharām" means that which captivates the mind of Kāmarāja, the Lord of Desire (Kāmeśvara). Regarding "Śiva": Śiva's seed-syllable is *ha*; Śakti is *sa*; Soma is *sa*; Mādana is *ka*; Purandara is *la*; and Mahāmāyā is *hrīṃ*.
Thus, *ha sa sa ka la hrīṃ* constitutes the Vāgbhava-peak (kūṭa). He states the other two peaks with the word "Kāma": [the syllables] *kāma-śaktī*.

The meaning is: the peak-syllable of Kāmarāja and the peak-syllable of Śakti. "As before" means as in the case of the Kāmarāja-vidyā. Furthermore, in the *Tantrasāra*, after stating "then again, the Śākta-Lopāmudrā," it says: "The seed-syllable of Śiva, the moon of Śakti, and Mādana [the letter 'ma'], together with Purandara [the letter 'la'], joined with the void [the letter 'ha'] and fire [the letter 'ra'], and the fourth vowel with the bindu."
As before, one should extract the King of Desire (Kāmarāja) together with the peak-syllable of Śakti.
By this, the production of the remaining two *kūṭas* from the second and third *kūṭas* of the *Kāmarāja-vidyā* itself has been stated.
This mantra is shown by the drawing of lines as follows:
(Śāktalopāmudrā).
The Vāgbhava-kūṭa, the Kāmarāja-kūṭa, and the Śakti-kūṭa.
Ha ha sa.
He is he.
That is *kala*.
Ka ha hrīṃ
la la hrīṃ

Hrīṃ 35–36. Now, while explaining the nine-syllabled Vidyā, he first states the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*): "Śiva" and so forth. Śiva is the letter *ha*; Śakti is the letter *sa*; Bhuvaneśī is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha sa hrīṃ* is the *vāgbhava*.
(Śaktikūṭa) Brahmā, Śiva, and Mahāmāyā are proclaimed as the nine syllables.
(Its conformity with the Eastern Tradition:)
This goddess is the power of Rudra; she is indeed the leader of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya).
(Declaration of the exposition of the Lopāmudrā-vidyā according to the Southern, Northern, and Middle traditions:
Now, however, I shall proclaim the Southern, Northern, and Middle [traditions]. 37.
(Therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
Mādana, Pañcavaktra, Lohitā, Rudrayoginī, Purandara, and Mahāmāyā constitute the supreme seed-syllable Vāgbhava. 38.
(In the *kāmarāja-śakti-kūṭa*):
As before, the supreme practitioner should know that which is called *kāma-śakti* is the *kūṭa*.
He states the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*: "The king of the twice-born" (*dvija-rāja*) is the letter *sa*; "five-faced" (*pañca-vaktra*) is the letter *ha*; and "great illusion" (*mahāmāyā*) is [the letter *ī*].

Hrīṃ. Thus, "sa ha hrīṃ" is the Kāmarāja-kuṭa. He states the Śakti-kuṭa: "Brahmā. Brahmā is the letter *ka*, Śiva is the letter *ha*, and Mahāmāyā is *hrīṃ*. Thus, "ka ha hrīṃ" is the Śakti-kuṭa. Śiva, Śakti, Bhuvaneśī, and the Vāgbhava seed-syllable are supreme.
O Goddess of the Gods, Kāma, Vyoma, and Mahāmāyā—beyond that [is the ninth]; Kāma, Vyoma, and Mahāmāyā are proclaimed as the nine syllables.

According to the statement cited in the *Tantrasāra*, however, the specific distinction is seen as the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja, namely *ka ha hrīṃ*, and the *kūṭa* of Śakti. This mantra is demonstrated by the following layout of lines:
(the nine-syllabled Rudra-Śakti).
The Vāgbhava peak, the Kāmarāja peak, and the Śakti peak.
Ha sa ka
He laughed.
hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ

37–39 | Having thus expounded the Vidyā according to the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), he now pledges to expound it sequentially in accordance with the Southern, Northern, and Central Traditions, beginning with the words "Now, however" (*idānīṃ tu*). Therein,
first expounding the Tripurā Vidyā according to the Southern Tradition, he first—
He states the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* with the words beginning "mādanam" and so forth: "This *mādana* is designated as *śāmbhava* (the *śākta lopāmudrā*)."
And now I shall describe that which pertains to Śakti.
(Therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
Bhṛgvīśa, Gaganam, Hāntam, Kāla, Indra, and Maheśvara;
enriched with the left eye, fire, and the moon—this is the supreme Vāgbhava-kūṭa. (40)
(In the *Kāmarāja-śakti-kūṭa*):
One should extract the *kāmarāja* and the *śakti-kūṭa* as before.
(Its conformity with the Southern Tradition.)
The right one, the slayer of Dakṣa, the liberator from all suffering. || 41 ||

The letter *ka* [is one face], the letter *ha* has five faces, the letter *kṣa* is red, the letter *ma* is Rudrayoginī, the letter *la* is Purandara, and *hrīṃ* is Mahāmāyā. Thus, *ka ha kṣa ma la hrīṃ* is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa. "As before" means that its two kūṭas called Kāmaśakti—the Kāmarāja-kūṭa and the Śakti-kūṭa—are like the Kāmarāja-vidyā; by that, [the sequence is] *ha sa ka*.
*Ha-la-hrīṃ* is the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*; *sa-ka-la-hrīṃ* is the *śakti-kūṭa*. By the drawing of the lines, this *vāgbhava-kūṭa* and *kāmarāja-kūṭa* are clearly demonstrated.
The peak-syllable of power is *ka-ha*.
He indeed is he.
ka kṣa ka
Lama Ha (The Great Mother)
Hrīṃ La La
Hrīṃ hrīṃ 39. This is indeed called Śāmbhava-Lopāmudrā, as indicated by the statement: "This is declared to be Śāmbhava."

40–41. Explaining the Śāktalopāmudrā Trikūṭā, he first states the *vāgbhava* kūṭa with the words beginning "Bhṛgvīśa" (*bhṛgvīśam*). Bhṛgvīśa is the letter *sa*; Gaganam is the letter *ha*; Hānta is the letter *kṣa*;
Kāla is the letter *ma*; Indra is the letter *la*; Maheśvara is the letter *ha*, which is further enriched by the left eye (*va*), fire (*ra*), and the moon (*u*).
The meaning is that it is adorned with the vowel *ī*, the letter *ra*, and the lunar bindu; by this, "hrīṃ" is obtained. And thus, "sa ha kṣa ma la hrīṃ" is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
(Now follows the promise to define the Madadravā-vidyā.)
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another [mantra] that fulfills all desires:
(The Mantra of Madadravā).
One should recite the element [BHA] joined with the Bindu, and below that, the word "Klinne. (42)

The *mādana* (the letter *ka*) conjoined with *śakra* (the letter *i*), endowed with the *mūrti* (the letter *u*) and the *bindu* (the nasal dot), [is placed] in the liquid of intoxication (*madadrava*). [Then] the letter *o*, ending with the *kādi* (the consonant *k*), situated upon the moon (*candra*). 43.
After that, the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), adorned with the sixth vowel;
Indra joined with Jhiṇṭīśa; Viyat; Soma; and Graheśvara. (44)
Mahāsena follows after her; she is the southern heroine sung [in this context].
She is said to be Madadravā, who causes the playful manifestation of power (śakti). || 45 ||
It concludes thus. Having thus explained the *vāgbhava* peak (*kūṭa*), he states the arrangement of the other peaks, beginning with "the *kāmarāja*":

the meaning is that one should extract its *kāmarāja* peak and *śakti* peak as before, according to the previously described *kāmarāja-vidyā*. And so it should be understood that the *kāmarāja* peak is *ha sa ka ha la hrīm*, and the *śakti* peak is *sa ka la hrīm*. Thus, this...
The combined mantra is shown as follows:
(the Ṣoḍaśī Śāktalopāmudrā), the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
The peak-syllable of Kāmarāja and the peak-syllable of Śakti.
Ha sa ha.
That is indeed *ka-kṣa*.
Kalama
Ha Hrīṃ La
la hrīṃ hrīṃ

Regarding "the southern": the meaning is that it follows the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya). 42–45. He states another mantra with the words beginning "bhautika" and so forth. "Bhautika" refers to the vowel *ai*; and when that is joined with the *bindu*, the result is *aiḥ*. Below that—immediately after *aiḥ*—one should recite "klinne. Regarding "mādana": "mādana" refers to the letter *ka*. That...

And [the syllable] joined with *śakra* (the letter *ka*) and the letter *la*; the form (*mūrti*) is the vowel *ī*, and the dot (*bindu*) is the *anusvāra*—it is endowed with these two. By this, "klīṃ" is obtained. Then comes "madadrave. The letter *sa* situated on the moon (the letter *u*) is joined with the vowel ending in *o* (the letter *au*), with the letters beginning with *ka* (the letter *k*), and with the *visarga*. By this, "sauḥ" is obtained.
(p. 341) (Now, the promise to describe the vidyās following the Uttarāmnāya:
Now, I shall explain the Uttarāmnāya in detail. (46)
(Therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
Viṣṇu, Īśa, then the letter Ha, Kāmeśa, then Pṛthivī, then Bhuvaneśī; thereafter follows the Vāgbhava seed-syllable of Śambhu. 47.
(The arrangement of the *kūṭas* of Kāmarāja and Śakti):
One should extract the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja and the *kūṭa* of Śakti as before.
(The fruit of propitiating this mantra).
This supreme knowledge should be known as the bestower of all accomplishments. || 48 ||

"Kāmabīja" means the seed-syllable of desire, which is the letter *ka*; it is adorned with the sixth vowel, *ū*. By this, *ku* is obtained. "Indra" means the letter *la*; it is joined with the "Lord of Jhiṇṭī," which is the vowel *e*. By that, *le* is obtained. "Viyat" means the letter *ha*; "Soma" is the letter *sa*; "Graheśvara" (the Lord of Planets) is the Sun-maker, the vowel *o*; and "Mahāsena" is the visarga. By this—
"hsauḥ" is thus obtained. And so, the complete mantra is: *ai* / *klinne klīṃ madadrave sauḥ kle hsauḥ*.

Regarding "the Southern Mistress," the meaning is: the Śakti propounded in the Southern Tradition (*dakṣiṇāmnāya*). He states that the name of this Vidyā is "Madadravā" by means of the phrase "this Madadravā."

46–48 | Now, having made the formal promise (pratijñā) with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth to expound the Vidyā as set forth in the Northern Tradition (*uttarāmnāya*), he first states the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) with the words beginning "Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇu*). Viṣṇu is the letter *a*; joined with that, Īśa is the letter *ha*. This is explained in exactly the same way in the *Tantrasāra*.
The end of *ha* (*hānta*) is the letter *kṣa*; Kāmeśa is the letter *ma*. In the *Tantrasāra*: [text continues]
"Viṣṇu, Īśa, then Ha, Kāleśa, and then Pṛthivī"—

since the word *kāleśa* is seen in such statements, and since its commentary shows that *kāleśa* refers to the letter *ma*, it should be understood that in the present context, the word *kāmeśa* refers to Mahākāla and thus signifies the letter *ma*. *Pṛthivī* is the letter *la*, [and] *Bhuvaneśī*...

*Hrīṃ*. Thus, it results in *ha kṣa ma la hrīṃ*, which is the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. "The seed of Śambhu" means the *bīja* of Śambhu. The placement of the qualifier at the end (*paranipāta*) is due to the fact that the rule regarding the prior placement of words is generally applicable.
He states the arrangement of the other two *kūṭas* with the words beginning with "the Kāmarāja," etc.; "Kāmarāja" means the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja.

"As before" means as in the case of the *kāmarāja-vidyā*. This is stated in the *Tantrasāra*: "O Dear One, the *kāmarāja* and the *śakti-kūṭa* have been described as before. Thus, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* is the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, and *sa ka la hrīṃ* is the *śakti-kūṭa*. Therefore, this is the complete mantra consisting of three *kūṭas*: *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ sa ka la hrīṃ*
(The fifteen-syllable [Lopāmudrā]:
the Vāgbhava peak and the Kāmarāja peak.
The peak of power:
*ha ha*
He is the syllable *kṣa*.
Ka-ma-ka (Kāmaka)
la la ha (lalaha)
Hrīṃ hrīṃ la.
Hrīṃ (another mantra; therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa):
Māyā, Śiva, Nṛsiṃha, Kāma, Śakra, and Sureśvarī.
This Vāgbhava-kūṭa, however, is the Kāmarāja [kūṭa], established as before, along with the Śakti-kūṭa.
Likewise, the Śaktikūṭa and the Vidyā are indeed extremely difficult to obtain. || 49 ||
(Now, the promise to describe another form of the sixteen-syllable Vidyā: Now I shall proclaim the sixteen-syllable Vidyā according to its various manifestations; therein [is] the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
Brahmā, Nṛsiṃha, Kāleśa, Candra, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 50 ||

49. He states another mantra consisting of three peaks (*trikūṭa*) with the words beginning with *māyā* and ending with *paramadurlabhā*. Here, *māyā* is the power (*śakti*), the letter *sa*; *Śiva* is the letter *ha*; *Nṛsiṃha* is the letter *kṣa*; *Kāma* is the letter *ka*; *Śakra* is the letter *la*; and *Sureśvarī* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *sa ha kṣa ka la hrīṃ* is the *vāgbhava* peak. However, if the reading is *kāla*, then *kāla* is the letter *ma*, and by that [the mantra is formed].

The syllable *kṣamalahrīm* would constitute the Vāgbhava-peak; however, in that case, there would result a redundancy with the sixteen-syllable mantra previously set forth in such statements as "Bhṛgvīśa, Gaganam, Hāntam," and so on. Therefore, it should be understood that the reading *kāmaḥ* alone has been inserted into the root text. He states the arrangement of the Kāmarāja- and Vāgbhava-peaks with the words "as before."
The meaning is that it is like the previously mentioned *Kāmarāja-vidyā*. Thus, this combined mantra—the sixteen-syllable *Vāgbhava-kūṭa*—is as follows: [the mantra].
The peak-syllable of desire-passion,
the peak-syllable of power,
that.
Ha sa ha.
That is indeed the moment.
Kalaka (The Black One)
ha hrīṃ la
la hrīṃ hrīṃ
50–52 | He promises to explain another such *vidyā* as the *ṣoḍaśī*, beginning with the words "and the *ṣoḍaśī*," and so forth.

Therein, he first states the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*: "Brahmā," etc. Brahmā is the letter *ka*; Nṛsiṃha is the letter *kṣa*; Kāleśa is the letter *ma*; Candra is the letter *sa*; and Bhuvaneśvarī is *hrīṃ*. Thus, the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* is: *ka kṣa ma sa hrīṃ*.
(The Peak of Kāmarāja): Śiva, Nṛsiṃha, Kāleśa, Śakra, and after that Śiva;
then, following that, Mahāmāyā.
(Śaktikūṭa) Listen now to the Śaktikūṭa. || 51 ||
Candra, Nṛsiṃha, Kāleśa, Śakra, and Bhuvaneśvarī—
this is that supreme Vidyā (another mantra).
I shall speak further.
(Therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa: Of this [goddess], the Vāgbhava-kūṭa (and the Kāmarāja-kūṭa).
And hear now of Kāmarāja:
Maheśa, Krodha, Kāma, Kāleśa, Pṛthivī, and Hara. || 53 ||

"Śiva" means the letter *ha*; "Nṛsiṃha" is the letter *kṣa*; "Kāleśa" is the letter *ma*; "Śakra" is the letter *la*; "Śiva" is the letter *ha*; and "Mahāmāyā" is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha kṣa ma la ha hrīṃ* is the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa*.
Regarding the *Śakti-kūṭa*, he says: "Listen to the *Śakti-kūṭa*" and so forth. "Candra" means the letter *sa*; "Nṛsiṃha" [is the letter *kṣa*].

The letter *kṣa* is Kāleśa; the letter *ma* is Śakra; the letter *la* is Bhuvaneśvarī; and *hrīṃ* is [Bhuvaneśvarī]. Thus, *sa kṣa ma la hrīṃ* is the Śaktikūṭa. Now, the mantra composed of these three *kūṭas* is shown:
(the Ṣoḍaśī).
The Vāgbhava peak, the Kāmarāja peak, and the Śakti peak.
Ka-ha-sa
kṣa kṣa kṣa
ma ma ma
Sala-la!
hrīṃ ha hrīṃ

*Hrīṃ* 52–54. Now he states the seventeen-syllable [mantra] with the words beginning "parāñca" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of this": immediately following [the previous mantra is] *Mahāmāyā*. Then, after that...
(The arrangement of the Śaktikūṭa): The Śaktikūṭa is as before. (Its excellence:)
This seventeenth Vidyā bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
(Another mantra:
The *praṇava* is proclaimed as the great seed-syllable (*mahābīja*) of the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*).
(The mantra following the Lower Tradition [*adhāmnāya*]:)
The tradition has declared that the great seed-syllable of Mahāmāyā is situated below. || 55 ||
(Thus, the conformity of the mantras to the tradition:
In this very manner, the six traditions (āmnāyas) have been proclaimed. || 56 ||

The meaning is "of the preceding sixteen-syllable [mantra]. By this, it should be understood that here too, as in the previously mentioned sixteen-syllable [mantra], the *vāgbhava* peak (*kūṭa*) is indeed *ka kṣa ma sa hrīṃ*. He states the specific detail regarding the *kāmarāja* peak with the words beginning "Listen to the *kāmarāja*," and so on. *Kakāraḥ* is the letter *ka*, *śakraḥ* is the letter *la*, and *bhuvaneśvarī* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *sa ha ka la hrīṃ* constitutes the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*). The separate seed-syllables are as follows: *kāma* means the letter *ka*; *śiva* means the letter *ha*; *brahmā* means the letter *ka*; *śakra* means the letter *la*; and *bhuvaneśvarī* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ka ha ka la hrīṃ* is the *śaktikūṭa*. This mantra, which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of these three *kūṭas*, is demonstrated by the drawing of lines: [Diagram] The three *kūṭas* are: *ka ha ka la hrīṃ*, *ka ha sa ka la hrīṃ*, and *ka ha sa ka la hrīṃ*. The first is the *śaktikūṭa*; the second is the *śivakūṭa*; and the third is the *brahmakūṭa*. These three *kūṭas* together constitute the *mūlamantra*. The *rekhāpāta* (drawing of lines) is as follows: [Diagram] The *mūlamantra* is: *ka ha sa ka la hrīṃ ka ha sa ka la hrīṃ ka ha sa ka la hrīṃ*. This is the *mūlamantra* of the *Śrīvidyā*. It is composed of thirty-two syllables. It is divided into three parts: the first part is the *śaktikūṭa*, the second is the *śivakūṭa*, and the third is the *brahmakūṭa*. Each *kūṭa* consists of eight syllables. The entire *mūlamantra* is thus the union of these three *kūṭas*. The *rekhāpāta* clearly illustrates this structure. The *mūlamantra* is the essence of all mantras and the source of all powers. It is the supreme secret of the *Śrīvidyā* tradition. One who recites this *mūlamantra* with devotion attains liberation and all worldly desires. It is the very heart of the *Tripurasundarī*. Therefore, one should always recite this *mūlamantra* with great care and reverence. It is the king of all mantras. It is the destroyer of all sins. It is the bestower of all siddhis. It is the supreme means to attain the state of Śiva. Thus ends the description of the *mūlamantra* and its *rekhāpāta*. One should not reveal this secret to anyone who is not a true disciple or who lacks devotion. It is to be kept strictly confidential. Only those who have been initiated by a qualified guru may receive this *mūlamantra*. Otherwise, it leads to misfortune. Therefore, one must protect this *mūlamantra* with the utmost care. It is the life-force of the *Śrīvidyā*. Without it, there is no attainment of the supreme goal. Thus, the *mūlamantra* is established. One should meditate upon it constantly. One should worship it daily. One should offer oblations to it. One should perform *japa* of it. One should contemplate its meaning. By doing so, one quickly attains the state of the Supreme Goddess. The Twelfth Chapter: (An Investigation into Pure, Impure, and Mixed Mantras; therein, the determination of Meru; the various types of mantras propitiated by sages and deities; the *dīpanī*; and the definition of the nature of the *vāmakeśī* vidyā.)
(Declaration of the threefold classification of mantras: Mantras have pure results, impure results, or are designated as both;
they belong indeed to Subhagā. That very [classification] is now being declared. (1)
(Meru of the mantras to be spoken hereafter:
Earth, Moon, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhvamādana, the Half-moon, and the Bindu—these nine syllables are called Meru. || 2 ||
(The origin of the Mahātripurasundarī mantras from Meru): The mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from Meru. (3)
(The etymological derivation of the earth and others, and their origin from the letter *la* and Mount Meru as the cause):
From the letter *la*, the earth was born, together with its mountains, forests, and groves;
it is endowed with fifty sacred seats (*pīṭha*), consists of all holy fords (*tīrtha*), and is supreme.
1. Regarding Subhagā Lopāmudrā: "Pure" (śuddha) means those that have pure fruits, those that have impure fruits, those designated as both, and those that have both pure and impure fruits. 2.
Now, wishing to demonstrate the origin of the mantras of Mahātripurasundarī from the letters which constitute its Meru, [the author says:]...

First, he indicates the colors of Meru with the words beginning "the earth," and so forth. "The earth" is the seed-syllable of the earth, the letter *la*; "moon" is the letter *sa*; "Śiva" is the letter *ha*; "māyā" is the letter *ī*; "śakti" is the letter *e*; "the black path" (kṛṣṇādhvā) is fire, the letter *ra*; "mādana" is the letter *ka*; the half-moon and the bindu are well known. "Nine syllables" (*navārṇa*) means that which possesses nine syllables, such as *la* and the others.
The meaning is "Meru.
With the words beginning with "mahā," he explains how the mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from the etymological Meru:
"born from Meru" means produced from the phonemes of the etymological Meru.
4. Now, with the words beginning with "from the letter *la*," he explains the arising of the earth and other elements from the letters that constitute Meru.
Thus, because it is the seed of the earth, the letter *la* is designated as the "seed of the earth" (*pṛthvībīja*). The same applies elsewhere.
From the letter *sa*, [arises] the nature of the moon, the stars, the planets, and the gods.
Through the conjunction with the letter *a* and the syllable *chi*, she is established in the sphere of space (*vyomamaṇḍala*).
From the vowel *ī* arises this supreme Māyā, which possesses an agent and consists of the fourth state (*turyātmikā*);
from the vowel *e* arises the Vaiṣṇavī energy, intent upon the protection of the universe.
From the letter *ra*, she is endowed with splendor and is the nature of supreme light;
from the letter *ka*, she is the granter of desires, possessing a form at will, radiant and imperishable.
In the form of the half-moon, she is proclaimed as the source of the universe;
through the *bindu* in the form of Śiva, she is the witness in the form of the void.
Together with this [energy], whose nature is the immutability of pervasion everywhere,
such a form— the form of Brahman— is produced by means of this Meru.
Tripurā is now described by means of these nine syllables.

8–9 | He describes the essential nature of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the point (*bindu*) with the verse beginning "half-moon," etc. By means of the half-moon, which is of the nature of *nāda*, Śakti is the source of the universe; that is to say, she is the cause of the universe. Since it has been stated that creation proceeds from *nāda* alone, the meaning is that *nāda* is the cause with respect to creation. Regarding "by the point": by means of the point, which is of the nature of the void (*śūnya*), of the essence of the void, and of the form of Śiva.
"Witness" means having the nature of a witness. "By this" means by this Viśvayoni (the source of the universe), the Self, the Bindu, which is Śiva;

"immovability of pervasion" means the immovability of the inseparable concomitance of pervasion. The meaning is that wherever Śakti exists in the form of the Half-moon (*ardhacandra*), there Śiva exists in the form of the Bindu. By this, the non-difference of Śiva and Śakti follows as a matter of course.

10. "By these" means by those previously mentioned. "By the nine-syllabled letters" means by such letters as consist of nine *arṇas* (syllables)—that is, by the letters that constitute the mantra, beginning with the letter *la* as previously described. Tripurā is thus described.
By the word "now," it is indicated that the Kāmarāja-vidyā—which is about to be explained as the source of other mantras—is indeed composed of the aforementioned letters.

By that which was stated previously—namely, "sa ha kṣa ma la hrīm" and so forth—it is indicated that in the case of the sixteen-syllable mantra (*ṣoḍaśī*) and similar instances, there is no fault even if the mantra is composed of letters other than these [specific ones]. (p.
351) (Worshipped by Manu).
One should extract the seed-syllable of the Earth from the Kāma and Ākāśa [syllables], which are the Śakti and Turya [syllables].
Having written this Vāgbhava, one should extract all the vidyās. || 11 ||
The younger brother of Madana is called Kāma, while the elder brother of Madana is said to be Śiva; setting aside the younger brother Śiva, this supreme knowledge is honored by Manu.
(That which was propitiated by Candra): Kāma, together with his younger brother [Aniruddha], [is to be worshipped] in speech; Śiva, excluding Kāma’s younger brother [Aniruddha].
From this point forward in this *Prakāśa*, the *vidyās* propitiated by those various deities and sages are to be explained.

In this context, while explaining the *trikūṭā* vidyā worshipped by Manu, he first states the *vāgbhava* kūṭa: "Kāma," etc. "Kāma" is the letter *ka*; "ākāśa" is the letter *ha*; "śakti" is the letter *e*; "turya" is the fourth vowel, the letter *ī*; "bhūḥ" is the letter *la*; and "māyābīja" is *hrīṃ*. The meaning is that one should extract these [letters]. And thus, *ka*...

"Ha-e-ī-la-hrīm" is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa. Regarding the statement "one should extract all the vidyās," by this it should be understood that its nature as a *meru* (central axis) exists within the mantras to be described hereafter. He states the Kāmarāja-kūṭa with the word "madana": in the *kāma*, that is, in the Kāmarāja-kūṭa, "madanānujahaḥ" refers to the letter *ha* situated below the letter *ka*—which is the younger brother (*anuja*) of *madana* (the letter *ma*), the first constituent of that kūṭa—which itself resides within the previously mentioned Vāgbhava-kūṭa.

The letter *ha* is the elder brother of *mada*; the meaning is that it should be the elder brother of *mada*. By the words beginning with *śakti*: *ka* is the letter *ka*; *śakti* is the letter *e*; the pair of fires (*vahni-yugala*) is the two letters *ra*; the earth (*bhūḥ*) is the letter *la*; fire is the letter *ra*; and Bhuvaneśvarī is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ka e ra ra la ra hrīṃ* is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.

Then there is the letter *ha*, the letter *la*, and *māyā* (*hrīṃ*). Thus, *ha ka la ra ha la hrīṃ* is the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja. He states the *kūṭa* of Śakti with the words beginning with "sara-ka": *sa-ra-ka-kṣmāgni-maṇḍitā*. This is an epithet of *māyā*. It consists of the letters *sa*, *ra*, and *ka*; then *kṣmā* is the letter *la*, and *agni* is the letter *ra*. *Māyā* (*hrīṃ*) is adorned by these. Thus, it is *sa-ra-ka-la*.
*Ra hrīṃ* is the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of Śakti. This mantra is demonstrated by the drawing of lines as follows:
(Candrārādhitā) KA-Śakti, BAINDAVĪ, VAHNI, KṢMĀ, MĀYĀ, HAKALĀ, LARAU.
This Māyā, honored by Soma, is the illusory power of Sahaka, Śakra, and Agni. || 47 ||
(Īśānārādhitā) consists of Kāma and Ākāśa; Kṣamā, Māyā, Śiva, Kāma, Ha, Bhu, and Bhuvā;
then Māyā and Kāma in the Śaktikūṭa; [this is] Sakalā Bhuvaneśvarī.
This Vidyā, propitiated by Īśāna, fulfills all desires.

47. Now, he explains the [mantra] propitiated by Candra with the words beginning with "Ka-śakti": therein, by the phrase *ka-śakti-baindavī-vahni-kṣmā-māyā*, the *vāgbhava* peak (*kūṭa*) is shown. *Kaḥ* is the letter *ka*; *śakti* is the letter *e*; *baindavī* is *māyā*, the letter *ī*; *vahni* is the letter *ra*; *kṣmā* is the seed-syllable of the earth, the letter *la*; and *māyā* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, it is *ka-e-ī-ra-la-hrīṃ*.

The *vāgbhava* peak (*kūṭa*). Regarding the *kāmarāja* peak, he says: "Ha-ka-la, la-rau, māyā. This means: the letter *ha*, the letter *ka*, the letter *la*; again the letter *la*, the letter *ra*, and *māyā* (*hrīṃ*). Thus, *ha ka la la ra hrīṃ* is the *kāmarāja* peak.
Regarding the *śakti* peak, he says with the words beginning with "sa-ha-ka," etc.: the letter *sa*, the letter *ha*, the letter *ka*; *śakra* is the letter *la*, and *agni* is the letter *ra*.
*Māyā* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *sa ha ka la ra hrīṃ* is the *Śaktikūṭa*. This mantra is presented according to its division into *kūṭas*:
*(Candrārādhitā)*.
The Vāgbhava-kūṭa, the Kāmarāja-kūṭa, and the Śakti-kūṭa.

Hrīṃ Hrīṃ 48. Now, declaring the Vidyā propitiated by Īśāna, he first states the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
By the words "Kāma, Ākāśa," and so forth: *kāma* is the letter *ka*, *ākāśa* is the letter *ha*, *kṣmā* is the letter *la*, and *māyā* is *hrīṃ*.
Thus, *ka ha la hrīṃ* constitutes the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*). He states the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable with the words "Śiva," and so forth;
[the phrase] "Śiva-kāma-ha-bhū-bhuvaḥ" is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).
(Ratipūjitā):
At the end of the pair [of the Kāmarāja-vidyā], Jīva, Kṣmā, and Madana constitute the supreme [Vidyā] worshipped by Rati.
This Vidyā, propitiated by Rati, accomplishes all desires and goals. (49)
(Adored by Nārāyaṇa, she consists of six peaks.
One should write that [Vidyā] in reverse order at the end of the Vidyā presided over by Kāma.
This supreme goddess consists of six peaks and is adored by Nārāyaṇa. (50)

The third [syllable] is *māyā* together with that; this is the connection. In the *kāma* [kūṭa], *śiva* is the letter *ha*, *kāma* is the letter *ka*, *haḥ* is the letter *ha*, *bhūḥ* is the letter *la*, and after that again *bhūḥ* is the letter *la*; together with that, *māyā* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha ka ha la la hrīṃ* is the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*. He states the *śakti-kūṭa* with the words beginning "in the *śakti*" (*śakti-ityādinā*). In the *śakti-kūṭa*, *sa-ka-lāḥ* are the letter *sa*, the letter *ka*, and...
The letter *la*, followed by *bhuvaneśvarī*. Thus, *sa ka la hrīṃ* is the Śaktikūṭa. Its configuration is demonstrated by the drawing of lines—(worshipped by Īśāna).
The Vāgbhava peak, the Kāmarāja peak, and the Śakti peak.

La Hrīṃ 49. Now, while declaring the Vidyā propitiated by Rati, it is indeed the previously mentioned Kāmarāja-vidyā.

Because two additional syllables are joined to the *vāgbhava* peak (*kūṭa*) of that [mantra], it becomes the Vidyā propitiated by Rati; this very point he states with the words beginning "of Kāmarāja. By joining these—namely, the "life-force" (the letter *sa*), "earth" (the letter *la*), "Madana" (the letter *ka*), and "Parā" (*hrīṃ*)—to the end of the pair at the conclusion of the long *īkāra* within the *vāgbhava* peak of the Kāmarāja Vidyā, one obtains the Vidyā propitiated by Rati.
This is the realized meaning. This mantra is shown by the drawing of lines:
(worshipped by Rati), the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.

50. He speaks of the lore (*vidyā*) propitiated by Nārāyaṇa, beginning with "Kāma... This refers to the lore presided over by Kāma, which was taught in the tenth chapter starting with "Now I shall proclaim the lore served by Kāmadeva," and is [also] known as the Śāmbhava [lore] worshipped by Brahmā. (p. 371) (Brahmapūjitā)
In the *vāgbhava* [syllable], there is *kāma* (kām) at the beginning; in *kāma*, there is *ha-ha-kṣ-mā-parā*.
In *śakti*, there is the *vāk-kūṭa* of Agastya. This is the Vidyā worshipped by Brahmā. || 51 ||
At the end of the Kāmarāja-vidyā consisting of three peaks (trikūṭā), one should write that same Kāmarāja-vidyā in reverse order.

Having thus written the Kāmarāja-vidyā, one should again write at the beginning the Śakti-peak of the Kāmarāja, then the Kāmarāja-peak, and finally, at the very end, the Vāgbhava-peak. By this, following the previously mentioned Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja [mantra], after the three peaks, [it is written] in reverse order.
The essential meaning is that by joining those three peaks, this vidyā, worshipped by Nārāyaṇa, becomes six-peaked.
This mantra is shown through the drawing of lines as follows:

51. Now, he describes the Vidyā worshipped by Brahmā with the words beginning "the first of Kāma," and so forth. In the *Vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), "the first of Kāma" means the *Vāgbhava* peak-syllable which is the first of the *Akīlita-Kāmarāja* as taught in the eleventh chapter with the words "the syllable *bhaga* with the left eye," and so on. By this, it is concluded that the *Vāgbhava* peak-syllable is *ī e ka la hrīṃ*.

He explains the *kāmarāja-kūṭa* with the words beginning with "kāma": in the *kāma*, that is, in the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, there is the letter *ha*, the letter *ka*, again the letter *ha*, *kṣmā* which is the letter *la*, and *parā* which is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha ka ha la hrīṃ* is the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*. He explains the *śakti-kūṭa* with the word "in the *śakti*": in the *śakti*, that is, in the *śakti-kūṭa*, there is the *agastyavāk-kūṭa*.
The meaning is that here the Śakti-kūṭa is indeed the Vāgbhava-kūṭa of Lopāmudrā, who was worshipped by Agastya as her second [consort].
This [Kūṭa] was propitiated by Brahmā. Its configuration is demonstrated by the drawing of lines:
(Brahmapūjitā).
The Vāgbhava peak, the Kāmarāja peak, and the Śakti peak.
Ha Ka E
Ka e ka.
Ha la la!
la hrīṃ hrīṃ
Hrīṃ (worshipped by Bṛhaspati),
the speech-born [mantra] of Agastya, and the final pair of the Brahma-vidyā in the mouth.
This great lore, worshipped by Jīva, bestows all desires. || 52 ||
(The purity, impurity, and variegated nature of the twelve previously mentioned vidyās:
Through these twelve divisions, the Supreme Goddess Mahāvidyā is to be known as variegated, pure, and impure by the most excellent practitioners. (53)
Having written down the pure vidyās, one should then write the reversed ones;
for these very same [vidyās] are indeed always distinguished by the difference between being pure and impure.
(Regarding the number of divisions beginning with the pure:
As many as there may be divisions of the pure, so many also [arise] from the sequence; likewise, the auspicious (bhadra) divisions of the variegated (śabala) pairs indeed come into being. 55.

52. Now, he describes the lore worshipped by Bṛhaspati with the words beginning "O Agastya," and so forth. Therein, he states the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) with the words "In speech" (*vāci*). Regarding "in speech"—that is, in the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable—one should employ the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable of Lopāmudrā, the second [form] worshipped by Agastya. Thus, it is established that the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable is: *ka e ī la hrīm*.
He states the arrangement of the *kāmarāja* and *śakti* *kūṭas* with the words beginning "Brahma" (*brahma*).

The meaning is that one should employ the final two [syllables] of the *vidyā* of Brahma—namely, the *vidyā* of the worship of Brahma mentioned immediately prior—as the *kāmarāja-kūṭa* and the *śakti-kūṭa* respectively in this context. This meaning is clearly demonstrated by the layout of the lines:

53. "By these" refers to those previously mentioned. They are called "variegated" (*śabala*) because they possess the nature of being pure, impure, or both. 54. He establishes that these possess the nature of being pure, impure, or both, with the words beginning "Vidyā. The meaning is: having written down the pure ones as previously described, one should write the impure ones in reverse order from what was previously described. And thus...
The meaning is that these divisions possess purity and impurity due to their being pure, impure, or variegated (*śuddhāśuddha-śabala*).
(Their essential nature and the fact that they are to be known through the teacher's instruction:
They are profound knowledge, of the nature of Brahman, and bestowers of liberation.
It must be understood through the mouth of the Guru; otherwise, one shall incur a curse. || 56 ||
(Their agreement with authoritative tantras:
This doctrine is proclaimed as that of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-tantra. || 57 ||
(Now, the Illumination and its Result):
Next, I shall explain the *dīpanī* of the illustrious Tripurasundarī, specifically for the purpose of purifying defects such as being dormant (*supta*), locked (*kīlita*), or severed (*chinna*). 58.
(The state of being asleep and other defects as obstacles to accomplishment:
"By the first [syllable] she is asleep; by the middle one she is pinned down; by the last one she is severed. Therefore, the vidyā is not accomplished. (59)
(The Sequence for the Removal of Those Defects):
Therefore, in order to destroy those defects, I shall describe the supreme doctrine, which is exceedingly difficult to attain, according to the sequence stated in the *Śrīkramamantranirṇaya*. (60)
(The application of the illuminator in the fifth [syllable], Vāgbhava:
One should join the seed-syllables of Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā at the beginning of Vāgbhava.
(In Kāmarāja—)
The Praṇava, Lakṣmī, the Vāgbīja, Manmatha, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 61 ||
Having thus recited [the mantra], the knower of mantras should utter that which ends with the one called Vāgbhava;
[specifically] in the *Svapnāvatī*,
he should utter the Praṇava, the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, and Ramā-Manmatha-Māyā.

61–64 | First, demonstrating the *dīpanī* (illuminator) of the fifth [vowel] which has been previously attained, he states one sequence beginning with the words "Speech" (*vāk*) and so forth. The fifth [vowel], consisting of five *kūṭas*, has already been specifically demonstrated.
Of that [fifth vowel], being composed of a great *kūṭa* (*mahākūṭa*), one should recite it while concentrated in meditation, together with *Svapnāvatī*.
In Madhumatī, one should worship Manmatha, Adhara, Kāma, and Ramā, the sovereign lady of the world. || 63 ||
Then, having recited the Madhumatī [mantra], one should [recite] Māyā (Śrīṃ) and the seed-syllable of Varma (Hūṃ) within the Śaktikūṭa.
Having uttered this seed-syllable, which begins with the syllables *phaṭ* and *praṇava* (oṃ) and is encapsulated by Śiva and Śakti, one should then recite the *śaktikūṭa*.

First, he describes the ritual application concerning the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) with the words beginning "Speech, Māyā," etc. At the beginning of the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable, one should join the three seed-syllables: Speech (*vāk*), which is the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable *aiṃ*; *Māyā*, which is the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*; and *Kamalā*, which is the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*. The resultant meaning is that having uttered these—*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*—one should recite the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable. He now states the arrangement for the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable:

Regarding the passage beginning with "the *praṇava*," etc.: the *praṇava* is *oṃ*; the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is *śrīṃ*; the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbīja*) is *ai*; Manmatha is *klī*; and Bhuvaneśvarī is *hrīṃ*.
Thus, having uttered *oṃ śrīṃ ai klīṃ hrīṃ*, the meaning is that one should recite the *kūṭa* (syllabic cluster) of Kāmarāja ending with the so-called Vāgbhava.
Next, he explains the arrangement of the third *kūṭa*, named Svapnāvatī, with the passage beginning with "the *praṇava*," etc.; thus: *oṃ ai śrī klī*.
The meaning is that having uttered *hrīṃ*, one should utter the fourth peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) known as Svapnāvatī.

Next, he explains the arrangement of the fourth peak-syllable called Madhumatī with the words beginning "Manmatha" and so forth. Thus, having uttered *klīṃ aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*, one should utter the peak-syllable Madhumatī. Then, he explains the arrangement of the Śakti peak-syllable with the words beginning "Māyā" and so forth.

*Māyā* is *hrīṃ*, then *śrīṃ*, then the armor-seed *hūṃ*, then the syllable *phaṭ*. Regarding the term "with the *praṇava*": it means one should join that mantra, preceded by the *praṇava*, with the seed-syllables *haṃ* and *saṃ* at its beginning and end—enclosed within *Śiva* and *Śakti*, meaning enclosed by the letters *ha* and *sa* of *Śiva* and *Śakti*. This should be applied before the *Śakti-kūṭa*. [The letter] *ha* is the word for *Śiva*.

Even though [the seed-syllable] indicates only the letter *sa*, in this context the letters *ha* and *sa* must be understood as being joined with the *bindu* and *visarga*. This is because it is seen in the *Tantrasāra*:
"O Goddess, that which begins with the *praṇava* is enclosed within the *bīja* of the *haṃsa*. Therefore, the practical application is as follows:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ* (this is the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*).
Oṃ śrīṃ ai/ klī/ hrīṃ ha sa ka la hrīṃ (this is the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable);
Oṃ ai/ śrīṃ klīṃ hrī/ ha ka ha la hrīṃ (this is the *svapnāvatī* peak-syllable). (Her nature as the vital breath and her bestowal of spiritual accomplishments.)
This illuminating vidyā, which is the ajapā in the form of vital breath, is the supreme fifth vidyā; it then becomes the bestower of siddhi.
(Another Method [of Prāṇa]): Now, there is another method regarding prāṇa which is extremely difficult to attain. 66.
(Regarding the application of seed-syllables at the beginning of the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
One should apply the seed-syllables Ramā, Māyā, and Haṃsa at the beginning of the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.
(Regarding the application of seed-syllables at the end of the Śakti-kūṭa:)
And at the end of the Śakti-kūṭa, there is also Haṃsa, Māyā, and Ramā. || 67 ||
(The meditation on the seed-syllable in the three middle peaks; therein, in the [first] Kāmarāja):
In the triad of Kāmarājas, the Kāma-bīja has a radiance equal to the sun;
it stands in the center of a throbbing triangle, enveloped by many rays of light. (68)
*klīṃ aiḥ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīḥ ka ha ya la hrīṃ* (this is the *madhumatī-kūṭa*);
*haṃsaḥ oṃ hrīṃ śrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ haṃ saḥ ha ka la sa hrīḥ* (this is the *śakti-kūṭa*).

Thus is the application of the illuminator (*dīpanī*) for the first and fifth [syllables]. In this same manner, the application of the illuminator is to be performed for the other fifth syllables as well.
It is to be inferred by practitioners.

(65) "Thus" means: "The Vidyā becomes accomplished. This means that through the recitation of the mantra associated with the aforementioned *dīpanī* at the beginning and end of one's own recitation of the mantra to be practiced, the Vidyā becomes accomplished. Regarding the rules for recitation, it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
One should recite it first, and then recite it seven times in succession. Thus [it is said].

66–71 | He states the *dīpanī* (the illuminator) by another method, beginning with "atha" and so forth. "Prāṇa" means that the *dīpanī* is the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the Vidyā. In that regard, he states the application of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) prior to the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* with the words "ramā" and so forth.
The seed-syllable of Ramā is *śrīṃ*, the seed-syllable of Māyā is *hrīṃ*, and the seed-syllable of Haṃsa is *haṃsaḥ*. Thus, at the beginning of the fifth *vāgbhava-kūṭa*:
The meaning is that one should join these seeds, namely *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *haṃsa*. With the words beginning with "śakti," he states the joining of the seeds at the end of the Śakti-kūṭa.

The meaning is that at the end of the Śakti-kūṭa, one should join this triad of seeds: *haṃsaḥ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*. Having then recited the Kāmarāja [kūṭa]—which is the illuminator of the three Kāmarāja-kūṭas—[one should proceed].
Having meditated upon Lakṣmī, who is utterly pure, as the Great Goddess herself within the thousand-petaled great lotus in Svapnāvatī; 69.
Immediately after that, one should recite the second Kāmarāja mantra:
(in the Madhumatī [seat]) the great seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire. (70)
The object of meditation should be placed upon the excellent solar petal within the lotus consisting of the *kula* and *akula*;
then, by reciting the *Madhumatī*, a person shall obtain every desire.
(The nature of this as the vital breath:
This vital breath is a great secret, hidden within the extensive knot. (72)

By the phrase "the three Kāmarājas," and so forth: here, as before, one should not employ the conjunction of seed-syllables (*bīja-yoga*), but rather perform the meditation on each respective seed-syllable alone;

thus he states that sequence: "the three Kāmarājas. The meaning is that one should meditate upon the Kāma-seed, *klīm*, which resides in the center of the triangle—that is, situated within the triangle at the pericarp of the Mūlādhāra lotus, enveloped by many rays and possessing a radiance equal to the sun—and then utter the Kāmarāja.

The state of the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) within the aforementioned triangle has been explained by us in detail right here, in the commentary on the sixth verse beginning with "In the region of the mouth called Vajra," in the sixth chapter. Thereafter, he states what is to be done, beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*).

Having meditated upon the Great Goddess Lakṣmī herself as the syllable *Śrīṃ*, the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, within the thousand-petaled great lotus (*sahasrāra-mahāpadma*), [one should contemplate] the second...

The meaning is that one should utter the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable (*svapnāvatī-kūṭa*). Then, having meditated upon the great seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī, *hrīṃ*, which possesses a radiance equal to blazing fire within the twelve-spoked lotus consisting of *kula* and *akula*, one should utter the *madhumatī-kūṭa*.
To the question, "What happens when this is done? he says: "All... Thus, when the *dīpanī* has been performed according to this sequence...
The meaning is that practitioners attain the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus, this is the summarized sense: first *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *haṃsaḥ*; then the five peaks (*pañcakūṭa*) of the fifth [vowel];
then *haṃsaḥ*, *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*; then, having visualized the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, radiant as the sun, within the triangle at the *mūlādhāra*.

The *kāmarājakūṭa*; then, having visualized the white seed-syllable *śrīṃ* in the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*), one should recite the *svapnāvatīkūṭa*; then, having visualized the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* in the heart-lotus, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire, one should recite the *madhumatīkūṭa*.
Thus [it is said]. (72) He states its secret nature with the words beginning "atha hi" and so forth.
(p. 377) (Another Method) Now I shall explain another supreme method that is difficult to obtain.
(The sequence therein is as follows:)
And likewise with Māyā-Śrī-Madana and also with Śrī-Māyā-Madana. || 73 ||
Śrī with Madanas and Māyā, Śrī with Madana and Māyā, and Śrī with Māyā and Madanas—this is declared to be the Tripañcikā. 74.
(Its Praise:
There exists no other knowledge equal to this in the three worlds;
this knowledge within the Mahātantra of Bhairavī is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (75)
Bestowing success, stainless, peaceful, and bringing the three worlds under control, one should indeed recite the "Five-Fifth" mantra after having offered it into the five peaks and so forth. 76.

73–74 | He states another method with the words beginning "atha" (now). Here, while explaining the sequence of the application of seed-syllables (*bīja*), he first describes the procedure for joining the seed-syllables within the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) with the words beginning "māyā. Thus, having uttered "hrīṃ śrīṃ klīm," one should utter the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable. And by the phrase "śrī-māyā-madanaiḥ" (with Śrī, Māyā, and Madana), meaning "śrīṃ hrīṃ klīm," one should utter the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable.

The meaning is as follows: having uttered *madanair māyayā śrīś ca* (i.e., *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīm*), one should utter the *svapnāvatī-kūṭa*; having uttered *śrīś ca madanamāyayā* (i.e., *śrīṃ klīṃ hrīm*), one should utter the *madhumatī-kūṭa*. Having uttered *māyayā madanaiḥ śrīś ca* (i.e., *hrīṃ klīṃ śrīm*), one should utter the *śakti-kūṭa*. Regarding the term "three pentads" (*tripañcikā*), it refers to each *kūṭa*.
The meaning is that by the conjunction of three seed-syllables (*bīja*), there are fifteen seed-syllables.
Thus, the resultant meaning is as follows: first *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*, then the *vāgbhava* peak;
*śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, then the *kāmarāja* peak; *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, then the *svapnāvatī* peak; *śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ*, then...

The *madhumatī* peak is *hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ*; thereafter, one should recite the *śakti* peak. (75–76) Thus, he speaks of the excellence of the mantra when illuminated by the application of the *dīpanī*, beginning with the words "There is no other than this. Regarding the word "five":
the meaning is that one should recite the seed-syllables (*bīja*) explained according to the previously mentioned sequence at the beginning of the five peaks. "Five times the fifth" means...
This means the fifth [syllable] of the fivefold [mantra] mentioned previously. Thus ends the arrangement of the *dīpanī-yoga* for the fifth vidyā.
(The *dīpanī* of the *trikūṭa* and other vidyās:
Now I shall declare the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of all other vidyās. (77)
(Regarding the sequence therein:
The seed-syllable *haṃsa*, preceded by *vāgbhava* (*aiṃ*) and followed by *ramā* (*hrīṃ*) and *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), is very difficult to obtain.
At the end of *śakti* (*sauḥ*), however, are *haṃsa*, *mahāmāyā*, and likewise *ramā*.
Endowed with these, one should certainly perform the recitation of the vidyā. || 79 ||
(The fruit of the application of the explained seed-syllables:
By means of the *ramā* seed-syllable, she constantly bestows the happiness of dharma and liberation;
by the syllable *hrīṃ*, she eternally grants sons and provides a multitude of various riches. (80)
When recited with the *haṃsa* seed-syllable (*bīja*), she bestows various desires;
however, liberation—certainly difficult to attain—is [granted] when the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) is placed at the beginning and the end. 81.
77. Next, he states the *dīpanī* (the illuminating mantra) for the *trikūṭā* and other vidyās with the words beginning "anyāsām" (of others).
"Others" refers to the *trikūṭā*, *catuṣkūṭā*, and so forth.

78–79. Therein, he states the sequence for the application of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) with the words beginning "ramā" (ram). "Vāgbhavādi" means at the beginning of the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* and the rest.

One should employ the seed-syllable of Ramā, the seed-syllable of Māyā, and the seed-syllable of Haṃsa; that is to say, after "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ," one should utter the Vāgbhava-kūṭa. At the end of the Śakti-kūṭa, however, first the seed-syllable of Haṃsa, then the Great Māyā "Hrīṃ," and then the seed-syllable of Ramā "Śrīṃ"; the meaning is that at the end of the Śakti-kūṭa, one should utter "Haṃsaḥ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ. By this—

The essential meaning is that one should recite the mantra encapsulated by the three seed-syllables: *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *haṃsaḥ*. Regarding the definition of "encapsulation" (*saṃpuṭa*), the *Tantrasāra* states:
"One should utter the entire mantra first, followed immediately by the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)."
"Furthermore, when it is reversed at the end, that is known as *saṃpuṭa*.
Regarding the phrase "by these": it was previously stated that there are seven types of recitation (*japa*).
[Verses 80–81] He states the fruit of the recitation of the seed-syllables *Ramā*, *Māyā*, and *Haṃsa* with the words beginning "by the seed-syllable *Ramā*" for those who seek liberation.

He states the specific distinction with the words "But liberation," and so forth. Accordingly, in this case, one must apply the *praṇava* (Oṃ) at the beginning and the end of the mantra—which has been previously described as encapsulated by the seed-syllable *haṃsa*—along with the syllables *śrīṃ* and *hrīṃ*. Thus, the sequence for the illuminator (*dīpanī*) is: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, then the mantra, then haṃsaḥ hrīṃ śrīṃ Oṃ.
This essence has been explained; now I shall describe another method. || 82 ||
The Vāgbhava [bīja] is formed by the Tāra, Māyā, Ramā, Kāma, and Vāgbhava;
that same [sequence], when reversed, is the Kāmarāja, which one should then recite.
The essence of consciousness is said to be the Vāgbhava [syllable] together with the Star, Kāma, Rāmā,
and Māyā (an alternative formulation).
And furthermore, I shall now speak.
One should join the seed-syllable of Kamalā (Śrī), which is the illusory power of speech (vāṅmāyā), at the beginning of the Vāgbhava [mantra].
Then, one should place the first of the Vedas (Oṃ) in the Lakṣmī and Speech seeds, followed immediately by Manmatha (Klīm). || 85 ||
Then, having given the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should extract that which is called Vāgbhava; at the beginning and the end is Tāra and Māyā, with the Śrī-bīja joined in the middle. (86)
At the end of *tāra* (om), the *vāgbhava* and the *kāmabīja* are likewise situated;
having thus pronounced this, one should pronounce the *kāmarāja*. (87)

82–84 | He states another method with the words beginning with "and the other" (*parañca*). Therein, he describes the conjunction of seed-syllables (*bīja*) prior to the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* with the words beginning with "the *tāra*" (*tāra*). *Tāra* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ); *māyā* is Hrīṃ; *ramā* is Śrīṃ; *kāma* is Klīṃ; and *vāgbhava* is Aiṃ.
The meaning is that when these are joined before it, the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* becomes conjoined with the illuminator (*dīpanī*). Thus, [it becomes] Oṃ...

The meaning is that having uttered *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiḥ*, one should recite the *vāgbhava* cluster (*kūṭa*). Now, regarding the *kāmarāja* cluster, he states the application of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) with the words beginning "that very same," etc. The meaning is that having uttered the aforementioned five seed-syllables arranged in reverse order—that is, in the inverse sequence—one should recite the *kāmarāja* cluster. And thus, having uttered *aiḥ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ*, [one recites] the *kāmarāja* cluster.

"One should recite" is the resultant meaning. Regarding the application of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) within the Śaktikūṭa, he says "with the Tāra," and so forth.
