"With the Tāra" refers to the Vāgbhava; "Tāra" and "Vāgbhava" [are synonyms]. Then, it is endowed with Kāma, Ramā, and Māyā—this is an adjective for the Śaktikūṭa which is understood by implication. Thus, the resultant meaning is that one should recite the Śaktikūṭa immediately after: *oṃ aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*.

84–89 | He states another method with the words beginning "and the other" (*parañca*), etc. Therein, this is the sequence: one should place the *vāgbhava* at the beginning; in the middle of this very *vidyā*, one should insert *kāma*; and the lower [syllable] situated after *manmatha* is the *śrībīja* placed between [two instances of] *manmatha*. (88)
Having thus joined them in sequence, one should then utter the Śaktikūṭa.
This is the illuminating Vidyā, hidden in all the Tantras. (89)

The meaning is: "at the beginning of the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. Regarding the phrase "speech," etc., the meaning is that one should join these three seed-syllables: "speech" (*vāk*) is the *vāgbhava-bīja* (ai), the *māyā-bīja* (hrīṃ), and the *kamalā-bīja* (śrīṃ). He states the application of other seed-syllables prior to these three seed-syllables with the words "beginning with the Vedas," etc.: the "beginning of the Vedas" is the *praṇava* (oṃ); "Lakṣmī" is śrīṃ; the "speech-seed" is ai; and "Manmatha" is klīṃ.

The connection is as follows: having first placed this pentad of seed-syllables—namely *hrīṃ* (the seed of *māyā*)—before the *vāgbhava*, *māyā*, and *śrī* seeds according to their etymological order, one should recite the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. This is because of the statement "one should join the beginning of the *vāgbhava*" here, from which it is understood that the seed-syllables of *vāk*, *māyā*, and *kamalā* (Śrī) must occur immediately prior to the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*.

The prior placement of the five seed-syllables beginning with *veda* (oṃ) must be understood by implication. Thus, the resultant meaning is that one should utter the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* after pronouncing "oṃ śrīṃ ai/ klīṃ hrīṃ ai/ hrīṃ śrīṃ. Regarding the conjunction of seed-syllables prior to the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, he says "beginning and end" (*ādyanta*). Here, the state of being the beginning and the end refers to what will be described below.

With reference to the seed-syllable *śrī* (*śrīṃ*). Thus, at the beginning of the *śrī*-seed there is the *tāra* (*oṃ*) and the *māyā*-seed (*hrīṃ*), and likewise at the end there is the same application of *tāra* and *māyā*;

by this, *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ* is obtained. Regarding "at the end of the *tāra*": after the initial *tāra*, the *vāgbhava*-seed (*aiṃ*) and the *kāma*-seed (*klīṃ*) are placed. By the phrase "situated thus," the application of the *vāgbhava* and *kāma* seeds is also stated for the end of the final *tāra*. By this, *oṃ*... [is obtained].

The collection of these seed-syllables (bījas) is: *ai*, *klīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *oṃ*, *ai*, *klīṃ*, and *hrīṃ*. The meaning is that having thus pronounced this group of nine seed-syllables (*etadbījanavakam*), one should then utter the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa*.
Now, he explains the application of the seed-syllable prior to the *Śakti-kūṭa* with the words "of this" (*etasyāḥ*). This refers to [the syllable] to be employed at the beginning of the *Kāmarāja*.

This means [the application] of the *dīpanī* mantra. One should employ the *kāma-bīja* in the middle. The underlying intention is as follows: the illumination (*dīpanī*) of the *śakti-kūṭa* is exactly like the illumination of the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*; the only distinction here is the reversal of the sequence of certain seed-syllables (*bījas*).
To demonstrate that very distinction, he says: "one should apply the *kāma* [seed-syllable] in the middle. As for the employment of the *kāma-bīja*, it must indeed be placed before the *śrī-bīja*.

It must be placed [there], because it will be stated later that "the Śrī-bīja is between Manmatha and [the others]. And thus, by the method of the Kāmarāja-dīpikā, since the Kāma-bīja is taken in place of the Māyā-bīja and the Vāgbhava-bīja is taken in place of the Kāma-bīja, it follows by implication that the Māyā-bīja must be inserted before the Vāgbhava-bīja. Accordingly: Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ oṃ.
Having uttered "aiḥ klīṃ hrīṃ," one should utter the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*); this is the established conclusion.
(Another kind of illuminator: One should apply *ramā*, *māyā*, and the *haṃsa* seed-syllable at the beginning of the *vāgbhava*.
After that, the best of practitioners should recite the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja, then the seed-syllable of Brahmā nearby, and finally the seed-syllable of Haṃsa at the end of Śakti. (90)
(Another kind of illuminator:
Alternatively, having recited the Praṇava, Lakṣmī, the Mānmatha, the Vāgbhava, and Parā, the best of practitioners should utter that which is called the Vāgbhava. 91.
Having likewise recited the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), Ramā, and Manmatha along with Māyā,
one should then utter the Kāmarāja mantra.
Having joined the Praṇava at the beginning, then Kāma, and then Ramā, the Supreme Goddess,
one should recite the Śakti-kūṭa in this sequential order.
And this essence has been declared, which bestows all accomplishments;
all these vidyās are most secret and are the bringers of consciousness. (94)

90. He describes the *dīpanī* (the illuminator) by another sequence, beginning with the word "Ramā": one should apply the seed-syllable *Ramā*, the seed-syllable *Māyā*, and the seed-syllable *Haṃsa* at the beginning of the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. The meaning is that after [uttering] "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ," one should utter and recite the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. Regarding "Kāmarāja": then, having uttered the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, [one should utter] the *brahma-bīja*.

The meaning is that one should utter the *praṇava*. Regarding "ending with Śakti": having then uttered the *kūṭa* of Śakti, one should mutter the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the two syllables "haṃsa," which is the seed-syllable *haṃsa*. It should be understood everywhere that the muttering (*japa*) is performed in conjunction with each respective *kūṭa*.
(91–93) Now, stating a different kind of *dīpanī*, he first describes the application of the seed-syllable within the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*:
Alternatively: *praṇava* is *oṃ*, *lakṣmī* is *śrīṃ*, *mānmatha* is *klīṃ*, *vāgbhava* is *aiṃ*, and *parā* is *hrīṃ*.

Thus, having recited *oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ*, one should then utter the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*; this is the meaning. Regarding the application of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, he says "and *praṇava*" and so forth. And thus, having recited *oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ*—

The meaning is that one should utter the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja. By the words beginning with "the *praṇava*" (*praṇavam*), he states the conjunction of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) prior to the *kūṭa* of Śakti.
Thus, having recited *oṃ aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*, one should utter the *kūṭa* of Śakti; this is the meaning. (p.
382) Having uttered any one of these, one should recite the Vidyā with a concentrated mind. || 95 ||
(Regarding the specific feature of the Vāmakeśī-vidyā in the Dīpanī:
Furthermore, the specific feature of the Vāmakeśī-vidyā is stated again:
[it consists of] the Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Śakti-kūṭa, in that respective order. (96)
By means of the three seed-syllables of desire alone, the *dīpanī* and so forth are prescribed;
seven times each, in sequence, at the beginning and at the end of the recitation. (97)
(Declaration of the description of the essential nature of the Vāmakeśī-vidyā) Now,
I shall briefly describe the form and power of that Vāmakeśī-vidyā, which is the very nature of Śabdabrahman. 98.

95. Regarding the phrase "of these": the meaning is that one should recite the *vidyā*—one's own desired mantra—after having applied any one of those various *dīpanīs* previously shown. Furthermore, he himself will state that the recitation of the *dīpanī* must be performed seven times at both the beginning and the end of the recitation of one's own desired mantra.

96–97. Having thus explained the yoga of illumination (dīpanīyoga) as common to all vidyās, he states the specific [procedure] for the Vāmakeśī-vidyā with the words beginning "In the Vāmakeśī," etc., and "Vāgbhava," etc. The meaning is that here, at the beginning of each of the three *kūṭas*, one should join the three seeds of desire (*kāma-bīja*), namely "klīm. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "illumination, etc.," there is the inclusion of vital breath (*prāṇa*), consciousness (*caitanya*), and so forth.

He teaches the procedure for the recitation of the *dīpanī* [mantras] with the words "of the recitation" (*japasya*). Thus, in the recitation of one's chosen mantra and so forth, there is a sevenfold recitation of the *dīpanīs*;
likewise, it is done at the end of each respective number of recitations.
98. Now, the nature and power of the *Vāmakeśī-vidyā*, whose essence is the *Śabda-Brahman*, [are described].

He promises to explain [this] with the words beginning with "Vāmakeśī," and so forth. Now, who is this one called Vāmakeśī? It is said: in the tenth chapter, that very *Kāmarāja-vidyā* of Śambhu—which is served by the hosts of gods and described as being "fixed" (*kīlitā*) by the verse beginning with "Kandarpa joined with Viṣṇu, together with the lower face, the letter above the right ear" (verse 159)—is stated therein to be the *Vāmakeśī-vidyā*. Thus it is said in that same place:

"She is Vāmakeśī, the Śāmbhavī, proclaimed by the Eastern Traditions (pūrvāmnāya). She is to be known as the 'Pinned' (kīlitā) Vidyā; she does not bestow accomplishment on the surface of the earth" (verse 162). By this [statement], it is established that the very Vidyā of the previously mentioned Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja is indeed Vāmakeśī. By the phrase "she whose nature is the Word-Brahman" (śabdabrahmasvarūpiṇī), it is indicated that the phonemes constituting the mantra possess the nature of the deity. Of her...

Thus, I shall briefly describe the power of that form consisting of the phonemes contained within the mantra— the nature of the Vāmakeśī-vidyā to be explained [herein], specifically the meaning of the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*).
In the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, a triangle is situated at the crown of the head;
right there, the seed-syllable of Mādana rests upon the bindu like a lamp.
Resembling ten million moons, consisting of consciousness and bliss, supreme, the unsurpassed state, secret, and situated above the forehead. (100)
The bhaga has the shape of a support and is situated upon the triangular plane. || 101 ||

The meaning is: "I shall establish [this] through words. Regarding the reading *rūpaprabhedañca*, the meaning is: "I shall explain the *prabheda*—the preeminent distinction regarding the meaning—of those syllables that constitute the mantra *ka e ī la hrīm* within the *rūpa* (form).
(99–100). In this context, while explaining the *vāgbhavakūṭa* as *ka e ī la hrīm*, [the author first discusses] the letter *ka*.
He states its essential nature with the words beginning "sahasra" and so forth: within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, a triangle is situated.
This has been stated in the sixth chapter of this very work, concerning the thousand-petaled lotus:
"Within that, a triangle constantly flashes forth, having the form of lightning."

"In that very place" means: having resorted to the supreme *bindu*—which is the identity of Śiva and Śakti as described in the sixth chapter, which is the void within that aforementioned triangle, served by all the hosts of gods, and exceedingly secret—the letter *ka*, which is the *mādana* or seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), exists there; this clearly states the essential nature of the supreme *bindu*.
In the *Saubhāgyasubhagodaya*, as cited in the commentary on the second chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya* composed by Amṛtānandanātha:
"The red *bindu* is Śakti; the white [bindu] is Śambhu; beyond that is their identity (*aikātmya*).
And thus, based upon the supreme *bindu* which consists of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti, the seed-syllable *mādana*—the letter *ka*—exists like a lamp.

This is what is meant: "like a lamp" means that just as a lamp manifests its own radiance only by depending on jasmine flowers and the like, so too the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) does so only by depending on the supreme *bindu*. He describes its essential nature with the words "resembling ten million moons," and so forth. "The state beyond the unsurpassed" (*anuttarapada*) means that in relation to which there is no further or final state for practitioners. And thus:

Through the propitiation of that [deity], whose essential nature consists of a radiance like ten million moons, the state of being composed of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), and so forth, and through the contemplation of identity with it, the attainment of that very nature occurs. This should be understood in the same way for other cases as well.
(101) Now, he explains the second letter *E* with the words beginning "Bhaga": *Bhaga* is the seed-syllable of the womb, *E*.

The "supportive configuration" (ādhārasaṃsthāna) is situated in the *mūlādhāra*. There too, it is "resting upon the triangular place," meaning it is located within the triangular space shaped like a womb (*yoni*) in the center of the pericarp of the *mūlādhāra* lotus. This is to be connected with the action to be described later by the word "one should contemplate."
That source of the universe is said to have the form of a lotus fiber;
she is the fourth [state], residing in the heart-lotus by taking her stand upon Mount Meru. (102)
The supreme and yet lower power of Śambhu consists of will, knowledge, and action;
she takes the form of the half-mora of the letter *ha*, with a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning. (103)
One should meditate upon Śakra as blazing in the middle of the forehead. || 104 ||
Resembling a mass of lightning, this fifth [syllable] is located in the eyes and nose;
it is the Vāgbhava Mahāvidyā, which bestows the status of Lord of Speech. 105.

102–103 | Now he explains the third vowel, *ī*, with the words beginning "mṛṇāla" (lotus fiber). The meaning is that the fourth [vowel], which consists of the fourth letter among the vowels starting with *a*, is the form of the vowel *ī*. The connection is as follows: the supreme and yet non-supreme power (*parāparā śambhuśakti*) of Śambhu is established, having taken recourse to Mount Meru within the heart-lotus called Anāhata. He further qualifies her as being "in the form of a lotus fiber" (*mṛṇālatanturūpā*), [referring to] the lotus fiber...

She is exceedingly subtle. Likewise, she is the source of the universe; because the syllable *ī* is the nature of Śambhu’s power (*śakti*), its creation and dissolution occur again and again eternally.
Therefore, power is primary, and this entire world is pervaded by power.

Thus, because the *Gandharvatantra*, in its third chapter, declares that the creation of the universe proceeds from *Śakti* alone, she possesses the status of being the source of the entire world (*viśvayonitva*). She is said to consist of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). Śambhu, known as *Prakāśa* (Light), is characterized primarily by the power of will; the supreme *Śakti*, whose nature is *Vimarśa* (reflective awareness), is characterized primarily by the power of action; and the predominance of the power of knowledge is common to both. And therein:

Since there is no difference between the two whose nature is light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarṣa*), it is established that the power whose form is reflective awareness possesses the nature of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). It is precisely with this intention that she is said to be "of the form of the half-mora (*kalā*) of the letter *ha*. The meaning is: *ha* is Śiva, and she is of the form of his half-mora, sporting as the half-body of Hara. Likewise, her radiance is equal to ten million flashes of lightning. As it has been said:

In the sixth chapter, concerning the *anāhata* lotus, it is said: "The power (*śakti*) shining within the pericarp of this lotus is called the triangle (*trikoṇa*), its body as tender as the tip of a lightning bolt," and so forth. Thus ends the determination of the nature of the fourth vowel.
(Verses 104–105) Now, he explains the fourth syllable, the letter *la*, with the word "Śakra": Śakra is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Indra, the letter *la*.

The connection is that it is "situated in the middle of the forehead. By this, the nature of this seed-syllable (*bīja*) as being the form of Indra is indicated; its specific details will be explained later. Now, he explains the fifth *māyā*-seed-syllable with the words beginning with "dīpitām" (the illuminated). It is in the form of the fifth letter with respect to the letter *ka*. "Netranāsike" is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of the eyes (*netrāṇi*) and the nostrils (*nāsike*).

In that [state], likewise, within the three eyes and the two nostrils, Śiva— resplendent like a mass of lightning, the meaning of the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, conjoined with that which is called knowledge— is established within the three voids (*triśūnya*). (106)
Resembling ten million suns and situated upon a great lotus, the supreme letter *Sa* is like the rising sun in the center of the mouth. (107)
And one should contemplate Mādana, glowing like the java flower, within the stomach. || 108 ||

By means of the syllable *ha*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the wind (*vāyu*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) resembling the *haṃsa*, exits to a distance of twelve finger-breadths. || 109 ||
The tip of the thousand petals consists of sixteen digits (kalās);
Indra is there in the center, distinguished by the form of the syllable Om.
The syllable *hrīṃ* is in the center of the heart, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
on the two breasts are two dots (*bindu*), and between the pair of breasts is a half-moon with the luster of the *javā* flower.
And at its tip are Nāda and Bindu, joined with Śiva and Śakti;
it is the supreme great seed-syllable of Kāmarāja, which effects attraction.

The meaning is that one should contemplate [the syllables] as illuminated. By this, it appears that the contemplation of the letters *ha*, *ra*, and *i* in the three eyes, and of the *nāda* and *bindu* in the two nostrils, has been taught. Having thus explained the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*, he states its fruit with the words beginning "This is the *vāgbhava*," and so forth.

106–108. Now, while explaining the second peak-syllable of Kāmarāja, namely *ka-ha-la-hrīm*, he first states the meaning of the letter *ha*: "Śiva. The letter *ha* is Śiva; "joined with that which is called knowledge" means it is endowed with the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*), will (*icchā*), and action (*kriyā*). It is "established in the three voids," meaning it resides within the triad of points (*bindu*)—above, below, and in the middle.

Upon the thousand-spoked [wheel] above the great lotus, he explains the second meditation on the letter *sa* with the words "the letter *sa*" (*sakāram*). He explains the third, the letter *ka*, with the words "intoxication" (*mādanam*).
109. He explains the fourth, the letter *ha*, with the passage beginning "by the letter *ha*" (*hakāreṇa*), etc. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) resides at the tip of the mouth and nose.

Vāyu; the letter *ha* denotes the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Here, by means of the letter *ha*, it is stated that the vital breath, which is wind, goes out to the extent of twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*). Now, as to what the essential nature of the letter *ha*—which is a synonym for *prāṇa*—is, he says: "having the luster of a swan" (*haṃsābha*). "Having the luster of a swan" means white in color; the meaning is that the Supreme Lord Śiva [is so].

110–112 | He states the fifth letter, *la*, with the words "of the thousand" (*sahasrasya*). The meaning is that sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon shine upon the tips of the petals of the thousand-spoked [wheel]. "Indra" means one should contemplate the letter *la* there.
(The meaning of the *Śakti-kūṭa*)
In the triangle of the navel-lotus is the syllable *sakāra*, which has the luster of a pomegranate;
and in the two petals of the lotus is the *mādana* (the letter *ma*), resembling yellow in color.
In this same manner, one should contemplate Śakra, whose nature is splendor, upon the back and the private parts;
and on the fourth [occasion], one should meditate upon him as illuminated within the center of the womb.
The seed-syllable of Śiva as well becomes a pair of eggs;
one should contemplate the supreme seed-syllable of the Goddess as the womb. 115.
I shall further explain the true nature of meditation with a concentrated mind; the reality of meditation is of a different kind [than previously described]. (116)

Now he states the seed-syllable of Māyā with the words beginning "Oṃkāra": the meaning is that one should meditate upon the syllable *hrīṃ*, which is the differentiator of the form of *oṃ* and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns, within the heart. Regarding the word "bindu" (*bindu*): the connection is that one should meditate on the two breasts in the form of two *bindus*, having a color like the *javā* flower—that is, red like a *javā* blossom—and on the half-moon at their apex, as well as the *nāda* and *bindu*.

113–115 | Now, while explaining the *śaktikūṭa* as "ka la hrīṃ," he first explains the letter *sa* with the words beginning "nābhi" and so forth. The meaning is: in the triangle of the navel-lotus. The meaning is that one should contemplate the letter *sa*, which has the luster of a pomegranate, i.e., red in color. The fourth [syllable] is the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*. Since this has already been explained previously, it will not be explained again here.
It is elaborated [as follows]. 116. Now, with the words beginning with "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), he describes the nature of the Vāmakeśī-vidyā in another way.

Regarding the phrase "the reality of meditation" (*dhyānatattvam*): meditation (*dhyāna*) is the contemplation of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-cintā*); its "reality" (*tattvam*) is its accordance with truth (*yāthārthyam*). This refers to the non-duality of the mantra and the deity.

The meaning is as follows: since this is well-established in all the scriptures, "meditation" (dhyāna) is simply the contemplation of the manner in which the individual phonemes constituting each mantra denote their respective deities, so that practitioners may experience the non-difference between the two; its "essence" (tattva) is this very thing. Regarding the term "composed" (samāhita): because it is impossible for the essence of meditation—which is difficult to grasp due to its extreme subtlety—to enter a distracted mind, one must be composed.

Thus it has been said. By this, it is indicated that the reality of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) enters the sphere of experience, in some manner, only for those whose minds are concentrated, and not for others.
(In this regard, the meaning of the *kūṭa* [peak] of Kāmarāja:)
In the great peak of Kāmarāja, there is the pair consisting of Śiva as creation and maintenance;
and right there is the seed-syllable of Śakti, which is the three-eyed form of Śaṅkara.
The letter *ha*, being of the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), bestows eightfold sovereignty;
the second [letter, *sa*], being of the nature of maintenance (*sthiti*), grants great enjoyment. The letter *sa*, being of the nature of emanation, ordains enjoyment within those [realms].
The three peaks are the syllable Hrīṃ, and the three eyes of the Goddess are auspicious.
The Sun of the Māyā-bīja situated within the Vāgbhava-kūṭa:
the letter *ha* is the Śāmbhava state, and the letter *ra* possesses unimpeded luster.
From the letter *ra*, indeed, Mahāmāyā bestows all-pervasive power. (120)

117. Therein, he analyzes the meanings of the letters constituting the *kāmarājakūṭa* of the fifteen-syllable *Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja-vidyā*. Regarding "Kāmarāja": the letters forming the *kāmarājakūṭa* are six, namely *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *ha*, *la*, and *hrīṃ*. Among these, he states the meaning of the two *hakāras* with the words beginning with "sṛṣṭi" (*sṛṣṭi*-etc.). The "two Śivas" refers to the two *hakāras*.

It consists of the forms of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and maintenance (*sthiti*); therein, the first *ha*-letter is of the nature of emanation and the second is of the nature of maintenance. As it is said in the *Saubhāgyasubhagodaya*:
"In this context, the *ha*-letter situated between the vowels (*kala*) possesses the essential nature of maintenance."
"Its supreme state of abiding is illuminated by the form of the Mother of Consciousness.
Thus, because these two are described as having the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and maintenance (*sthiti*), they should be understood as being the very essence of the powers of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

Regarding the phrase "the seed-syllable of Śakti": the seed-syllable of Śakti is the letter *sa*, which is one of the letters constituting the aforementioned *kuṭa* (the seed-syllable *kūṭa*), and it represents the three eyes of Śaṅkara.

The meaning is that its nature is the third eye, which is the form of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). By this, it is understood that this letter *sa* is the Raudrī power of withdrawal. He will explain later the nature of the three *ka*s situated within the three *kūṭas*.
(118) Having stated that the aforementioned letters have the nature of creation and so forth, he declares their fruit with the words beginning "the letter *ha*."
"Sovereignty is eightfold" means the eight sovereign powers beginning with *aṇiman*. "The second" means the second letter *ha*;
the meaning is that the second *ha*, by virtue of being the nature of persistence (*sthiti*), serves as the means for experience (*bhoga*).
119. "The letter *sa*... [and so forth].
Now, he explains the three *hrīṃ* syllables that constitute the final part of the three *kūṭas*, beginning with the words "trikūṭa" and so forth.
(Verse 120) Having thus described in general the essential nature of the three *hrīṃ* syllables situated within the three *kūṭas*, [he proceeds] to the distinction of the *kūṭas*—
(The meaning of the seed-syllable of Māyā situated in the peak of Kāmarāja):
I shall explain the fruit of the syllable *hrīṃ* of Kāmarāja thereafter. (121)

The letter *ha*, because it is of the nature of *laya* (dissolution), withdraws the continuum of differentiation. The letter *ra*, being of the nature of the fire of time (*kālāgni*), effects the destruction of the flood of sins.
*Mahāmāyā*, the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*), is the illuminator of consciousness and bliss. 122.
(The meaning of the seed-syllable of Māyā residing in the Śakti-kūṭa:
One obtains this very fruit from the syllable *hrīṃ*, which is the seed of Śakti.
The letter *ha* indeed destroys death, and the letter *ra* is the illuminator of all. (123)

He states its essential nature with the words "the letter *ha*," and so forth. The state of Śambhu (*śāmbhava-bhāva*) means having an existence that is not distinct from the existence of Supreme Śiva;

in other words, it consists in the state of identity with Supreme Śiva—this is the meaning of the letter *ha*. Regarding "the letter *ra*": the letter *ra* is the constituent of the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*;
it is "of unimpeded luster," meaning its radiance is not overcome by *māyā*. Regarding "from the letter *ra*": [it refers to] Mahāmāyā, who revolves from the letter *ra*.

The vowel *ī* bestows all-pervasive expansion. Thus, the meaning of the syllable *hrīṃ*, which constitutes the *vāgbhava* peak, is that the Blessed Goddess— whose nature is the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) with Supreme Śiva and whose radiance spreads unimpeded— abides pervading the entire universe consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) from Śiva down to Earth.
121–122. Now, he explains the *hrīṃ* syllable of the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa* with the words beginning "of Kāmarāja" (*kāmarājasya*). Regarding the letter *ha*:

because it is of the nature of *laya* (dissolution) and because it is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). The letter *ha* has the nature of withdrawal by virtue of being the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śiva.

Thus, the meaning is that this letter *ha*, being of the nature of withdrawal, should withdraw the continuity of duality—that is, the knowledge of difference between the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) and the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*).
Regarding the syllable *repha*: it means that, by its nature as the fire of time (*kālāgni*), it burns away the entire mass of sins. Regarding *mahāmāyā*:

*mahāmāyā* is the vowel *ī*; the *kāmakalā* is the very essence of the fourth consciousness (*turīya-caitanya*), and for that reason, it is the illuminator of consciousness and bliss. Thus, the *hrīṃ* syllable, the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of the Kāmarāja-bīja, having preceded the dispelling of all dualistic knowledge, reduces the heap of sins to ashes.
The essential meaning is that [the mantra] reveals the nature of Brahman, which consists of consciousness and bliss, within the heart of the practitioner.

(123–124) Having thus explained the *hrīṃ* syllable of Kāmarāja, he explains the *hrīṃ* syllable situated in the Śakti-kūṭa with the words beginning "of the seed-syllable of Śakti" (*śaktibījasya*). "This very thing" refers to the form that is about to be described. He states that very same thing with the words beginning "the letter *ha*" (*hakāra*).

The syllable *ha* destroys death; the meaning is that for one who possesses it, there is no death caused by being bound by the noose of Yama. The letter *ra* is Māyā consisting of universal consciousness and bliss; one should contemplate its identity with consciousness.
The three eyes of the Goddess have been explained [as having the meanings of the three peaks, the three places, and the three forms]; now I shall describe the remainder. 124.
The letter *la* also bestows great sovereignty because it is the form of Indra;
the letter *la* always grants the sovereignty of form because it is the lord of the earth. (125)
The letter *la* bestows great sovereignty in the form of liberation;
Śakra is the king of the three worlds, established upon the three peaks. (126)
(The meanings of the letter *ka* situated in the three peaks:
In the three peaks and in the letter *ka*, Kāma, the Lord of the Three Worlds, bestows a form consisting of consciousness and bliss; of this there is no doubt. (127)
The letter *ka*, because it is the form of desire (*kāmarūpa*), bestows great luster;
subsequently, the letter *ka* at the end of the head [of the mantra] is the state beyond reality (*tattvātīta*). 128.
The "illuminator" (prakāśaka) means that which illuminates everything whose nature is light and reflective awareness (vimarśa). Regarding "consciousness" (cit):

one should contemplate—that is, bring about—the unity with consciousness, meaning non-difference from Brahman whose nature is consciousness; [this refers to] Māyā, which consists of consciousness and bliss, whose essence is knowledge and bliss, and which is the vowel *ī*. One should effect this identity with the Brahman that is of the nature of consciousness.

Thus, the essential meaning is that this syllable *hrīṃ*, having dispelled the suffering of death and having revealed the nature of Brahman as established by the Vedic scripture "All this, indeed, is Brahman," brings about the realization of the nature of consciousness-bliss (cidānanda).
(Verses 124–126) Now, he promises to explain the meanings of other phonemes situated within the three peaks (*trikūṭa*).
With the words "and the remainder," etc., he first explains the letter *la* situated within the *vāgbhava*-kūṭa by means of the passage beginning with "the letter *la* also," and so forth.

Because it is the form of Indra and because it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Indra, the letter *la* bestows unsurpassed sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). The sense is that since Indra is the sovereign lord of supreme sovereignty, it follows all the more clearly that his seed-syllable possesses the capacity to grant supreme sovereignty.

Now, he speaks of the letter *la* situated in the second peak with the words beginning "The letter *la*, because of being the lord of the earth," and so forth. He explains the letter *la* situated in the third peak with the words beginning "The letter *la*," and so forth. He states the resulting conclusion with the words beginning "Śakra," and so forth.
(Verses 127–128) Now, while declaring the essential nature of the three *ka*s situated within the three peaks, [he first...]
(Its being the source of all: This is the womb of great desire; this is proclaimed as Śakti.
Such is the Great Vidyā; Śiva is Ardhanārīśvara. 129.
(The Meaning of the Saubhāgyā Mantra):
I shall declare the most wonderful variety of seed-syllables (bīja) belonging to Saubhāgyā. (130)
There are two *ha*-letters at the beginning and the end, and two *ha*-letters in the middle;
Śiva, the four-Veda Śambhu, is established in the four directions. (131)
In the first and middle *kūṭas*, two *ka* syllables are proclaimed;
in the *śakti-kūṭa*, there are two *ka* syllables, which belong to the four-faced Brahmā.
The seed-syllable of Indra is within the three peaks; the supreme Earth is triangular.
Tripurā and Mahāmāyā are proclaimed as the one Śakti. || 133 ||
He explains the letter *ka*, which resides in the *vāgbhava* cluster, with the words beginning "the letter *ka*" (*kākāra*).

Since the letter *ka*—by implication—resides in the *vāgbhava* cluster, desire (*kāma*) is situated therein; for since *ka* is the seed-syllable of desire, the presence of desire there is logically established. It is the Lord of the Three Worlds.

Furthermore, because of its sovereignty over the three worlds and because its nature as consisting of ineffable consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*) is invariably present there, its form consists of consciousness-bliss.

"It bestows its own nature upon the practitioner"—this is the ellipsis. Now, he explains the letter *ka*, which is situated as the second peak of the Kāmarāja-mantra, with the words beginning "the letter *ka*. Because of the identity between the signified and the signifier due to the nature of desire (*kāmarūpatva*), and because it is the very essence of desire, the connection is that "it bestows great luster" (*mahākāntim*). And thus, regarding the letter *ka*:

The sense is that, because it conveys the meaning of the form of Kāmadeva—who is the locus of incomparable beauty—it is logical that it possesses the skill of bestowing extraordinary splendor. Now, he explains the third syllable, the letter *ka*, situated in the Śakti-kūṭa, with the words beginning "beyond the principles" (*tattvātītam*). Thus, the letter *ka* residing in the Śakti-kūṭa is the supreme state beyond the principles.
The meaning is that it bestows the state of Brahman, which is Nirvāṇa and liberation; this is the grammatical connection.

(Verses 130–133) Previously, in the eleventh chapter, beginning with the words "Now I shall explain Saubhāgyā" (verses 59–60), the fifteen-syllable Saubhāgyā-vidyā was presented; [herein follows] the description of the syllables constituting its three peaks (*trikūṭa*).

He explains the essential nature [of the mantra] with the words "of the fortunate one" (*saubhāgyāyāḥ*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the difference between the seeds" (*bījabhedam*): the meaning is the difference in the referents of the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Regarding "at the beginning and at the end":

in the first part, the *vāgbhava*-kūṭa, there is one letter *ha* (in *sa ha ka la hrīm*); and at the end, in the *śakti*-kūṭa, there is another (in *ka ha ka la hrīm*). Thus, the meaning is that there are two letters *ha* in the two *kūṭas*. Likewise, in the middle, [there is] *ha ka ha la hrīṃ*.
(391) (The fruit of the knowledge of this vidyā):
He who knows the great vidyā, the auspicious and supreme syllable, shall partake of heaven and be liberated; he is the son of the Goddess upon the earth. 134.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 12 ||

In the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, there are two *hakāra*s; thus, taken together, there are four *hakāra*s. He describes their essential nature with the words beginning "the knower of the four Vedas" (*caturveda*).
Then, he explains the four *kakāra*s with the words beginning "the first. In the first *vāgbhava-kūṭa*...

In the middle *kāmarāja* peak (*kūṭa*), as previously shown, there are two *ka*s; likewise, in the *śakti* peak, there are two—thus, there are four *ka*s in total. He states their essential nature with the words "of Brahmā" (*brahmaṇas tu*). Since the letter *ka* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Brahmā, the meaning here is that the four *ka*s constitute the nature of the four faces of Brahmā. Now, regarding the three *la*s situated in the triple-peak (*trikūṭa*):

He explains with the words beginning "In the three peaks" (*trikūṭeṣu*), etc. The meaning is that in the three peaks is the seed-syllable of Indra, the three *la*s, which is the nature of the triangle and the earth.

Regarding "Tripura": Mahāmāyā is the triad of seed-syllables *hrīm*; likewise, the single energy is the syllable *sa*. Thus, Tripurā is proclaimed. (134) Regarding "Ya": *Para* is Paraśiva; those whose measure (*mā*) is by him [are the *paramākṣarī*].

The connection is as follows: he who knows that fifteen-syllabled mantra (*pañcadaśākṣarī*) consisting of the aforementioned syllables, which are of such a nature—that is, whose form is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti.
This is the thirteenth chapter.

(The Definition of the Sixteenfold Knowledge) (The Promise to Describe the Nature of the Sixteenfold Knowledge) Now I shall declare that knowledge, which is the first of all and the bestower of all accomplishments.
She consists of the eternal Śabdabrahman, whose nature comprises sixteen syllables;
she is the very essence of the knowledge of Brahman and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 1 ||

(The Fault in Reciting the Śrīvidyā Mantra Without Initiation) The wise person who recites the Śrīvidyā without the instruction of a guru shall become food for the Yoginīs, even by the command of the venerable Guru. (2)
(Prohibition against bestowing the Śrīvidyā upon the unqualified):
One should never give the sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā to just anyone;
one may give away a kingdom, one may give away wealth, but this boon must never be given.
"From [excessive] manifestation, there would be a loss of accomplishment"; thus was the command issued by Śambhu.
Even to a king who bestows his kingdom, or to a son who gives one’s life,
one may give away one’s entire empire, one’s son, one’s friend, or one’s wife—
even one’s head along with one’s life— but the sixteen-syllable mantra must never be given.

1. Having thus explained the Śrīvidyā mantras in detail through the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth chapters, the author specifically defines the previously mentioned Ṣoḍaśī in this chapter, beginning with the words "atha" (now), etc.
3. Regarding the term "ṣoḍaśārṇām" (consisting of sixteen syllables): "A boon may be given, a kingdom may be given, wealth may be given, but this [mantra] should never [be given]."
The meaning is "it should be given.
(Regarding its secret nature: This Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā) should always be concealed, like one's own private parts. || 6 ||
(To be given to one devoted to the Guru):
Just as salt dissolved in water becomes truly indistinguishable,
so too does the mind become truly absorbed at the feet of the venerable Guru.
Then, out of compassion, the sixteen-syllable Mahāvidyā should be bestowed.
(The Inexpressibility of the Ṣoḍaśī-vidyā):
All those mantras that are being uttered are traditionally held to be vocal;
the reality devoid of utterance is the sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā. (8)
(I shall describe its fourfold nature:
I shall explain this most rare [teaching] in four distinct ways. || 9 ||
(The Determination of the Ṣoḍaśī Vidyā) Whatever vidyā has been extracted from the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra,
each and every one of them is the Ṣoḍaśī Vidyā in its entirety, differing only according to its seed-syllables (bīja). 10.
(The attainment of the waking state of Vidyā):
[The letters] beginning with *ca* and ending with *va*, together with those from *śa* onwards, are distinct;
they are enriched by the left eye (*vāmākṣi*), the point (*bindu*), and the resonance (*nāda*), and consist of the digits (*kalā*) of the Universal Mother (*viśvamātṛ*).
And by the very application at the beginning of the Vidyā, the sixteenth [kalā] takes on the form of the waking state.

10. "Samuddhṛtā" (extracted) means in the eleventh chapter. 11. Now he states the sixteenth [syllable] according to its technical definition: "Candrādyam" (the first of the moon). The seed-syllable of the moon is *sa*; that which precedes it is *ha*. Likewise, "varuṇāntam" (ending with Varuṇa): the seed-syllable of Varuṇa is *va*; that which ends with it is *śa*. "Śakrādīti": Śakra is...

The letter *la* is at its beginning, and it is accompanied by the letter *ra*. By the word "separately" (*pṛthak*), it is indicated that the previously mentioned letters *ha* and *śa* are each joined with the letter *ra*. By this, *hra* and *śra* are obtained. Regarding "the left eye" (*vāmākṣī*): the left eye is the vowel *ī*; [along with] the *bindu* and *nāda*, [this constitutes] the practitioner’s state in the form of waking (*jāgrad-rūpatā*).
Arising, wakefulness, awareness, and the constant withdrawal of the mind—these four aspects are established in the waking state. (12)
(The nature of the waking state:
The waking state is said to consist of the quality of sattva, and it is purely of the nature of power (śakti). || 13 ||
(Regarding the transformation of the *trikūṭā* and other vidyās into the *pañcakūṭā* and others:
Indeed, all the *trikūṭā* divisions become *pañcakūṭā*. Vaiṣṇavī shall consist of eight *kūṭas*, and likewise Nārāyaṇī shall be so. (14)
This second method would be difficult to find within the three worlds. || 15 ||
This very [Vidyā] is of the nature of Śiva, and because of its pervasiveness, it is immovable;
for, being of the nature of deep sleep, it is directly of the nature of Brahman. (The state of deep sleep of Vidyā) || 16 ||

The meaning is that it is appropriate for them to be enriched by what is well-known; the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) is also connected here. And thus, through the individual conjunction of the vowels *hr* and *śr* with the fourth vowel (*ū*), the nasal dot (*bindu*), and the sound (*nāda*), the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* are obtained. Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of the Vidyā":
here, the author of the *Tantrasāra*, having introduced the topic with "In the *Jñānārṇava*, he states the technical [sixteenth vowel]," says:

O Goddess, one who is the manifest embodiment of Brahman itself should join at the beginning of the Vidyā the [syllables] ending in Candra (m) and Varuṇa (v), each accompanied by Śakra (k) and the others, enriched with the left eye (ī), the bindu, and the nāda, and consisting of the kalās of Viśvamātṛ.
These two statements of identical sequence have been cited above. Furthermore, it has been explained that the letter *ha* ends with the moon (*candra*).

Here, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "the *ha* of which the first [element] is the moon"—the word *candrādya* (beginning with the moon) refers precisely to the letter *ha*; thus, there is no contradiction with the statement from the *Jñānārṇava*. The phrase "at the beginning of the Vidyā" means at the beginning of the twelve Vidyās mentioned previously.

This has been explained in the *Tantrasāra*. Thus, here too, by joining at the beginning the previously mentioned twelve Vidyās worshipped by Anva and others with the aforementioned seed-syllables (*bīja*), the meaning is that Maheśvarī becomes the sixteen-fold [Vidyā] in the form of the waking state.
(12) Regarding the Goddess’s state as the waking form, he describes the fourfold condition of the practitioner with the verse beginning "origination" (*utpatti*).

14–16 | Regarding the application of the two seed-syllables at the beginning of the Vidyā and so forth, which was previously stated in the passage beginning with "first, the moon and so forth," he now states its result:
(the state of the practitioner therein is as follows: death, forgetfulness, fainting, and sleep shrouded in darkness.
The state of deep sleep (suṣupti) should be known as its digit; deep sleep is the very form of Śiva. || 17 ||
Śāmbhavī, however, is of the nature of waking through the singular application of the seed-syllable.
(The state of the Vidyā is that of dreaming);
at the end of deep sleep and at the beginning of waking, the dream-state consists of rajas. 18.
(In that regard, the state of the practitioner: Longing, delusion, reflection, and mental recollection of sense objects—this fourfold set of arts is prescribed for the dream state. (19)
"—*trikūṭā* and so forth. Also, in the *Tantrasāra*, after stating from "ending with *candra*" and "ending with *varuṇa*" up to "she is directly the nature of Brahman," it says:
'The *trikūṭās* are indeed all the divisions; they become the *pañcakūṭās*.'"
"It is said: 'The Vaiṣṇavī [vidyā] consists of eight kūṭas, while the Śāṅkarī should consist of six kūṭas.

Thus, in the present case, when the two single-syllable kūṭas *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* are joined at the beginning of the various three-kūṭa [mantras], there results a five-kūṭa [form]. Likewise, prior to the vidyā worshipped by Viṣṇu, which consists of six kūṭas..."
When combined with the two previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*), there is the state of having eight peaks (*kūṭa*).

For example: *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *ka e ī la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, *sa ka la hrīṃ*—this is the five-peak [mantra]. For example: *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *ha sa ka la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, *sa ka la*.

*Hrīṃ* | *Sa ha ka la hrīṃ* | *Sa ha sa ka la hrīṃ* | *Ha sa ka la hrīṃ*. Thus is the eight-peaked [mantra]. According to the statement in the *Tantrasāra*, "In this way, Nārāyaṇī becomes [the mantra]; the six-peaked one becomes Śāṅkarī," the meaning here is that Nārāyaṇī is Śāṅkarī. And likewise, by the passage beginning with "The two-fold Vidyā... (12.21), that which was practiced by Śaṅkara...

The four-peak (*catuṣkūṭā*) Vidyā has been shown; its resultant meaning is that it becomes six-peaked (*ṣaṭkūṭā*) through the conjunction of two peaks consisting of the two seed-syllables *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*.
And thus: *hrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *ka e ī la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, *sa ha sa ka la hrīṃ*, *ka*...

*e ī la ha sa ka ha la sa ha sa ka la hrīḥ*. This is the six-peaked (*ṣaṭkūṭā*) [mantra]. It should be understood that for the twelve varieties previously mentioned, there is an increase in the *kūṭas* according to the method just described. Because they do not deviate from having sixteen syllables, these are designated by the technical term "the Sixteen" (*ṣoḍaśī*). The same applies elsewhere as well.
(The specific application of the *praṇava* in the case of the Vidyās consisting of five peaks:
Whatever sixteen-syllable [Vidyā] consists of five peaks and embodies Śiva and Śakti, when adorned with the beginning of the Vedas (*oṃ*), it becomes composed of Śiva and Śakti. (20)
(This is the fruit of this meditation: By the mere remembrance of her, there shall be the merit of giving away a hundred elephants. (Conclusion)
These three divisions have been declared as the great essence, more essential than the essential. || 21 ||
(The distinction between Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja and the first Lopāmudrā):
The specific difference and distinction between Vāmakeśī and Lopā is now declared;
it is difficult to find, having been observed in the various divisions of the *Samayāṅka-mahātantra*. (22)
(The threefold nature of the sixteen-fold Kāmarāja):
The sixteen-fold [vidyā] called Kāmarāja becomes threefold by virtue of its seed-syllables. (23)

20. Regarding the phrase "consisting of five peaks": previously, through the passage beginning with "first, the moon and so forth," and "all the divisions consist of three peaks" and so on, various Vidyās were shown which consist of five peaks—comprised of Śiva and Śakti as the Māyā-āramā-yoga-nirvāhya—and which consist of Śiva and Śakti in the form of the two aforementioned seed-syllables (*bīja*). Each such Vidyā is adorned by the Vedādi; "Vedādi" [refers to the syllable *oṃ*].
The meaning is that the Vidyā consists of six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭā), being adorned with the Praṇava and preceded by the Praṇava.

Here, this should be noted: previously, the state of having five peaks was shown for the three peaks through their conjunction with the two seed-syllables *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*; here, by joining the Praṇava before those two (*hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*), they attain the state of having six peaks. In this regard—

The phrase "consisting of five peaks" (*pañcakūṭātmikā*) is an illustration; practitioners should infer that those [mantras] previously shown consisting of eight peaks and so forth may also consist of nine peaks and so on. This is clearly stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
"O Goddess, when [the mantra] is adorned with the beginning of the Vedas, it consists of Śiva and Śakti."
Then, O Supreme Goddess, all the divisions consist of six peaks;
Vaiṣṇavī consists of nine peaks, and Śāṅkarī consists of seven peaks.

Thus: *Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ ka e ī la hrīḥ; ha sa ka ha la hrīḥ; sa ka la hrīḥ*. In this way, a mere indication of the divisions of Trikūṭā is shown. Other divisions, however, should be inferred according to this sequence.
(Therein, the first:)
Having bestowed the seed-mantra of Gopāla before Kāmarāja,
the sixteenth [vowel] known as Kāmarāja is considered to have been propitiated by Kandarpa.
(Its Praise:
By the grace of this [image], even Kāma, endowed with victory over the three worlds and made beautiful by every form of loveliness, may bring the three worlds under his control. (25)
(Second verse:
This sixteenth Vidyā, preceded by Māyā, is difficult to obtain in all respects;
it is said to have been propitiated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
(Its Praise:
From whom Īśvara himself arose;
by whose grace Kṛṣṇa himself maintains the three qualities. (26)
(Third [verse]):

The illustrious sixteen-fold Vidyā bestows all prosperity. (24–25) Now, he describes the divisions of the Kāmarāja-Ṣoḍaśī with the words beginning "having given," etc., in the tenth chapter, concerning the Vidyā.

Beginning with the words, "I shall proclaim that which was practiced by Kāmadeva," and continuing with "Kandarpa [was joined] with Viṣṇu," etc., that very Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja-vidyā which was demonstrated here is to be understood by the term "named Kāmarāja," because it is encountered first and because it is heard that it was propitiated by Kandarpa. And thus: *ka e ī la hrīṃ* | *ha sa ka ha la*.

*Hrīṃ* | *Sa kala hrīṃ*. Thus, if one were to prefix the seed-syllable of Gopāla, *klīṃ*, to the previously shown fifteen-syllable Śāmbhava Kāmarāja-vidyā, that constitutes one variety. (26) Regarding the phrase "preceded by Māyā": if the aforementioned Kāmarāja-vidyā is preceded by Māyā—that is, by *hrīṃ*—[that is another variety].
If it is preceded by the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*), then it is the second.
Regarding "Śrīmatī": if that [mantra] is Śrīmatī and begins with "Śrī," being thus joined with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī (*śrīṃ*), then it is the third. As it is said:
"The Vidyā worshipped by Lakṣmī possesses the three qualities. (p. 398)
(Its Praise:
By whose grace the Vaiṣṇavī Lakṣmī, the beloved of Viṣṇu, came into being. (27)
(Declaration of the description of the nature of another type of Ṣoḍaśī) And I shall further proclaim another Ṣoḍaśī, which is difficult to obtain at all times. || 28 ||
(The sequence therein: Having recited the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja and so forth, along with the Śrī of the Kāmayoni in due order, the best of practitioners attains the state of Lord of Speech. (29)
(1) *klīṃ* *ka e ī la hrīḥ* | *hasakala hrīḥ* | *sakala hrīḥ* | (2) *hrīḥ* *ka e ī la hrīḥ* | *hasakala hrīḥ* | *sakala hrīḥ* | (3) *śrīḥ* *ka e ī la hrīḥ* | *hasakala hrīḥ* | *sakala hrīḥ* |

By the phrase "of Vāmakeśī and Lopā," it is taught that this triad of divisions belongs to the first Lopāmudrā as well, just like the previously mentioned Kāmarāja-vidyā; that too is now demonstrated:
(1) *klīṃ ha sa ka la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, *sa ka la hrīṃ*.

(2) Hrīṃ ha sa ka la hrīṃ | Ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ | Sa ka la hrīṃ | (3) Śrī/ Ha sa ka la hrīṃ | Ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ | Sa ka la hrīṃ | Here, it should be understood that by adding one syllable to each of the fifteen-syllable mantras, they become sixteen syllables.

28–30 | He promises to explain the *ṣoḍaśī* (the sixteen-syllable mantra) by another method, beginning with the words "And others... and so forth. Regarding "Kāmarāja" and so on: the meaning is that one should first recite, in sequence, the *Kāmayoni* and *Śrī* [mantras] before the fifteen-syllable *Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja-Vidyā*. Here, "Yoni" refers to the *Māyā-bīja*, the syllable *hrīṃ*. By "in sequence," it means: *Kāmayoni-Śrī*, *Yoni-Śrī-Kāma*, [and *Kāma-Yoni-Śrī*].
And [the mantras] beginning with Śrī, Yoni, and Kāmā. The meaning is that if one should join these in sequence, then there arise three Vidyās consisting of eighteen syllables;
this point is obtained by the word "in order" (kramāt). He states this clearly in the *Kuloḍḍīśa* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"The [mantras] preceded by Kāma, Māyā, and Ramā, and likewise Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Smara."
Ramā, Māyā, and Kāma; the syllable consisting of eight and one [letters] is threefold.
Thus, and in this way—(p.
399) its secret nature and excellence [are shown]: "This most secret Vidyā has been concealed within all Tantras."
A science equal to this has never existed, nor will it ever exist.
(I Ajapā-vidyā) Furthermore, I shall specifically declare the supreme secret:
the Ajapā is the Great Vidyā, stainless throughout all Tantras. (31)

(1) *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīḥ* | *ka e ī la hrīṃ* | *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* | *sa ka la hrīṃ* | (2) *hrīṃ śrīḥ* | *klīṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ* | *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* | *sa ka la hrīṃ* | (3) *śrīḥ* | *hrīṃ klīṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ* | *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* | *sa ka la hrīṃ* |
Thus, it should be understood that for Lopāmudrā I, there are three mantras formed by the previously mentioned application of seed-syllables (*bīja*).

Furthermore, because it was stated previously that "the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) or difference regarding Lopāmudrā of the Vāmakeśī [tradition] is being declared," and because it will be stated later: "Just as the method of Kāmarāja has been proclaimed, such is remembered to be the method of the lore (*vidyā*) known as Lopāmudrā."
Now, this seed-yoga (*bījayoga*) with Lopāmudrā is demonstrated as follows:
(1) *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ha sa ka la hrīṃ | ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ | sa ka la hrīṃ |* (2) *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ ha sa ka la hrīṃ | ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ | sa ka la hrīṃ |*

(3) Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ ha sa ka la hrīṃ | ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ | sa ka la hrīṃ | 31 | Now, he promises to state the *ajapā* mantra with the words beginning "the other," etc. Regarding "ajapā": the *Tantrasāra* states the *ajapā* mantra as follows:
The sky [A], the half-moon [I], and the letter white as the moon [U], followed by the beginning of creation [M]—
this two-syllabled mantra, known as Ajapā, is declared to be the celestial wish-fulfilling tree.

Thus [it is said]. Its meaning is as follows: *viyat* is the seed-syllable of space, the letter *ha*; and that is adorned by the half-moon, the *anusvāra*. By this, *ham* is obtained. Regarding the phrase "that which begins with it": the beginning of that *ha* is the letter *sa*, and that is joined with *sarga*, the *visarga*.
By this, *saḥ* is obtained. Thus, it is stated that *haṃsaḥ* is the *ajapā-mantra*. He states the seed-syllable for this [mantra] named *ajapā*:
In the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra-ṭīkā* as cited in the *Prāṇatoṣaṇī*:
"O Goddess of gods, for the practitioner of mantra, recitation occurs even without [physical] recitation;
therefore, this is called 'Ajapā' (the non-recited), which severs the bonds of worldly existence."
Through recollection, recitation, meditation, and complete dedication [to her], she who adorns the throat of Śiva bestows the accomplishment of all desires. (32)
(Declaration of the description of another Ṣoḍaśī: Now I shall proclaim another [form of] Ṣoḍaśī, which bestows the state of Lord of Speech. || 33 ||
Therein is the supreme Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), beginning with the seed-syllable *Gīr*, which was served by Bṛhaspati and worshipped by Jīva;
by whose grace the preceptor of the gods attained the status of Lord of Speech.
Preceded by the seed-syllable *bījapūra* and garlanded with *bindu*, she is served by Śiva and worshipped by Śambhu. || 35 ||

32 | Regarding the passage beginning with *yatsmṛteḥ*: the connection is that by the recollection (*smṛti*) and so forth of this *ajapā*, the Power (*śakti*) adorned upon the throat of Śiva becomes the bestower of the accomplishment of all desires.
33–34 | He describes another aspect of the nature of the Blessed Goddess, the sixteen-year-old deity (*ṣoḍaśī-devī*), starting with the word *atha*. Here, this should be noted:

The previously mentioned Śāmbhava, Kāmarāja, and Vidyā [forms], as well as the first Lopāmudrā, are threefold—beginning with the Gopāla-bīja, beginning with the Māyā-bīja, and beginning with the Śrī-bīja; likewise, there are three others beginning with the Gīr-bīja, beginning with the Śakti-bīja, and beginning with the Praṇava. Thus, according to the Samayāṅka doctrine, six varieties of the Ṣoḍaśī are taught. Having bestowed upon them therein...

By the passage beginning with "gopālabījam" and ending with "viṣṇuvallabhā," the first three divisions have been shown. Now, while stating the final three divisions, he first describes the one beginning with the seed-syllable of Speech (gīrbīja) through the words "atha aparām" and so forth. "Gīrbījādyā" means that which begins with the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava. And thus—
Aiṃ Ka E Ī La Hrīṃ | Ha Sa Ka Ha La Hrīṃ | Sa Ka La Hrīṃ. Thus the sixteen-syllable mantra is finalized. In this same manner, for the first Lopāmudrā as well:
Aiṃ Ha Sa Ka La Hrīṃ | Ha Sa Ka Ha La Hrīṃ | Sa Ka La Hrīṃ.
Thus, the sixteen-syllable mantra is to be understood.

(35) He states the second [mantra]: "bindusrag" etc. Here, "bindusrag" is the seed-syllable *saur*. This is because of the agreement with the *Āgamacandrikā*, which states: "*saur* is Parā, beginning with the seed-syllable. And therefore—
sauḥ ka e ī la hrīṃ | ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ | sa ka la hrīṃ | (The equality of Kāmarāja and Lopāmudrā: Just as the method of Kāmarāja has been proclaimed, [so too is that of Lopāmudrā].
Such is the method remembered for the vidyā known as Lopāmudrā. || 36 ||
(Its secrecy and praise:
"But that [tantra] is the most secret within the tantras, the granter of all heart's desires. (37)
(The status of the Kāmarāja-vidyā as the Ṣoḍaśī through its conjunction with the Praṇava): The great Kāmarāja-vidyā preceded by the Tāra (Om) is the Ṣoḍaśī;
this was to be worshipped by Nārada, from which his mental attainment arose. (38)

Thus is the sixteen-syllable mantra composed with the *parā* seed-syllable. That which begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ), however, will be described in verse 38. According to this method, the first *lopāmudrā* mantra is also as follows:
*sauḥ ha sa ka la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, *sa ka la hrīṃ*.
Thus, the sixteen-syllable mantra is to be understood.

As for the phrase "but as," by this it is taught that, just like the Kāmarāja-vidyā, the first Lopāmudrā also possesses sixteen syllables through the application of the aforementioned seed-syllables; the sequence, however, has already been demonstrated.

38. Regarding "Kāmarāja": this too is indeed the Śāmbhava Kāmarāja-vidyā. If that [vidyā] is preceded by Tāra (the syllable Om), beginning with the Praṇava, then it is another variety of the Ṣoḍaśī. This is because, after concluding the discussion on Kāmarāja and Lopāmudrā with the passage beginning with "As previously stated" (*yathā tu*) and ending with "such a method is remembered" (*prakāra īdṛśaḥ smṛtaḥ*), there is again a mention of the Kāmarāja-vidyā alone; therefore, it begins with Tāra.

The intention of the authors of the treatises appears to be that [this] is indeed the Kāmarāja-mahāvidyā, and not the first Lopāmudrā as well. Alternatively, because the word "ca" (and) is joined after "Kāmarāja-mahāvidyā," it should be understood that the inclusion of Lopāmudrā here is also intended. For in works such as the Āgamacandrikā, the status of being the Ṣoḍaśī is attributed to Lopāmudrā as well when preceded by the Praṇava.

Because it is explicitly stated. Here, this should be noted: previously, the state of being the *ṣoḍaśī* (the sixteen-syllable mantra) was demonstrated for the Śāmbhava, Kāmarāja, and Lopāmudrā [mantras] by means of the respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) at the beginning; it should be understood that these same varieties apply to the Śākta Kāmarāja and Lopāmudrā as well, provided they are preceded by the aforementioned seed-syllables. As stated in the *Āgamacandrikā*:

Having thus stated the Śākta-Kāmarāja mantra as *ī e ka la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, and *sa ka la hrīṃ*, [it is noted that] because it has been explicitly stated that there are six varieties— namely, those beginning with the Śrībīja (*sauḥ*), those beginning with *aiṃ*, those beginning with the Bīja *hrīṃ*, those beginning with the Bīja *oṃ*, and those beginning with the Bīja *klīṃ*— [the following applies].
(A different sixteen-fold Vidyā) Now, however, I shall proclaim the sixteen-fold [Vidyā] which is difficult for all to obtain;
by the mere knowledge of which, Brahman is directly realized—of this there is no doubt. (39)
(Its essential nature:

The supreme digit, the Fourth State (*turyā*), which is characterized by mere radiant manifestation from deep sleep up to the end of waking, has attained the state of being the culmination of all states.
It is declared to be free from both existence and non-existence, and transcending the qualities (guṇas). || 40 ||

(Its four parts are: dispassion, the desire for liberation, stainless meditative absorption, and a mind that discerns between the real and the unreal; these are the parts of the Fourth State (turyā). || 41 ||
(Its Praise:
By whose grace Lord Śiva, the all-pervading sovereign of the worlds, [attained his state];
she is the supreme knowledge among all sciences, difficult to obtain in any scripture. (42)
By a single utterance, millions of great sins are destroyed.
Thousands of ritual baths at sacred fords, hundreds of sacrifices and gifts, hundreds of thousands of gold-gift ceremonies (tulāpuruṣa), and hundreds of horse-sacrifices— || 44 ||
They do not equal it anywhere; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
What then to say of the absolute Brahman, which is attained by a single utterance alone? 45.

Thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices, circumambulations of the earth, and pilgrimages to holy sites such as Kāśī, numbering three and a half crores, do not equal [the merit of this] anywhere; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (46)
39. Now, he undertakes to describe a different kind of *ṣoḍaśī* with the words "Now, however" (*idānīntu*), etc. (This is the promise to define the nature of the previously mentioned *vidyā*).
"By means of the secret convention, through the grace of the venerable Guru, I shall proclaim the supreme [Vidyā]."
One should protect this knowledge in every way, if one desires one's own welfare.
(The nature of the Vidyā:

[The syllable] ending with *sa* (Śa), joined with the seventh preceded by *Śiva* (Ha), conjoined with the mantra ending with *Sūkṣmā* (Sa); [then] the Goddess (Ī), the right arm (Ra), the eye of Indra (Ū), and Kāma (Ka) marked with a digit (the crescent moon).

The seed-syllable with its face turned upward between the teeth, possessing living fangs, and joined with the remainder [of the mantra]—this fivefold [mantra] is thus proclaimed as the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals. || 48 ||

(The Application of Other Seed-Syllables): One should first utter the seed-syllable of the Vedas, then the three-fold Ramā, followed by Lopāmudrā served by Kāma; or again, the five [syllables] in the reverse order as before.

48. Now he speaks of another kind of *ṣoḍaśī* with the words beginning "sāntāntam" and so forth. That which has "sa" as its end is *sānta*, namely the letter *ṣa*. That which has that *ṣa* as its end is *sāntānta*, namely the letter *śa*. This is joined with the seventh [letter] preceding "Śiva. "Śiva" is the letter *ha*; the seventh letter preceding it, when read in reverse order, is the letter *ra*. Joined with that [it becomes] *śra*. By this, *śra* is obtained.

The subtle *ikāra* is at its end, and the *īkāra* likewise; "with the head" (*mastam*) means with the *anusvāra*. Thus, "endowed with" (*anvitam*) means joined with those two, the *īkāra* and the *anusvāra*; this is the qualification "ending with *sa*" (*sānta*). By this, the seed-syllable of Ramā, *śrīṃ*, is obtained. Now, he states the seed-syllable of Māyā: "the Goddess" (*devīm*), which is *hrīṃ*.

This means the seed-syllable of Māyā. Next, he states the seed-syllable of Kāma with the words beginning "dakṣiṇa" (the right): the right arm is the letter *ka*, and Śakra is the letter *la*; where there is their "leading," that is, their union, such is Kāma, the Bindu. It is marked by Kāmakalā, which is the letter *ī*. By this, the seed-syllable *klīṃ* is obtained. Regarding the phrase "the upper face at the end of the teeth": the end of the teeth is the letter *ai*.

"Upward-facing" means that there is a *bindu* above the face; by this, the Vāgbhava seed-syllable *ai* is obtained. Regarding "with life": "life" (*jīva*) is the letter *sa*; together with that, one should write the "tooth" (*daśana*), which is the vowel *au*, joined with the "face," which is the *visarga*. The word "seed-syllable" (*bīja*) refers to the five seed-syllables of the aforementioned form: *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiḥ sauḥ*.
The connection is that [the mantra] is "joyful" because it bestows the accomplishment of all aims.

(49) Following the five previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*), he states the syllables to be joined with them, beginning with the words "the first of the Vedas" (*vedādya*): the first of the Vedas is the *praṇava* (Oṃ); *triguṇā* is *māyā* (Hrīṃ); and *ramā* is *śrīṃ*. The connection is that one should utter [these]. Now, [the sequence is]: Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ.

(Its Praise) This is Śrī, the supreme, higher than the highest, the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims; more essential than the essence, the source of origin for all worlds, and auspicious. (49)

She who is the manifest embodiment of Brahman, saluted by hosts of gods and sages, whose nature is bliss, the sole essence of saṃsāra, the mother of the three worlds, and the source of the rise of righteous action—
she is this venerable Brahmavidyā, consisting of all qualities yet devoid of qualities and free from phenomenal expansion.
This knowledge is the primordial of all, bestowing benefit upon the whole, the infinite form of the power of consciousness.
(Its secrecy and praise: Even the sovereignty of an empire, a boon, one's own head, gold, and jewels should be given to a king;
likewise, a son, a friend, a wife, and all one's retinue may be given—or else, she herself must not be given at all.

The Śrīvidyā of sixteen syllables, consisting of all auspicious qualities, is the sole object of worship for the God of gods; she is to be worshipped through all the sacred traditions (āmnāyas), she bestows benefit upon all, and must be guarded with great effort. || 51 ||
(The Ineffable Nature of this [Śrīvidyā]):
Even with thousands of mouths and hundreds of tongues, this sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā can never be fully described. (52)

After the aforementioned seed-syllables *sauḥ*, *oṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*, one should utter the Vidyā of Śambhu’s Kāmarāja-mantra as served by Kāma— namely *ka e ī la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, and *sa ka la hrīṃ*— or else the first Lopāmudrā, namely *ha sa ka la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, and *sa ka la hrīṃ*. This is the syntactic connection.

He speaks again of the application of the seed-syllables (*bījayoga*) with the words "once more" (*punareva*). The connection is as follows: one should utter, in reverse order, the five seed-syllables previously stated in the passage beginning with "the pentad ending with *sa*" and ending with "Ramā"—namely, *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ*—in the sequence *sauḥ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.
(Non-manifestation by *vaikharī* and the other levels of speech): Because it consists of the nature of the expressed object, *vaikharī* is incapable of describing its qualities;
for the reality is beyond syllables (*nirakṣara*), and therein *parā* is the cause.

53–54 | Regarding the statement that her nature is indefinable (*nirupākhyarūpatva*) in the passage beginning with "by thousands of millions of mouths," he states the reason for this with the verse beginning "Vaikharī. Here, the following should be noted: speech is divided into four types—*parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*.
Their essential natures are briefly analyzed here. [This is] in the first chapter of the *Sāradātilaka*, in the section on creation (*sṛṣṭiprakaraṇa*).
Following the description of the creation of objects, at the occasion of defining the creation of sound,
[it is said]: "The omnipresent Kuṇḍalinī, who consists of the Śabda-Brahman and is the Mistress of the Universe, being multiplied by forty-two at the root, brings forth [the phonemes]."
From that [the Absolute] comes Śakti, from that Dhvani, from that Nāda, from that Nirodhikā;
from that comes Ardhendu, from that Bindu, and from that arose Parā.
It is said: "The *paśyantī*, the *madhyamā*, and the *vaikharī* are the birthplace of sound. And thus, Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is the Śabdabrahman, first gives birth to *śakti*;

from that, *dhvani*, and from that, *nāda*, and so forth. In this sequence, the states ending with *bindu* are merely different manifestations of the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*). [These are not detailed here] for fear of making the text too voluminous.
These are explained; however, the details should be sought in the *Sāradātilaka* and its commentary composed by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.

From that *bindu*, there arises the supreme (*parā*) creation of sound, which consists of *nāda*. From that very *parā*, there sequentially arise the threefold creation of sound known as *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. Among these, *parā* is subtle and resides in the *mūlādhāra*.

She is of the nature of pure light. Rising from there, she is the *paśyantī* in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; rising further than that, she is the *madhyamā* in the heart; and rising even further than that, she is the *vaikharī* in the mouth. As these attain increasingly gross forms in succession, the *vaikharī*, reaching the ultimate degree of grossness, generates the manifold expansion of sound (*śabdaprapañca*). And so it is stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
The statement:
"The subtle Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature consists solely of light, resides within the center;
being beyond the range of the ears, she rises upward from there, moving upwards."
Self-luminous Paśyantī becomes dependent upon the Suṣumṇā;
reaching the heart-lotus, she herself becomes Madhyamā, whose form is sound.
Then, from that mere internal discourse, there arises the undivided upward-moving [power];
it resides in the chest, throat, and palate, and is situated in the head, nose, and teeth.
Vaikharī speech, which is grasped by the ear, originates from the root of the tongue and the lips, encompasses all phonemes, and gives rise to the manifold expansion of sound.
Thus, it is also stated in the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*:
"By the impact of the power of one's own will, arising from the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) at the *mūlādhāra*, the supreme sound called *parā* is produced."
That very [vital energy], led upward and expanded within the Svādhiṣṭhāna, attains the name Paśyantī; likewise, it proceeds gradually further upward.
In the *anāhata* [cakra], joined with the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), it is called *madhyamā*;
likewise, impelled upward from those two by that [wind], it reaches the region of the throat in the *viśuddhi* [cakra].
Then, that which is called Vaikharī [arises] from the head, throat, palate, lips, and teeth;
likewise from the root, tip, and back of the tongue, and in sequence from the tip of the nose.
The letters, from the beginning up to the final *kṣa*, have arisen in succession from the throat, palate, lips, and throat-lips, as well as from the teeth and both lips.
The nature of these [phonemes] as "syllables" (akṣara) has been declared based on their beginning with vowels (ādi), their being consonants (kṣānta), and their interval (antara).
Among them, the vowels (svaras) are independent; by means of them, the consonant (vyañjana) is manifested.
Thus (5–10). And so, for all living beings, [the power] consisting of pure light resides in the *mūlādhāra*.

"The wind arising from the *mūlādhāra* receives the names of *prāṇa* and so forth"—as stated in the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Tantrarāja*. By the impact of the Supreme Self’s own will-power (*svecchāśakti*), [it assumes] the nature of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) whose form has been thus described.

It is said that the supreme speech (*parā vāk*), whose essence is sound (*nādātmikā*), has arisen in an exceedingly subtle form; this is its first state. That same supreme speech, whose essence is sound, impelled by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) of the Supreme Self, moving progressively upward, unfolds within the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and, having previously been in a manifest form, assumes the name "Visionary" (*paśyantī*). Impelled by that very same power of will...
Gradually expanding within the *anāhata* lotus, it acquires the name "Madhyamā. Then, likewise impelled by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*),

expanding in turn within the wheel (*cakra*) called *viśuddha* located in the region of the throat, it attains the name "Vaikharī" as it proceeds according to its own will through the head, throat, palate, lips, teeth, and so forth.
By way of connection, she creates the fifty-one phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. With this very intention, Lakṣmaṇācārya also states in the first chapter of the *Sāradā*:
"In this sequence, Kuṇḍalinī creates the garland of phonemes."
Thus it has been said. Now we shall follow the subject at hand. Regarding the term *vaikharī*:
even at the end of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the fourteenth [state] is not to be spoken; rather, there is the sixteenth-syllabled *turīyā*.
She is the supreme reality beyond sound, whose nature is consciousness and knowledge.
For when she has become silent, the *paśyantī* becomes the *madhyamā*. (The Epilogue:
She is the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman, and she bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 54.
Even at the cost of one's life, the sixteen-syllable fourth [mantra] must not be spoken;
it is the supreme reality beyond sound, whose nature is consciousness and knowledge.
(Its status as the source of other vidyās:
From this mantra, thousands of great mantras emerge, just as sparks fly forth from a red-hot iron ball. (56)
(Furthermore, its secret nature: One must die with this knowledge; it should not be given to just anyone. || 57 ||
By the statement to be spoken hereafter, it will be established that this Vidyā has the nature of the consciousness of the fourth state (turya-caitanya);

and because its nature is the consciousness of the fourth state, it transcends sound and is ungraspable by the sense of hearing. For this very reason, it is the "Supreme" (parā) among the aforementioned distinct states of the Śabdabrahman—namely, Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī.

The first state is extremely subtle, residing solely in the *mūlādhāra*, and because it transcends sound, it is inexpressible. But how could *vaikharī*—which has as its object only gross sound that has become the domain of the sense of hearing and which manifests in the *viśuddhi* wheel located in the throat—ever grasp this *parāvidyā*, which dwells in the *mūlādhāra*, far beyond the subtle and the extremely subtle? Thus he says:

—By the passage beginning with "because of being an object of speech" (*vācyabhāvatvāt*), etc. "Because of being an object of speech" means because its nature (*bhāva*)—that is, its existence (*sattā*)—is an object of speech, i.e., a domain of words; the meaning is that it has as its sole object the phonemes (*varṇa*) which are within the range of the senses. The meaning is that *vaikharī* (the manifest speech), in the form previously described, is incapable of describing the qualities of this Vidyā, which has transcended the range of the senses. He states this very point with the passage beginning with "since," etc. Since...
This Vidyā is without syllables, being a reality that transcends the syllable; therefore, the connection is that Vaikharī, which manifests syllables, is incapable of describing its qualities.

If one asks, "Then what is capable? he says, "The Supreme (Parā)," meaning that Parā alone is the cause for describing its qualities, while the other power (Vaikharī) has become mute. Now, by means of the two other powers, Paśyantī and Madhyamā—

To the question, "How is it that her own nature is not perceived? he says: "become mute. By this, it should be understood that according to the reasoning stated previously, even Paśyantī and Madhyamā lack the capacity to describe her qualities. "Madhyamā would be the middle" means [she exists] between Paśyantī and Vaikharī.
(To be given to a worthy disciple: One should bestow the King of Mantras upon a disciple who is endowed with devotion and devoted to truthful speech.
(The sequence for the gift:
Having inscribed it in water, the practitioner [should proceed]. || 58 ||
Having placed his foot upon the head of the disciple according to the sequence of divine conduct,
[he should recite] one hundred thousand, or half that, or one thousand times the "Gajāntaka" mantra.
Having recited the mantra alone in the temple of Śiva, one should reveal it [to others];
this applies to the venerable Tripurasundarī (for there is a fault in reversing the aforementioned sequence).
Otherwise, it will not bestow accomplishment.
(Now, its other divisions:
Now, its other divisions are described according to the system of the Tantra. (In that regard, the sequence:)
From the middle of this, one should then omit either Kāmarāja or Lopāmudrā.
One should cast all the vidyās of the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra in their proper sequence;
then, all the divisions become the sixteenth [digit], which is the fourth state (turīyā). || 62 ||

Because she is present, the middle energy (madhyamā)—who stands in the middle and is named "the Middle"—has also become mute in the description of her qualities; such is the connection. Let this suffice for the detailed exposition.
