Having thus stated the division of the sixteen-syllable mantra with the words beginning "ending with *sa* and *ta*, joined with the seventh preceded by *śiva*," etc., [the author proceeds].

It was stated that "thousands of great mantras emerge from this mantra"; now, [the author] shows some of those very mantras, beginning with "from the middle of this" (*asyā madhyāt*) and so forth. Thus, one should pronounce the letters as before—those shown by the passage beginning with "ending with *sa* and *nta*" (*sāntāntam*)—recited in direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*viloma*) order at the beginning and end. This is the Nirukta-Śāmbhava-Kāmarāja.

Having omitted Lopāmudrā from the middle, one should sequentially insert all the *vidyās* taught therein in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra*, as previously shown. In this way, through the conjunction of those respective mantras with these seed-syllables (*bījas*), each individual *vidyā* is formed. (In that regard, the knowledge of even a single one of them brings about the state of Śiva.)
Having known any one of these, nothing further remains to be known;
he is the Lord, there is no difference—this is the truth, the absolute truth, firmly established. (63)
(The excellence of power produced in the practitioner through the repeated practice of this mantra:
Poison becomes non-poisonous; he certainly paralyzes water.
He turns the world into water, and he turns water into the world. 64.
One may turn fire into water and cause water to become fire;
through firm practice, one effects all such reversals—of this there is no doubt. (65)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 13 ||
The Fourteenth Illumination:
Morning Duties; therein, the exposition on the venerable Guru, the mantra, the nine Kulanāthas, the Guru-maṇḍala, and so forth.
(The Descent of the Worship of Śrīmat Tripurā): She who is the great manifestation of eternal bliss, whose face is smiling, whose three eyes are flickering,
who is beautiful with the glow of vermilion like the rising sun as her body-unguent, and who is the wish-fulfilling tree for devotees alone.
Having bowed to that supreme Tripurā, who is manifested in the lap of Paraśiva, [the author] performs the pure worship of her lotus feet with the breast of full-blown bliss. || 1 ||
(The Morning Duties; therein, meditation on the venerable Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus:

In the thousand-petaled lotus, [one should meditate on] the venerable Guru, radiant as the full moon, with hands like lotuses in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, embraced by his own lineage.
One should remember the Guru, whose face and eyes are serene, who embodies the form of all deities, seated upon a swan at the crown of the head, while first uttering his name.

(The worship of the Guru and Śakti, and the recitation of their mantras: At dawn, according to the prescribed order, one should worship the Guru, the Deva, and the Śakti, seated in the lotus posture, while contemplating them as Śiva and Śivā.

1. Having thus concluded this chapter with the preceding section by defining the *Śrī Tripurasundarī-vidyā*, the author, intending to describe the morning rites (*prātaḥkṛtya*) and so forth in this present chapter, first introduces the exposition of the ritual worship (*saparyā*), preceded by a salutation to the Goddess, beginning with the words "Nityānanda... and so on.

2. He describes the nature of the meditation on the venerable Guru with the words "sahasra" (a thousand), etc. Its explanation, however, is to be understood by looking at the commentary on the first verse of the work beginning with "daśaśatadalapadme" (in the lotus of a thousand petals). "By one's own lineage" means by one's own power. 3. Regarding the word "prātaḥ" (in the morning): this term should also be applied to the preceding verse; [it refers to] in the morning, upon the head.
Having worshipped with various kinds of ritual implements and other offerings, the practitioner of mantra should mentally recite that supreme mantra three times.

Having written the word *hasauḥ*, one should recite three times the syllables *ha*, *sa*, *kṣa*, *ma*, *la*, *va*, and *ya* joined with fire (*ra*), each preceded by the three long vowels of the east (*ā*, *ī*, *ū*). (4)
[One should place] the syllable joined with bindu, nāda, and kalā at the end of "Śrīparā," and then the word "pāraka," followed by the word "sarvārādhyapada" and then the word "sarvamūrdhapada. (5)
At the end of "Nātha Sarvaguru," the word "Guru" itself [is added], and then "Guru";
at the end of the word "Śrī Gurunātha," one adds the syllables sa, ha, kṣa, ma, la, va, and anila (ya).
One should write the first [syllable] joined with the long sound of the letter *ra*, endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*; then one should write the fourth [syllable].
Based on such observations as "the Guru, who has two eyes and two arms, upon a white lotus," [it is said]: "Guru, Deva, and Śakti" means the Guru, the Deva, and the Śakti.
"Abhirūpataḥ" means in their respective forms—that is, the Guru and Deva-Śakti, whose nature is Śiva and Śivā—[they are to be worshipped] with various kinds of implements and mental offerings;
this is the connection with the word "having fully worshipped."

5–9 | In the preceding statement, it was said that one should mentally recite "that supreme mantra" (*tan-manu-vara*). He now states that very mantra, beginning with *hasau* and ending with *gurormanuḥ*. First, one should write the word *hasau*; then, *ha sa kṣa ma la vānilān*. *Anila* is the seed-syllable of wind, the letter *ya*. By this, *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya* is obtained. [The phrase] *vahniyuktān* means joined with fire (*vahnī*).

The letter *ra* is joined with those; by this, *ha*, *sa*, *kṣa*, *ma*, *la*, *va*, *ya*, and *ra* are obtained. Furthermore, they are "endowed with the three preceding long vowels," meaning they are joined with the three preceding long vowels—the second, fourth, and sixth vowels—subsequently, at the final delimitation.
By this, the conjunction of the long vowels with the letter *ra* itself is stated. Likewise, they are endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.

The meaning is that one should divide the letters from *ha* to *ra* into three groups by sequentially distributing them according to the three types of long vowels mentioned in the etymology (*nirukta*).

Thus, the sequence results in: *hsauḥ*, *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rāṃ*, *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rīṃ*, and ending with *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rūṃ*. Regarding the phrase "at the end of Śrīparā": after "Śrīparā" at the end [of the mantra], the subsequent part is "pārakaṃ," which means "the supreme itself."

Regarding *pārakam*: although one should have said *para* here, the suffixes *aṇ* and *ka* are applied in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*) for the sake of metrical requirements (*chando'nurodhāt*). By this, *śrīparāpara* is obtained. Then [one writes] *sarvārādhyā*, and then *sarvamūrdhvanātha*;
thereafter, one should write the third and the second [names] as before.
The practitioner should again write the first [syllable] at the end of the venerable Śambhu-guru.
The fourth letter of the first peak-syllable, again the first, and the third—
this mantra of the Guru is adorned with forty serpent-colors.
(Another mantra of the Śrīguru:
Alternatively, one should extract the Vāgbhava, Māyā, and Lakṣmī-bījas;
namely, *ha sa kha phreṃ*, and likewise the one called Ānandabhairava, which is *sa ha kha phreṃ*.
One should remember the name of the Guru, as well as the name of the Śakti, and the Śrīpādukā.

The meaning is that immediately after saying "sarvaguru," one should say "gurusvayaṃguruśrīgurunātha. "Saha" refers to the letter *repha* (the letter *ra*). "Dīrghaśruti" means the third vowel among the long vowels, which is *u*. Thus, "endowed with *dīrghaśruti*" means joined with the letter *ra*. Likewise, they are "endowed with *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*"; by this, the syllable *rūṃ* is obtained. In its collective form (*samaṣṭi*), however, it is: *sa ha kṣa ma la va ya rūṃ*.
Thus it is obtained. Having formed a cluster (*piṇḍīkṛta*), one should write the first [syllable] in its collective form; by this, *hsauḥ* is obtained. Then, the fourth:

*ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rūṃ*; the third: *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rīṃ*; and the second: *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rāṃ*, which should be written as before. Then, after "the venerable Śambhu-guru" (*śrīśambhugurvante*), that is, immediately following "the venerable Śambhu-guru" (*śrīśambhuguv*):
The meaning is that one should again write the first [syllable] as *hasauḥ*. This reading appears to be erroneous. Regarding "the first":

it refers to the first *kūṭa*, *hasauḥ*; its fourth [letter] is *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rūṃ*. One should again write the first as *hasauḥ*. "The third" is in relation to the first *kūṭa*. Consequently, one should write *ha sa kṣa ma la va ya rīṃ*; this is the mantra of the venerable Guru.

This mantra is presented in its entirety: Hsauḥ Ha Sa Kṣa Ma La Va Ya Rāṃ | Ha Sa Kṣa Ma La Va Ya Rīṃ | Ha Sa Kṣa Ma La Va Ya Rūṃ | Śrī Parāpara Sarvārādhyasarvamūrdhanātha Sarvaguru Guru Svayaṃguru Śrīgurunātha Sa Ha Kṣa Ma La Va Ya Rūṃ | Hsauḥ Ha Sa Kṣa Ma La Va Ya Rūṃ ||

HA SA KṢA MA LA VA YA RĪṂ HA SA KṢA MA LA VA YA RĀṂ ŚRĪŚAMBHU (MAD) GURU HSAUḤ HA SA KṢA MA LA VA YA RŪṂ HSAUḤ HA SA KṢA MA LA VA YA RĪṂ. This is the Śrīgurumantra. The same authority is seen in the first chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, following the determination of the number of syllables in the mantra.

He concludes: "Forty. The meaning is that the nine *kūṭas* beginning with *hasakṣa*, being each a single syllable according to their respective *kūṭa*-nature, yield nine syllables; these, together with the other thirty-nine letters beginning with *hasau*, constitute this *gurumantra* consisting of forty-eight syllables in total.
10. He states another mantra, which was previously summarized, beginning with "Alternatively" (*athavā*) and so forth. *Vāgbhava* is *aiṃ*; *Māyā* is *hrīṃ*.
(The number of recitations for the aforementioned guru-mantra.)
The wise practitioner should recite this ten times, seven times, or even three times.
(The Offering of Recitation:
The mantra-practitioner should offer the recitation into the right hand of the venerable Guru. 11.
(On the necessity of reciting the *Śrīgurustotra* in the morning:
One should daily praise Him with these five verses for the attainment of all perfections;
by chanting them at the time of awakening in the morning, the day shall become auspicious. (12)
(Śrīgurustutiḥ) Salutations to you, O Lord, O Blessed One, Śiva in the form of the Guru,
who has assumed manifold forms for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of the descent of knowledge. (13)
Salutations to the one whose nature is Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is the Supreme Self, who is the sun that dispels the darkness of all ignorance, and who is the essence of consciousness. (2) 14.

To the independent one, whose form is fashioned by compassion, who is the essence of Śiva, and who bestows auspiciousness upon devoted and fortunate beings both in this world and the next. (3) || 15 ||

The seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is *śrīṃ*. Thus, one should first extract the triad of seed-syllables: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. Then [the syllables] *ha sa kha phreṃ*. And then the mantra of Ānandabhairava, known as Ānandabhairava, which is *ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yūṃ*;
this is the Ānandabhairava-mantra. Then [the sequence]: *sa ha kha phreṃ ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yūṃ*.

(To Ānandabhairava, vauṣaṭ) Sa ha kha phreṃ. The mantra concludes as: "I remember (or I worship) the venerable [Name]ānandanātha, the venerable [Name]īdevyambā, and the venerable pādukā. In this context, it is taught that the Guru ends with the title ānandanātha, while the Śakti ends with the title ambā.

Thus, from the observation of the statement in the seventh chapter of the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*, by the phrase "the name of the Guru and the name of the Śakti," one should understand that the names of the venerable Guru and his Śakti,
ending in *-ānandanātha* and *-ambā* respectively, are to be taken. "For the sake of discernment for the discerning, and for the sake of reflective inquiry for those who possess such inquiry..."
To the illuminator of luminaries, to the one whose form is knowledge for the wise. (4) || 16 ||
In front, at the sides, behind, above, and below, always with a virtuous state of mind, perform the service of your servitude. (5) 17.
(Śrīguru-namaskāraḥ) Having offered praises, one should then pay obeisance with this mantra: || 18 ||
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge. 19.
O Lord, by your grace I have accomplished my purpose in every respect;
I am liberated from the great noose of illusion and death, and I am Śiva.
(Description of the place for meditating on the Kulanātha [the venerable Guru]:
Thereafter, one should contemplate the Kulanāthas above the mouth of the Kula. || 21 ||
(Declaration of the exposition on the Kulanāthas and their worship) I shall proclaim the Kulanāthas, who assume the form of Śiva,
as well as their worship, which serves as a staircase for the descent of the Vidyā. 22.
21. Having thus described [the practice] ending with the salutation to the venerable Guru, he teaches the contemplation of the Kulanātha with the words beginning with "tataḥ" (then).
One should contemplate the Kulanāthas, who are the venerable Gurus. To the question "Where?", he says: "of the mouth of the Kula.
Here, by the word *kula*, the *suṣumnā* channel is meant, which is the path for the Kulakuṇḍalinī to travel to the *sahasrāra*; its "mouth" is below the *sahasrāra*.
The meaning is that one should contemplate the Kulanāthas above that, in the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*). As it is said in the *Pādukāpañcaka*:
"There, at the lotus-feet of the Lord, which are dripping with the honey-essence of saffron and wine..."
"His mind, cool as the nectar of the moon and the abode of auspiciousness, remembers the couple.
(22) Now, in response to the inquiry, "Who indeed are these so-called Kulanāthas?", he says: "The Kulanāthas," and so forth. (p. 415) (The description of the three divine Kulanāthas.)
"Furthermore, I am designated by different names in the world—such as 'Light,' 'Reflective Awareness,' and 'Bliss'—due to my divine form. (23)
(An Exposition of the Three Lords of the Siddha Family) From them three were born, and they are indeed those three Siddhas: Jñāna, Satya, and Pūrṇa; these are proclaimed as the [three] Śrīmukhas.
"Those who have assumed the form of Śiva" means those by whom the form—the essential nature—of Śiva, that is, Paramaśiva, is assumed.

By this, their state of being the very form of Śiva and their possession of an eternal body are stated. This is explicitly declared in the first chapter of the *Tantrarāja*: "Now I shall proclaim the Lords, who are my own forms and possess eternal bodies."

"Vidyāvatāra" means the descent (*avatāra*) of *vidyā*, that is, the descent of the *tantra-vidyā* which serves as a ladder. The essential meaning is that the Blessed Lord, Paramaśiva himself, having descended in the form of various *kulanāthas*, teaches all the *tantras* without exception. "In that same way, their worship":
the connection is that I shall explain the worship of those *kulanāthas*, just as [the descent was explained].

23. The Lords of the Family (*kulanātha*) are of three kinds: celestial (*divya*), perfected (*siddha*), and terrestrial (*bhauma*). Among these, he first describes the celestial ones with the words beginning "prakāśa" (light). I am Paramaśiva, whose nature is the fullness of *ahantā* (I-consciousness); the meaning is that, by means of the distinction of names—namely, the threefold distinction of the names light (*prakāśa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and bliss (*ānanda*)—I conceive of myself as having a celestial form, thinking "I am."

The remainder [is as follows]. Thus, because the primordial source, Paramaśiva, consists of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and bliss (*ānanda*), the three Lords (*nāthatraya*), who are his transformations (*vikṛti*), likewise possess those respective natures. By the phrase "by virtue of their divine form," their status as divine gurus is stated. This is explicitly declared in the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
Having indeed become a Guru, the Blessed One bestows the Great Vidyā;
that divine Guru, the Rishi, then reveals the divine knowledge.
O Pārvatī, listen now as I shall describe the disciples of Divyaugha-nātha:
there is Prakāśa, then Vimarśa, another, and also Ānanda.
"By means of my divine form, I manifest in the world under various names," and so forth.
(24) Having thus described the divine Kulanāthas, he speaks of the Siddhas with the words beginning "the three.
The meaning is that from those aforementioned divine [beings], such as Prakaśa and the others, three have arisen; these very ones are the Siddhas. Their designations are as follows:

He says [this] with the words beginning "jñāna" and so forth. Thus, it is established that these three—Jñāna, Satya, and Pūrṇa—are the Lords of the Kula (kulanātha), designated as Siddhas, who have arisen from the previously mentioned divine gurus. He qualifies them: "śrīmukhāḥ," meaning those preceded by the word "Śrī."
The divine Siddhas dwell eternally in the sky, and they also reside here upon the earth.
From them, the three Lords of the other families arise; thus, the three born from them likewise dwell there. (25)
(The three Lords of the Bhauma-kula):
By name they are Svabhāva, Pratibha, and likewise Subhaga;
being of the nature of Śiva, they dwell eternally upon the earth alone. (26)
(On the promulgation of the Tantra scriptures by the lords of the Nirukta lineage:
By these nine, who were non-different from Kadi and the other Śaktis, the Tantra was established in the world with its glory made manifest during the Kṛta Yuga. (27)
(Their form:

These [deities] have two eyes and two arms, endowed with graceful postures; they have serene faces, are smiling, and are equipped with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 28 ||

25. Now, he explains their abode with the words beginning with "divyāḥ" (the divine ones). In that context, the *divyāḥ*—who are of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), reflective awareness (*vimarṣa*), and bliss (*ānanda*), eternal, possessing eternal forms, and the Lords of the Kula—dwell in the *kha*, which is the void existing within the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
Here, in the passage of identical sequence found in both the first chapter of the *Tantrarāja* and the twenty-sixth chapter on the Gandharvas, [it says] "divyāḥ"...
The reading "nityam madantike" (always in my presence) is observed. He states the abode of the Siddhas with the words beginning "siddhāḥ":
the Siddhas, whose selves are full of knowledge and truth, dwell both here on earth and elsewhere. Now he speaks of the terrestrial Kulanāthas.
From those aforementioned Siddhas, three who are about to be described have arisen.

26. Now, as to what their names are, he says "svabhāva" and so forth. There are three Lords of the Kula (kulanātha) named Svabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga; the meaning is that they always reside on earth alone and nowhere else.
These three as well are of the nature of Śiva, being indeed identical with the essence of Śiva.
27. He states their status as initiators of the tantra with the words beginning "by these" (*etair*). By the nine Kulanāthas previously mentioned.
(Regarding their venerability: Such individuals are indeed to be venerated during worship within their respective maṇḍalas and so forth.
By her command, the goddesses, possessing divine forms, reside within the Śrīcakra.
All those [deities] whose names begin with three syllables are endowed with bliss;
they end in the term "Nātha" within their own mandalas, while in the [central] mandala they end in "Śakti."

(On the accomplishment of the nine-syllabled nature of the previously mentioned mantras: Likewise, Māyā, Lakṣmī, and the others became known as the nine syllables for the worship of the nine Śaktis and the [nine] deities. (31)

29. Regarding the phrase "in their respective maṇḍalas and so forth": the *maṇḍala* will be explained further on. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one's own head and other parts are also included. 30. Now, concerning the worship of the aforementioned nine Lords (*nātha*) in their respective *maṇḍalas*:

He defines the nine-syllable mantras with the verse beginning "tryakṣara" and so forth. Here, this should be noted: taking those nine Kulanāthas consisting of three syllables which were previously shown in the passage beginning "prakāśa, atha vimarṣa, anya," one should append the word "ānanda" (bliss) to the end of each and every one of them. By this means, they take forms such as *prakāśānanda*, *vimarṣānanda*, and so on.

The mantras consist of five syllables. Regarding the phrase "in their own maṇḍalas": in the maṇḍalas that will be described, those Lords (nātha) ending in [the word] *nātha*—if they end in two syllables, such as *prakāśānandanātha* and *vimarṣānandanātha*—then they become seven-syllable [mantras]. To demonstrate the nine-syllable [mantra] of Kulanātha and Śakti, he says: "ending in Śakti" (*śaktyantā*). These...

If the five-syllabled [mantras] end with Śakti, or if they end with the two syllables "Śakti," then likewise, by way of *prakāśānanda-śakti* and *vimarṣānanda-śakti*, there are seven-syllabled Kula-śakti mantras.
(31) He establishes their nine-syllabled nature with the words beginning with "māyā": those seven-syllabled [mantras] end with Nātha or end with Śakti.

Or [the syllables] such as *māyā* (hrīṃ) and *lakṣmī* (śrīṃ); that is, if the two seed-syllables *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* are joined before [the names] such as *Prakāśānandanātha* or *Prakāśānandaśakti*, then they become mantras known as "nine-syllabled" (*navārṇa*). With this intention, he says: "In that way, they became known as nine-syllabled."
And thus: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Prakāśānandanātha;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vimarṣānandanātha.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ānandānandanāthaḥ. (By the union of seven syllables, the aforementioned nine-syllable mantra becomes sixteen syllables.
This is the Vidyā that brings satisfaction to all and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
With that seven-syllabled mantra, the practitioner of mantras should perform worship preceded by the [deity's] name.
(The Seven-Syllable Mantra):
*Javī* joined with *marut*, and *gotrā* conjoined with *dharā*;
*prāṇa* also joined with *marut*, and the third [syllable] should be with *kha*. (33)
Again, *ja* is swift, endowed with the earth (*kṣmā*), and the bowstring (*jyā*) is accompanied by the wind (*vāta*).
The sixth [element] is the sky pervaded by the friend of the wind (fire), and fire is the seventh syllable. (34)
(Conclusion) Thus has the seven-syllabled mantra been declared, which bestows accomplishment within the Śakti-tantras. 35.
In this manner, nine-syllable mantras with ever-new phonemes are to be inferred. Their application within the mandala, however, will be demonstrated in its specific sequence [verse 32].
Now, regarding this nine-syllable mantra through its connection with the seven-syllable mantra to be described hereafter:
He introduces [the mantra] beginning with "The Vidyā... (verse 33–35) in order to accomplish its sixteen-syllable nature.
In the previous statement, it was said, "by that seven-syllabled one. He states that very seven-syllabled mantra with the words beginning with "javī" (swift).
*Javī* is the syllable *pa*; and that is "endowed with Marut," meaning joined with the letter *ā*. By this, *pā* is obtained. Regarding "gotrā"—
The cave (grotā) is the letter *da*, and it is joined with the earth (*dharā*), which is the letter *u*; by this, *du* is obtained. Regarding "vital breath" (*prāṇa*):

the vital breath is the letter *ka*, and it is joined with the wind (*marut*), which is the letter *ā*, with the seed-syllable of space (*nabhas*) which is *kha*, and with the drop (*bindu*) in the form of *ma*; by this, *kāṃ* is obtained. "The third" means the third syllable of the mantra. Again, "swift" (*javī*) is the letter *pa*, [joined] with the earth (*kṣmā*).

It is endowed with the vowel *ū*. By this, *pū* is obtained. *Jyā* is the letter *ja*, and that is joined with the wind (*vāta*), which is the vowel *ā*. By this, *ja* is obtained. Regarding "pervaded" (*vyāptam*): the pervader is the letter *ya*; the wind is as before, the vowel *ā*. By this, *yā* is obtained.
*Nabhaḥ* (the sky) is, as before, the letter *ma*; fire is the vowel *i*. By this, *mi* is obtained. Regarding "the seventh syllable": this refers to the mantra.

The meaning is that it consists of seven syllables. "In this way" means that [the mantra] "I worship the sandals" (*pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*) consists of seven syllables. The two statements beginning with *javī* and ending with *saptamākṣaram* are found in the *Tantrarāja* (p.
419) as the union of the two mantras.
One should join that [mantra] with the names of all the powers and deities preceded by their respective names, according to the common rules for success.
(The distinction regarding tantras other than Śakti-tantra:
In tantras external to the Śakti-tantras, there is recollection by means of the mind. || 37 ||
(When the nine-syllable and seven-syllable [mantras] are joined, they become sixteen syllables):
There are nine names for the nine [deities], each consisting of nine syllables;
through their conjunction with the seven-syllable [mantra], each becomes sixteen syllables.
(Regarding the nature of those sixteen syllables as the sixteen Nityās:
Those sixteen forms of the Nityās have arisen in their proper sequence. (38)
(The time for the worship of the maṇḍala of the gurus:
One should perform the worship of the maṇḍala of the gurus on the seven festival days.
(Regarding the specific names on the full-moon festival days:)
Having written the sixteen-syllable names during the full [moon] phases, one should worship them. || 39 ||
But on the other six festival days (*parva*), one should write down only the nine syllables.
(In the worship of both [the two forms], there is no difference in the mantra.
On each of those occasions, the wise person should perform the worship while reciting the seven-syllable mantra.
The same form is also seen in the first chapter. This very method for extracting the mantra was also demonstrated by its commentator, Subhagānandanātha.
(36) When the aforementioned nine-syllable mantra is joined with the stated seven-syllable mantra, the resulting mantra consists of sixteen syllables.

In order to demonstrate that [this] is so, he says "of all," and so forth. "Of all" means of the nine powers previously mentioned. "Of the deities" means of the lords (nātha). "By names" means by such names as Ānandaśakti, Ānandanātha, and so on.
The meaning is that one should join that aforementioned seven-syllable mantra preceded by the names, beginning with the names *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarṣa* (reflective awareness).
"As in the case of the common [elements]" means that one should join them—such as light (*prakāśa*) and the rest—as previously described, just as Ānandanātha has done.
(The fact that the worship of the *gurumaṇḍala* is accomplished by means of nine offerings:
In all worship of the *gurumaṇḍala*, nine [offerings] are prescribed.
Therefore, one should worship them with those ritual services; listen to those as well. (41)
(Resolution of the Ninefold Worship): Fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, food offering, betel, water for sipping, hymn, and the self-nature—these are declared [to be the ninefold worship]. (42)
(The Basis for the Construction of the Guru-maṇḍala) One of clear intellect should construct the guru-maṇḍala upon a pedestal,
or on a wooden plank, or even on a ground that is perfectly pure, level, and stable. (43)
(Resolution on the Materials for Constructing the Mandala) One should fashion the construction of the Guru-maṇḍala everywhere using pastes composed of red sandalwood, saffron, and light musk. (44)
(To be performed at the conclusion of the maṇḍala worship:
Having wiped [the face] at the end of the worship, one should apply [the remains] to the forehead, the chest, and both shoulders;
for him, Lakṣmī will be present everywhere and difficult for all others to attain. 45.
One should lay down ten threads—east-west and north-south—with intervals of five finger-breadths between them; these should be joined to form squares.
The mandala is square and consists of eighty-one sections.

46–47. Now, he teaches the construction of the *gurumaṇḍala* with the words beginning with "first" (*prāk*). One should cast ten lines from east to west, and likewise ten lines from south to north. The casting of these lines should be done with an interval of five finger-breadths (*pañcāṅgula*) between them. When this has been done, there arises a mandala consisting of eighty-one squares (*pada*) with intervals of five finger-breadths.

It is as follows: it should also be noted by the wise that this mandala consists of forty-five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), being composed of nine-by-nine square cells with an interval of five finger-breadths on all sides.
In the very center of all that is the first [square], and the second is situated directly in front of it.
And one should write the third [syllable] in the third [square], and likewise in all nine of the nine squares.
In this way, at all the festival occasions (parvan), one should perform the mandala endowed with ever-new [offerings]. || 49 ||
Having divided the ninefold [grid] into nine parts by applying two threads across the center,
one should write the nine syllables of the name within them and worship them in sequence.
48–49 | He describes the sequential arrangement of the Kulanāthas within this mandala with the words beginning with "tat" (that), etc.

The meaning is that in the center of all that—that is, in the middle of all those nine groups—one should write the first Kulanātha as previously specified, namely in the form "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Prakāśānandanātha," within the first group of nine. In front of that [is] his...

In the center of the nine-squares [grid] situated in front—that is, located in the eastern direction—one should write the second [syllable], *hrīṃ śrīṃ Vimarṣānandanātha*, within that nine-square section consisting of nine cells. And "the third": in the third [section], the southeastern nine-squares, one should write the third [syllable], *hrīṃ śrīṃ Vimarṣānandanātha*, in that same form. And "the third": in the third, the southeastern nine-squares...
One should write the third Kulanātha in the form "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ānandānandanātha.
In this very sequence, by way of circumambulation, one should write the other Kulanāthas in the other groups of nine as well.
By this, in the southern group of nine, [one writes] "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrījñānānandanātha," and in the south-western group of nine, "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ..."

One should write Śrī Satyānandanātha in the western group of nine; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha in the northwestern group of nine; likewise, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Svabhāvānandanātha in the northern group of nine; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Pratibhānandanātha in the northeastern group of nine; and Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Subhagānandanātha in the [eastern] group of nine—this is how it should be understood. The sacred joints (parvan) will be described further on.

50. Now, he teaches the ninefold division of the mandala with the words beginning "navakam" (the group of nine). "In the middle" means in the center of the mandala, having set aside three squares on each side. "By the laying down of two lines" means by the laying down of two lines—one extending from east to west and one extending from south to north—having thus divided [the area] into nine as a group of nine.
The Connection: Regarding those groups of nine, he explains the sequence for the arrangement of the ocean of the names of the nine lords with the words "In those...
In those groups of nine, one should worship after having inscribed the group of nine letters of the names according to the very order previously mentioned. This is what is meant:
first, in the center of the central group of nine, [one places] the first syllable of the nine-syllable mantra "hrīṃ śrīṃ prakāśānandanātha."

One should write: in the first square, the second syllable, *śrī*; in the third, the southeast, the third syllable, *pre*; in the fourth, the south, the fourth syllable, *ke*; in the fifth, the southwest, the fifth syllable, *śe*; in the sixth, the west, the sixth syllable, *ne*; in the seventh, the northwest, the seventh syllable, *ndai*; and in the eighth, the eighth syllable, *ne*.

"In the ninth [square], write the ninth syllable, *the*. And thus, in the central group of nine, one should write the nine syllables—*hrīṃ śrīṃ pra kā śā na nda nā*—one by one, starting from the center and proceeding clockwise. This is the procedure for the central group of nine.
In the same way, the application of the remaining eight Nāthas in the other eight squares is to be inferred by the wise.

To make it clearly understood, the illustration of the Guru-maṇḍala is shown: (p. 422) On the full moon day, having laid down three lines each in the center of that [space], and having thus formed sixteen [squares], one should indeed write those names within them.

Now, for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the previously mentioned sixteen-syllable Lord of the Family (*kulanātha*), [there is] a group of nine.
To achieve the perfection of sixteen squares, he states a specific detail regarding the mandala of eighty-one squares as defined by etymology, beginning with the words "pūrṇa" and so forth.

Here, however, within that previously mentioned group of nine, one should lay down three lines on both sides to form sixteen squares; the remainder of the instruction is that this is done by laying down three lines on each side. Within those very sixteen square compartments, those sixteen syllables are the names.
The meaning is that one should draw [the lines].

This is what is intended: in the center of the middle square among the nine squares of the previously mentioned *gurumaṇḍala*, one should draw three lines extending east-west and three lines extending north-south, each individually spanning three sets of nine squares.

They are to be drawn. When this is done, all the groups of nine become composed of sixteen squares. It is with this very intention that the phrase "having made [them] sixteenfold" (*ṣoḍaśīkṛtya*) was stated. Regarding the word "should write" (*likhet*): the meaning is that one should write there the names in the forms previously shown, such as *hrīṃ śrīṃ prakāśānandanāthapādakān pūjayāmi*, and so forth. Here, within the sixteen squares...

It should be understood that one should write one letter per square according to the rule for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sixteen letters of the name. As for the writing itself, it must proceed clockwise, as no specific direction has been stated; furthermore, since the rule for the placement of letters was previously described starting from the central square in the aforementioned maṇḍala, it should be noted here as well that one begins first with the group of four central squares and then proceeds to the outer squares.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the passage beginning with "pūrṇā" (the full) from the second chapter of the *Tantrarāja*, which possesses the same sequence [of words], Subhagānandanātha has stated that starting from the square situated below the left within the central group of four, one should proceed clockwise through the central group of four, and likewise proceed externally according to the aforementioned order. This refers here to the Kulanāthas.
And the arrangement of the letters of its name is shown by the second [diagram], the Guru-maṇḍala-citra:

(On the necessity of performing worship for the Guru, whether living or deceased, according to this sequence:
Thus, worship is prescribed for the Guru both while he is living and when he has passed away;
having formed a mandala of the [sacred] sites, worship and drawing [the deity] therein are considered appropriate.
(The fruit of worship performed according to the sequence of etymological derivation:
Thus, the wise person who, being attentive, worships the Lords on the sacred festival days—he becomes an excellent teacher and an adept; therefore, the attainment of the Vidyā is supreme. 53.
(The fault in the opposite case:
Otherwise, the attainment of both results in certain misfortune;
there will be suffering from disease, weapons, and the like, or death in a desolate place due to exhaustion. (54)
Furthermore, there is the attainment of such calamities as these, and death by the king's sword;
therefore, one should act according to the stated sequence alone for the sake of accomplishing all goals. (55)
(The Seven Parvas: The day of the Guru’s birth, likewise the day he attained knowledge, one's own birthday, or even the day of [the Guru's] spiritual pervasion (vyāpti). || 56 ||

52. Whether the Guru is living or deceased, this very sequence for the worship of the *guru-maṇḍala* remains the same; thus he says "worship in this manner" and so forth. However, regarding the worship of the *maṇḍala* when the Guru has passed away, he states the specific detail concerning that particular portion with the words "the locations" and so forth.

Therein, "having made the locations into a *maṇḍala*" means having drawn them in the form of a circle (*vṛtta*). Within that *maṇḍala* thus formed into a circle, "arcā" refers to the drawing [of the deities].

The worship consists of the writing of the syllables of the mantra; this is the meaning according to the [author's] view. (54) He states the fault in deviating from the sequence previously described for the worship of the mandala and so forth, with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).

The sense is that if performed otherwise—that is, by reversing the stated sequence—the attainment of both the teacher and the disciple leads to misfortune (*anarthāya*). [He now describes] those very misfortunes...
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "vyādhi" and so forth: (p.
425) "The day of the conjunction of the three syllables is the full-moon day; likewise, there are six distinguished parvas, making seven parvas including the new moon. (57)
(In this regard, the necessity of performing worship:
One should perform worship during these [periods], whether for a month or even for a year. || 58 ||
(In this regard, there is a distinction:

While the Guru is alive, one should always worship his son and so forth when he is occupied [with other duties], treating him as equal to the Guru himself and attending to him with prostrations and other services.
(In the event of the absence of the Guru, his son, and so forth, what should be done:
In their absence, one should worship someone of that lineage or someone instructed by them.
(The conclusion.)
In this context, the worship maṇḍala for the groups of lords has been described.

(Then, the arousal of Kuṇḍalinī: From the four-petalled Mūlādhāra, one should lead the Supreme [Kuṇḍalinī], radiant as a flash of lightning, subtle like the fiber of a lotus stalk, by means of the Haṃsa to the abode of liberation.
Having led [the deity] by means of the great, eternal Brahma-mantra, one should thereafter worship the single form of the Great Soul;
then, recollecting "I am He," one should pray at the root-lotus, which consists of nectar. || 61 ||

56–57. It was previously stated that the mandala, endowed with ever-new [elements], is [to be established] on all *parvan* days; he now points out those very *parvan* days by means of the passage beginning with "of the Guru" (*guror*). The day of obtaining the *vidyā* is the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

The day of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the day of the death of the Guru—this is the ellipsis. Regarding "the day of the conjunction of three syllables," this refers to two syllables of the [consonant] groups (*varga*).

Subhagānandanātha, in his commentary on the second chapter of the *Tantrarāja*, states that the day on which the three syllables—the *ghaṭikākṣara* and the other two—converge is called the "day of the conjunction of the three syllables" (*akṣaratrayasaṃpāta*). As for the specific nature of the syllables of the classes (*vargākṣara*) and so forth, it has been explained in detail in the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity.

58. Regarding "month by month": the connection is that one should perform worship every month; in the absence of that possibility, one should do so every year on these occasions, such as the day of the Guru's birth and so forth.
61. Regarding "the *mūlādhāra*": the meaning is this—having led her [to that state] in the sixth chapter...
This has been explained by us in detail in the commentary on the verse beginning with *kulakuṇḍalīm*, which sets forth the sequence for the arousal of Kuṇḍalinī.
(p. 426) [The casting of the foot from the bed onto the ground.]
One who knows the ritual procedure should leave the bed at dawn,
stepping upon the ground according to the sequence of the directions while contemplating the mantra spoken by Śiva.
It dispels all the faults of people. || 62 ||
(The mantra of supplication therein:
Oṃ! O Mother, whose girdle is the ocean and whose breasts are the mountain ranges;
O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you! Forgive my touch of your feet. (63)
(Instruction on placing the foot upon the ground with the Nirukta mantra: With this mantra, the practitioner should set his foot down upon the ground. (Beholding and bowing to the family trees.)
Then, having observed the family trees, one should pay homage to them unobserved.

64. Regarding "the family trees" (*kulavṛkṣān*): he states the family trees in the eleventh chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*: "The *śleṣmātaka*, the one called *karañja*, the *nimba*, the *aśvattha*, the *kadambaka*, the *bilva*, the *vaṭa*, the *udumbara*, and the *tintiḍī* is remembered as the ninth. Thus it is said.
Also, in the second chapter of the *Kaulāvalī-nirṇaya*:
"When a true practitioner has gone outside and sees a Kula-tree,
he should diligently pay homage to the Kula as well as the Lord of the Kula."
The aśoka, keśara, karṇikāra, and likewise the tila;
the nameru, the piyāla, and the sindhuvāraka and kadambaka.
"Maruvaka, the Campaka tree, and twelve family trees. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, another method in accordance with the previously mentioned *Kulārṇava* is stated in that very same work:
"Alternatively, I shall describe the family trees for the sake of perfect accomplishment."
"Śleṣmātaka, karañja, nimba, aśvattha, kadambaka, bilva, vaṭa, udumbara, and ciñcā is recorded as the ninth.
(p. 427) [The discarding of feces and urine, and the mantra for cleaning the teeth.]
Having performed the evacuation of feces, urine, and so forth with a restrained mind, one should remember the Root Mantra while feeling a sense of purity;
having thoroughly cleansed [the area] by sprinkling it with earth and water, facing the east,
one should [offer] all desires and objects of desire to the beloved who resides in the heart, using the dative case ending for "janat" (people).
This mantra for the cleansing of the teeth has been declared according to the sequence following the tantras. || 65 ||
(The rites beginning with the binding of the topknot and ending with the twilight worship:

Having performed the topknot-binding and the triple-ash mark and forehead-mark with the root mantra alone, one should then sip water in sequence, perform the visualization of Tripurā before oneself, and then carry out the two Nyāsa rituals for the hands and the limbs.
One should perform the supreme twilight worship (saṃdhyā) as described in the Śrīkrama-saṃhitā with a restrained mind;
having performed it and having propitiated the supreme Goddess Tripurā, one becomes a god. (66)
65 | He states the mantra for cleaning the teeth, beginning with "Kāmaṃ": *Kāma* is the seed-syllable of desire, *klīṃ*.

Then the word *kāma*, signifying Kāmadeva. Then the word *sarva*. Then from the word *jana*, the word *priya* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*). By this, *priyāya* is obtained. Joined with *hṛd* (the heart-mantra *namaḥ*), it ends with the word *namaḥ*. Thus: *klīṃ*.

"Salutation to Kāmadeva, who is dear to all people. Thus the fourteen-syllable mantra is finalized. Here, by the second word "kāma," the four syllables "kāmadeva" are to be understood. This is clearly stated in the first chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
One should write the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), the god of love (KĀMADEVA), and finally the word "janam" (people).
This mantra, ending with "priyāya hṛdaya," is for the purification of the teeth.
Thus it is said. Also, in the fifth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"One should write the syllable *klīm*, which is the essence of Kāmadeva, at the end of all [the names] of people;
ending with 'to my beloved, [O] heart' (*priyāya hṛdaya*), this mantra is for the purification of the teeth."

"One should wash the face with fourteen syllables for the sake of purification. Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti* as cited in the *Prāṇatoṣaṇī*, and similarly in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, *Gandharvatantra*, and other texts, since the word *kāmadeva* is seen to be a constituent part of the mantra, [the word] *deva* should not be omitted.

Furthermore, because there would otherwise arise a contradiction with the statements of the Gandharvas and others that "the face consists of fourteen syllables" and so forth, the conclusion is that in this context, the four syllables "kāma-deva" must be included as constituent parts of the mantra by means of the word "kāma.
66. Regarding the phrase "by the root [mantra] alone": here, by the word *sandhyā*, one should understand the mental *sandhyā* consisting of the morning rites and so on.
(p. 428) (Now, regarding the twilight [ritual], therein is the placement of the fifteen syllables upon one's own body:
Upon the head, throat, mouth, ears, eyes, nose, and arms;
and upon the heart, the private parts, the region of the back, the navel, the belly, and the anus.
One should place the fifteen-syllable mantra of Mahādevī on the foot and the ankle.
(Dhyāna:
One should contemplate the complete Vidyā in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), possessing a reddish glow;
one should remember her as bestowing great good fortune, consisting of sixteen syllables and flowing with nectar. (68)
(The application of the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī mudrā:
Then, one should rotate the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī [mudrā] over the region of the left shoulder. (The application of the Ripujihvā [mudrā:])
And one should joyfully place the tongue of the enemy within the soles of one's feet. || 69 ||
Thinking, "I am the creator of the three worlds," one should place [the mark] upon the forehead;
one should then apply it completely around the face as a circlet.
Then, one should place [the mantra] on the face and the upper part of the throat;
having performed the pervasion (vyāpakatva), one should cast the yoni-mudrā upon the mouth and pay obeisance.

In the fifteenth [verse], because the Tantric twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) will be described immediately after the bath, and because it is not the appropriate occasion for it here, the rest is easy to understand.
67. Regarding "the head": in the previous verse, as a constituent part of the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*),...
The mental twilight worship (*mānasa-sandhyopāsana*) as taught in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā* has been indicated; that very practice is now demonstrated with the words beginning "the head" (*śiraḥ*).
Thus, the meaning is that one should sequentially place each individual syllable of the fifteen-syllabled *Śrīvidyā* mantra previously shown upon the fifteen locations, starting from the head.
(p. 429) (The Form and Fruit of Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī) Having formed a fist with the palm, the practitioner should extend the index finger like a staff.
Named Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī, she punishes enemies in an instant. (72)
The *mudrā* for seizing the tongue of the enemy and the purification of the hands:
one should place the thumb within the fist; this becomes the *mudrā* for seizing the tongue of the enemy. (73)
The wise one, having rotated the ring finger around the head on all sides,
should cast it into the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head) and then place it upon the wrist.
The wise one, while recollecting the sixteen-syllable mantra, should place the ring finger on the forehead;
meditating upon the three worlds as crimson, he should keep Śrīvidyā in his mind. (75)
The syllable Oṃ is the peak (kūṭa) born of speech; the syllable Āṃ is that which belongs to the King of Desire (Kāmarāja);
it is joined with the end of the letter Śa and the beginning of the Ka-series, and conjoined with the end of the letter Ai. || 76 ||
Tripurā Parameśānī is prescribed for the purification of the hands. || 77 ||

72. Regarding the term "fist" (*muṣṭi*): here, by the word "palm" (*tala*), it should be understood as the palm of the left hand. In the section on mudrās in the *Tantrasāra*, it is said: "Having formed a fist with the left hand at the region of the ear, the best of mantra-knowers should straighten the index finger and rotate it."
The Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī mudrā is also indicated at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Because it is clearly stated thus by that statement.
73. Regarding "the thumb": in the *Tantrasāra*, however, it says:
"Having blocked this forefinger with the fist [placed] inside the thumb..."
The mudrā Ripujihvāgrahā is indicated at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa).
By this, it is seen that a specific distinction is made, namely that the closing of the index finger is also stated by means of the fist formed with the thumb.
(The meditation on the Vidyā):
Now, within the support, which is a triangle, is the Vāgbhava [syllable], the color of lightning.
Born from that, she has the color of lightning, possesses two arms, and has the form of a young girl. || 78 ||
Her lotus-like hands shine with a book and a rosary; she has three beautiful eyes, bimba-red lips, and a golden complexion, and she is as slender as a spider's thread.
One should merge her, whose essential nature is called Vāgbhava, into the Supreme Power (Paraśakti),
who resembles pure crystal and is like cow’s milk or silver.
Having the shape of a Kadamba bud, situated at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), she holds the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, a noose, and the Vidyā. 81.
(Tripurārghyadāna): Having uttered the Vāgbhava syllable, [one should say] "I worship the sandals of Tripurā, the Mistress of Speech"; thus one should present the arghya three times. (82)

78–81 | Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha ādhāra," the following should be noted here: that mental worship of the *sandhyā* which was previously indicated is to be performed during the four periods of time—namely, morning, midday, evening, and midnight; otherwise, [it would contradict the rule]: "In the evening, however, the seed-syllable of Śakti is white indeed in the lunar orb."

Because of the specific statements to be made later, such as "at midnight, within that interval" and "having uttered the fourth seed-syllable," the separate mention of evening and midnight would be redundant. Thus,

since evening and midnight are established in various places as the times for those [specific rites], it is settled that the two previously mentioned ritual procedures (kalpas) pertain to the morning and midday periods.

In this context, the procedures described by the passage beginning with "There, the head, the throat... and ending with "...are declared in the purification of the hands" are common to all four periods of time. However, by the passage beginning with "Now, the support (ādhāra)...", [the author] explains the procedure for meditation and so forth pertaining to the morning, which is encountered first. "In the support" means in the *mūlādhāra*; "in the triangle" means situated in the *mūlādhāra*.

The meaning is "in the triangle. The ellipsis is "having meditated upon the Vāgbhava-bīja, which is the color of lightning. The connection is that one should cause her—who arises from that [bīja], namely from that Vāgbhava-bīja; who has two arms; who possesses all the qualifying attributes such as "having the form of a child," and so forth—to enter into that Supreme Śakti residing in the *sahasrāra*. There too—
The meaning is that one should meditate upon her as qualified by such attributes as "resembling pure crystal" and so forth.
(82) Following meditation, he instructs on the offering of the *arghya* with the words beginning "vāgbhavantu," etc.
(Tripurāgāyatrī) (p. 431)
"May we know Tripurādevī; may there be the state of Vāgbhaveśvarī; may we meditate upon her; then, may liberation impel this for us. (83)
(The recitation of that [mantra] by way of inhalation and so forth):
Then the knower of mantras should recite it three times according to the procedure of inhalation (*pūraka*) and the rest. (84)
(The Meditation on the Goddess:
Seated upon the solar disc in the filament at the center of the heart-lotus is the second Kāmarāja, resembling the rising sun. 85.
Born from that [seed], she is red in color, four-armed, and three-eyed;
she holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and is endowed with youth.
(Therein, another sequence:

Alternatively, one should lead [the deity] who is blazing with the dawn-red glow, whose nature is the peak-syllable of desire (kāmakūṭa), into the thousand-petaled lotus and meditate upon her as possessing the brilliant splendor of the sun.
She has four arms, is greatly radiant, possesses three eyes, and has a beautiful countenance;
in her left [hand] she holds a book consisting of all knowledge, which is the essence of the Praṇava.
In her right hand she holds a rosary of beads with a luster equal to the sun, and with her right and left hands she, the Supreme Goddess, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

83–84: After the offering of the three *arghya*s, he instructs the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* in three ways—by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*)—with the passage beginning with "Tripurā" and ending with "should recite thrice.
85: Having thus described the procedure for meditation and other rites pertaining to the morning time, he now states the midday meditation.
"Situated in the center of the heart-lotus," and so forth. This should be understood to apply likewise in the places to be mentioned hereafter.
(The offering of *arghya*):
Having meditated thus, one should extract the *Kāmarāja* [seed-syllable] and the word *Tripurā*.
Having recollected the sandals of Kāmeśvarī, one should offer the arghya water three times.
(The Gāyatrī and its Recitation):
Having uttered the Kāmarāja [bīja], one should say: "O Goddess Tripurā, we know;
O Mahākāmeśvarī, we meditate upon; may that [power] be ours. From there, [one recites] word by word.
The practitioner, moistening [the tongue], should impel [the mantra] and recite this three times.
(The meditation on the Goddess at evening:
At evening, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable of Śakti as white within the lunar orb;
[the Goddess] born from that, white in color, wearing a crown of matted locks.
Three-eyed, two-armed, with slightly protruding fangs and fingers, and auspicious. || 92 ||
(Therein is another interpretation:
Alternatively, one should meditate upon her in the form of Power within a pure lotus. 93.
Abounding in all ornaments, she grants boons with her right hand;
in her left hands, she holds a rosary and a boon-granting gesture, as well as a book and the gesture of fearlessness.
(The Procedure for Offering the Arghya):
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Śakti, one should offer the arghya three times with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of Tripurā Amṛteśvarī. (95)
(The Gāyatrī and its Japa):
The practitioner of mantras should recite the Gāyatrī, which is the very nature of the Śakti-bīja. || 96 ||
We know Tripurādevī; we meditate upon the Mistress of our own power;
may she impel us toward immortality.
(Meditation at midnight)
At midnight, there is an interval. || 97 ||
Having uttered the fourth seed-syllable, which has a luster like a ruby,
one should invoke the Sovereign of the Gods into the sky of supreme bliss.
[He meditated on] the Great Goddess born from that [seed-syllable], possessing a luster like a ruby, holding a noose and a goad, bearing a bow, and having three eyes. (99)
(The sequence for the arghya offering: Having uttered the fourth seed-syllable, one should offer the arghya three times, saying: "I worship the sandals of Mahātripurasundarī. || 100 ||
(Therein, the Gāyatrī and its recitation:
The practitioner of mantra should recite the Gāyatrī, which consists of the fourth seed-syllable; after the word "Tripurasundarī," he should then say "vidmahe. (101)
"Kāmeśvarī dhīmahi, tanno klinne pracodayāt"—
one should recite this mantra one hundred and eight times, thirty times, ten times, or in ten ways.
(Conclusion) Thus, by way of incidental discussion, the entire sequence of the twilight rites has been fully described. || 103 ||
(The Necessity of Morning Duties): Now, having performed the morning rites, one should cease according to the sequence;
that which is performed by one who is devoid of the morning rites becomes as if unperformed. (104)
(p. 434) (The ritual performance in the temple):

Then, having gone to the sacred site of the deity and having removed the remains of previous offerings (*nirmālya*), the wise man should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), as well as the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*). 105.
One should provide water for washing the face, one should indeed provide a tooth-stick, one should provide water for sipping, and one should provide pure and auspicious clothing. (106)
Having paid homage, performed the recitation, offered praise, and bowed down, one shall become happy. || 107 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 14 ||
The Fifteenth Chapter:
(The Twofold Nature of the Sequence of Bathing) The method of bathing is twofold, distinguished by the categories of external and internal. (1)

(Therein, the promise to describe the internal bath: I shall respectfully describe the internal bath, though it is an extreme secret, for the sake of attaining the four goals of human life; of this there is no doubt. (2)
(The Procedure for Internal Bathing) The practitioner, being self-restrained, should perform the supreme mental bath preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), using the root mantra with the mind. (3)
Having recollected the threefold consciousness from within the midst of the three steps,
one [beholds] the flowing stream of being, consciousness, and bliss, which brings liberation from worldly existence.
For yogins, the means to liberation for men is through mere remembrance;
therefore, one should contemplate oneself as drenched by that [remembrance] for the sake of the cessation of worldly existence.
(Conclusion and fruit of internal bathing:
Thus, this internal bathing bestows the fruit of ten million sacred fords.
(Now, external bathing.)
Then, one should perform the external bath according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.

1 | Having described the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*) in detail in the previous exposition, in this exposition he first prescribes the bath with the words "the method of bathing" (*snānaprakāra*), etc., because one hears of the censure of one who has not bathed regarding the worship of the Goddess (*devīsaparyā*) to be described here. (In that regard, the sipping of water [ācamana]):
Then, one should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) as before with the inauspicious elements beginning with the self (*ātmatattva*).
(Invocation of the Holy Waters): Having meditated upon the King of Yantras within the water, one should perform the invocation of the holy waters (*tīrthāvāhana*).
(The mantra therein: O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī! Be present in this water. (8)

(The necessity of performing the invocation as prescribed with the Nirukta mantra and the goad mudrā): With this mantra and the mudrā known as the goad, the practitioner [should perform the invocation]. || 9 ||
(The Hook Mudrā): Having formed a fist with the right hand, one should extend the middle finger like a staff;
there, one should join the index finger in the form of a hook.
The great mudrā called the Hook is capable of attracting the three worlds. || 10 ||
(Consecration: While recollecting the root mantra, one should pour water three times upon the head with the rite called "the jar" (kumbha). || 11 ||
(Thighbone Seal): Having placed the right thumb upon the left thumb with both hands, the wise know the fist held slightly open to be the thighbone seal (*kumbhamudrā*). 12.
(Procedure for Immersion): Then, having closed the seven apertures, the wise one should immerse himself three times.
7 | "The King of Yantras" means the Śrīyantra that is about to be described.
9 | "By this" refers to the connection with the preceding [verse]: one should perform the invocation of the *tīrtha* by means of the mudrā known as the *aṅkuśa*.
13 | "The seven apertures" refers to the two apertures of the eyes, the two apertures of the ears, the two apertures of the nose, and one [aperture].
"The opening of the mouth" refers to the seven apertures. (p.
437) [This concludes] the instruction on the knowledge of another procedure for bathing from my own *Śyāmārahasya*. As for the other secret of bathing, it is indeed in my work titled *Śyāmā*.
This very point should be investigated here; however, it has not been stated [in detail] for fear of making the work too voluminous. || 14 ||
(Regarding the Tantric Sandhyā following the Vedic Sandhyā, therein the ritual rinsing of the mouth, etc.):
Then, having performed the Vedic Sandhyā and having rinsed the mouth according to the rules,
[one should perform] the Aghamarṣaṇa preceded by the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should then take water in the left hand.
Then, taking [the vessel] with the right hand, one should form a hollowed cavity (saṃpuṭa);
furthermore, one should do so three times with the seed-syllables of Śiva, Vāyu, Water, Earth, and Fire.

14 | "Another [work]" refers to the *Śyāmārahasya*, a treatise (nibandha) titled *Śyāmārahasya* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. In the first chapter of the *Śyāmārahasya*, following the description of the morning rites (*prātaḥkṛtya*), it begins with the words: "Then, having gone to a river or similar place, one should contemplate everything in the form of Kālikā," and so forth.
The secret of the ritual bath has been specifically described.

(16) One should form a hollow cavity with the right hand and cover [the vessel]. Having covered it, one should consecrate it three times with the seed-syllables of Śiva, Vāyu, Water, Earth, and Fire—namely *haṃ*, *yaṃ*, *vaṃ*, *laṃ*, and *raṃ*—using the *tattvamudrā*.

The connection [of the sentence] is that one should sprinkle that water upon the head seven times with the root mantra. Regarding the definition of the *tattvamudrā*, the *Gandharva-tantra* states in its seventh chapter: "The joining of the thumb and the ring finger is declared to be this *tattvamudrā*."
Even though it is not specifically stated here, one should perform the sprinkling on the head with drops of water falling from the gaps between the fingers of the left hand;
as stated in the sixth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"Having taken water in the left hand, [one should sprinkle] with the falling drops of water."
One should perform the sprinkling seven times upon the head while recollecting the mantra.
Having taken the remaining water in his right hand,
the practitioner should touch his nose with that water and then perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite.

Because it is clearly stated in such passages as these: "In this regard, by the statement 'thereby [is] the *aghamarṣaṇa*,' it is declared that the very washing away of sin (*pāpa*)—performed with water consecrated by the aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and drawn up through the nostrils—is what constitutes the *aghamarṣaṇa*. In the root text, however, it is said:
'Having drawn it up through the flowing nostril, one should wash away the sin. The procedure for drawing it up is described in the *Gandharvatantra*:"
In the sixth chapter: Having drawn [the water] through the *iḍā* [left nostril], the mass of sins within the body is washed away;
that water, black in color, is then expelled through the *vāmanāḍī* [right nostril].
Having consecrated it seven times with the root mantra and the *tattvamudrā*,
one should sprinkle that water upon the head, and place the remainder on the right side.
Having meditated upon that [breath] as consisting of light, one should lift it up through the left nostril and wash away the sin residing in the man's left side.
It has the murder of a Brahmin as its head, the theft of gold as its two arms, the drinking of liquor joined with its heart, and the violation of the Guru’s bed as its two hips. (19)
The pair of feet associated with that [form] was a sin against every limb and member;
its hair was minor sins, and its beard and eyes were red.
One should contemplate him as holding a sword and shield, cruel, black, and filled with wrath, his entire body covered by a multitude of various sins.
One should cast that accumulation of sins upon a diamond-stone (vajraśilā) on the ground.
(Instruction on the procedure immediately following the twilight ritual [sandhyā] and the libation [tarpaṇa]):
Then, having performed the Tantric twilight ritual, one should offer libations to the Supreme Goddess. 22.
"The mantra-practitioner, having visualized that [person] in the form of sin in his right hand, should cast it onto a vajra-stone in front [of him] with the *astra-mantra*.
(18–21) He describes the actual nature of the "sin-person" (*pāpapuruṣa*) with the words beginning "sin," etc.: "sin" refers to the person who is sin, the sin-person.
He qualifies that [deity] with the words "situated in the left abdomen," and so forth.

(21) Regarding "thereafter": following that aforementioned *aghamarṣaṇa*, having performed the remaining Tantric *saṃdhyā*, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). In this regard, in the *Tantrasāra*, within the section on *Śrīvidyā*, [it is stated] after the Tantric bath...
It has been stated that after performing the ritual actions up to the *aghamarṣaṇa* according to the Tantras, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
However, in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, Pūrṇānanda Guru, the Paramahaṃsa Brahmānanda, states that after the *aghamarṣaṇa*,
having washed one's hands and sipped water as before, one should meditate upon the Goddess within the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) and [proceed] with water.
Having worshipped with the five offerings and taken water in his joined palms, he stands up and recites: "O Vāgbhaveśvarī, we know; O Kāmeśvarī, we meditate;
may Śakti impel us. [He worships] the illustrious Mahātripura, preceded by the gods, sages, and ancestors, together with her weapons and retinue.
The wise man should offer libations to the Goddess either in water or within his home.

Having purified the water with the Vāgbhava [syllable], the lamp with the Kāmarāja [syllable], and the nectar with the Śaktikūṭa [syllable], one should satisfy the Supreme Goddess (Parā) with that very same [nectar]. 24.
Having meditated upon the King of Yantras in the water, one should then invoke the Goddess.
Having offered libations to Gaṇeśa and others, one should satisfy the lords of the Gaṇas;
having offered libations to Sarasvatī and others, one should satisfy the deities such as Bhadrakālī.

"O beautiful one, this is your *argha*; Svāhā!"—having thus offered three *arghas*, and having offered three *arghas* to the Sun with "Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ, to Mārtaṇḍabhairava together with the Śakti Prakāśā, this *argha*, Svāhā!", and having recited the Gāyatrī and the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) as much as possible, and having offered the recitation to the Goddess and dismissed her into the heart, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*). This is the Sandhyā.

Having stated this much, the procedure for libation (*tarpaṇa*) is taught by the words "Now, the libation," and so forth. In the second chapter of the *Kaulāvalī-nirṇaya*, after describing the rites up to the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite, it says:
"Having washed both hands, one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)."
One should then say: "The mantra consisting of *māyā* and *prāṇa*, for Mārtaṇḍabhairava united with the power of illumination (*prakāśaśakti*), *arghyaṃ svāhā*.
Having thus offered the *arghya* to the Sun, it is proclaimed as the *Śaktisandhyā*.
Having visualized the yantra before him and the Goddess there accompanied by her attendants,
the best of practitioners should then take scented water and a vessel of the kula, and duly perform the libation into the mouth of the deity according to the rite.

With these and other words, having described the sequence beginning with the washing of the hands and sipping water (ācamana) following the *aghamarṣaṇa*, and ending with the offering of water (*arghya*) to the Sun,

the libation to the Goddess (*devītarpaṇa*) was taught. In the present context, however, one should perform the Tantric twilight rite (*tāntrikī saṃdhyā*) after the *aghamarṣaṇa* and then perform the libation.

Because of the mention of "the supreme" (*parām*), because of the mention of "satisfying" (*tarpaṇāt paraṃ*), and because of the subsequent mention of "offering the arghya to the Sun," the intention of the phrase "having performed the twilight worship" (*sandhyāṃ kṛtvā*) is that one should complete the ritual— from the washing of the hands as approved by one's own guru, Brahmānanda, up to the offering of the arghya to the Goddess— excluding the recitation of the root mantra for the offering of the arghya to the Sun.

It appears that [this refers] to the Paramahaṃsas who are full of bliss (*pūrṇānanda*). Here, because differences of opinion among the teachers (*ācāryas*) are observed, one should adopt whichever position is appropriate according to one's own tradition; this is the general direction. (p. 440) At the four gates outside the Yantra, the propitiation of the Guru is prescribed.
And [the feet of] Amukānandanātha and the two feet of Amukāmbā. || 27 ||
One should worship the Supreme Guru in the southeast, Parameṣṭhin in the southwest,
Parāpara in the northwest, and the Guru’s consort in the center.
And having gratified the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) and the five deities beginning with Brahmā, || 29 ||
One should satisfy the goddesses, the invocation-mantras, and the Tithinityās;
and one should offer the root-mantra three times, or seven times according to one's capacity, with water.
Then, having gratified the Goddess who consists of the five languages, the fifth [goddess] Saubhāgyā, as well as Aṇimā and the others, and the eight deities beginning with Brahmāṇī; || 31 ||
Then, having manifested Tripurā through the mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhaṇī,
one should satisfy Tripureśvarī with the forms of Kāmākarṣaṇī and the others.
There, one should satisfy the well-guarded Yoginīs, beginning with Anaṅgakusumā, as well as the beautiful Sundarī, who is a Yoginī in a state of deep sleep.
And [he worshipped] the powers such as Saṃkṣobhaṇī, as well as Tripuravāsinī,
the traditions of the Yoginīs, and the deities such as Sarvasiddhi.
One should satisfy the auspicious Parā, the eternal Tripurā, the Kula-yoginī;
and having likewise satisfied Sarvajñā and the others, as well as Tripuramālinī.
There, one should satisfy the Yoginīs of Vidarbha, the eight deities beginning with Vaśinī, the perfected Tripurā, and likewise the secret Yoginīs.
Jambha and the others, the goddess Tripurā, the Yoginī of the supreme secret, the six-limbed young maiden, and the triad beginning with Kāmeśvarī. (37)
Then the mantra-practitioner [should worship] the Root-Vidyā, Mahātripurasundarī, the Cakra consisting of all bliss, and likewise the Supreme Goddess. (38)
Then, the wise practitioner should satisfy the goddesses of the four assemblies, the deities such as the Buddhas, and Vaṭuka and the others, each with a single handful [of water].
Then, having performed the libation twelve times upon the *bindu* at the respective station of the Great Goddess, one should complete the sprinkling three times over the body.
One should properly offer the arghya three times to the Sun and lift up his face.
(Meditation on Mārtaṇḍabhairava:
He whose innate luster possesses the splendor of a golden lotus and tender sprouts, who holds a beautiful khaṭvāṅga and a lotus,
a discus, a spear, a noose, a trident, a beautiful rosary, and a skull-cup;

We worship him who holds lotuses in his hands, who is beautiful with three eyes and the shining four faces of the Vedas, who has the Sun as his beloved half, who wears a jeweled crown, and who is radiant with necklaces. 42.
(The offering of *arghya* to Mārtaṇḍabhairava [the Sun]:
Having recollected the god Bhairava, known as Mārtaṇḍa, the Lord of the Universe, the practitioner of mantras should [offer] with the root mantra or with the mantra of the Sun. (43)
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), the word "Sohantu" is reversed;
this is declared to be the Sūrya-mantra, [to be used] with red flowers, water, and other offerings.
44–45 | Regarding "māyā": *māyābīja* is *hrīṃ*. By stating *so'haṃ* in reverse order, one obtains *haṃsaḥ*. (p.

442) Having offered the *arghya* libation to Mārtaṇḍabhairava—addressed with the dative suffix *-ṅe* and joined with the Śakti of Light—one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times. 45.
(Therein is the meditation on the Goddess within the solar disc:
Having meditated upon the Goddess within the orb of the Sun as bearing a digit of the moon,
possessing the luster of gold recently smelted, and having the form of the solar disc itself— (46).

[She is] crowned with a mass of radiant jewels, adorned with various ornaments, and [holding] the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon. (Now, the sequence for entering the place of sacrifice:)
And then, with the goad mudrā. || 47 ||
Having brought her into his heart and contemplating the mantra within his own heart, the yogi, with his mind not directed outward, should then enter the sacrificial ground.
(The Praised Sacrificial Grounds and the Procedure for the Worship of the Goddess therein): On a mountain with a single linga, on a cremation ground,
on the shore of a lake, within the Ganges, on its bank, at a confluence, or in an empty temple.

It may be so. And thus, *hrīṃ haṃsaḥ* is the mantra of the Sun. Therefore, having uttered either the root mantra or the aforementioned mantra of the Sun, one should say: "To Mārtaṇḍabhairava, accompanied by the Power of Radiance (*prakāśaśakti*), this is the *arghya* offering; svāhā!"—this is the meaning. (Verses 47–48) Regarding the word "pāśa" (*pāśa*): the ellipsis is to be supplied as "holding the noose, the goad, and the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons. Now, regarding the word "atha" (*atha*). Thus...
Immediately after the meditation, having brought her to the heart-lotus of the *anāhata* by means of the hook-mudrā— the remainder being that [she is brought] from the solar disc—
the definition of the hook-mudrā is stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Having made the middle finger straight, one places the index finger upon its middle joint."

"Having joined [the fingers], one should slightly bend them; this mudrā is known as the *aṅkuśa* (hook). Thus, while recollecting the mantra—contemplating the nature of its root-mantra—one should have the mind not turned outward, with the attention concentrated on one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) residing within the heart-lotus. The sacrificial ground (*yāgabhūmi*) is the place of worship.
49. He defines the places of worship with the verse beginning "at a solitary liṅga," and so forth:
"One should worship the Supreme Goddess at a solitary liṅga, on the bank of a river, or at the root of a *bilva* tree. (p. 443)
(The Characteristics of a Solitary Liṅga:
Where no other liṅga is seen within a distance of five krośas, that is declared to be an ekaliṅga; there, supreme accomplishment is attained. 50.
(Now, the worship of the door; therein, first is the washing of hands and feet:
Then, one should wash one's hands and feet at the door of the house of worship. || 51 ||
(On the gathering of dūrvā grass:
Without dūrvā grass, there is never any worship of the Goddess here;
therefore, one should take the auspicious dūrvā, which consists of all flowers. 52.
(Regarding the sipping of water:
Having placed a blade of dūrvā grass in his hand, he should sip water according to the prescribed rule.
(Dikpālapūjā) Having meditated upon the sandals of the venerable Guru within the full moon,
one should worship all the guardians of the directions according to the sequence beginning with the east. 54.

He will explain this further ahead. "In the land of the ancestors" means in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). "At a confluence" means at the junction of rivers; however, if the reading is *saṃgrāme*, it means on a battlefield. This is clearly stated in the *Muṇḍamālā-tantra* as cited in the *Śyāmā-rahasya*:
"On a riverbank, at the root of a *bilva* tree, in a cremation ground, or in an empty house."
On a mountain with a single linga, in a temple, at a crossroads,
upon a corpse, on a shaven head, in water up to the neck,
on a battlefield, in a womb, on dry land, or in a solitary forest.
"In whatever delightful place, or wherever the mind finds its absorption.
The specific details, however, are to be seen in the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*.
(50) Previously, it was stated, "on a mountain with a single liṅga," and so forth; he now describes the characteristics of such a site with a single liṅga as being within a radius of five *krośas*.
By such [passages] as these.
53. Regarding "one should sip water" (ācāmet): here, the author of the *Tantrasāra* has described the sipping of water by means of the *ātmatattva* and so forth.
54. Regarding "full" (pūrṇa): within the interval of the full moon—that is, within the interval of the full moon situated at the pericarp of the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
(p. 444) (Therein is another sequence:
Having first performed the general offering (sāmānyārgha), or else following the sequence, the practitioner should worship Indra together with his Śakti at the eastern gate. || 55 ||
And Yama at the southern gate, likewise Varuṇa at the western, Kubera at the northern gate, Vahni in the southeast, and Nirṛti in the southwest. || 56 ||
The practitioner of mantra should worship in the southwest, and likewise in the northwest;
Vāyu in the northeast, and similarly Īśāna above, as well as Prajāpati.
And one should worship below with infinite offerings of perfumes, flowers, and so forth. || 58 ||
(Astrapūjā) The wise one should worship the weapons, beginning with the Vajra, according to the sequence starting from the east. || 59 ||
(The weapons to be worshipped:
