One should worship the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, and the goad; then the mace, the trident, the lotus, and the discus in sequence. 60.

The meaning is: "having meditated upon the sandals of the venerable Guru. Regarding the word "all": the meaning is that one should worship all the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) by means of the sequence starting from the east and so forth, within the aforementioned full moon. The *Nirvāṇatantra*, in its tenth chapter, describes the abiding of the guardians of the directions, Indra and the others, in the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*), with reference to that thousand-petalled lotus:
"Thus Brahmā and the other gods, Indra and the other lords of the thirty-three, are all devoted to praise and devotion, eternally abiding in divine states.
(Verses 55–58). Regarding the worship of the guardians of the directions, he describes another sequence beginning with the words "the general *arghya*," etc., in this ritual manual (*kalpa*).

Having prepared the general *arghya* offering, one should worship Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera in sequence at the four gates of the pavilion—east and so forth—and Vahni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna in the four corners; furthermore, one should worship Prajāpati above and Ananta below.

(Verses 59–60). Regarding the phrase "east and so forth": the remainder is that these are the weapons, such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*), belonging to Indra and the others. Here, by the expression "by means of the sequential order starting from the east," [the sequence is established].

In the first ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the worship of the weapons (*astra-pūjana*) is performed according to the sequence starting from the east; however, in the second ritual procedure, one should worship the weapons of the guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, first according to the order of worship, and then the weapons of the lords of the intermediate corners, such as Agni, following the sequence of worship.
This is because there is no authoritative basis for deviating from the primary order of worship when performing the worship of the weapons that constitute its subordinate parts.
The object of meditation.
(p. 445) (The worship of Gaṇeśa and others in the order starting from the east:
Gaṇeśa, Kṣetreśa, Dvāraśrī, and Dehalī.
One should worship [the deity] at the eastern gate, and afterwards, Gaṇanāyaka at the southern gate.
And Durgā, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and likewise Kāmarati;
and him dwelling with Prīti, as well as the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma. || 62 ||
Having worshipped Ratnasopāna in the west,
one should fully worship Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Māyā, and Durgā in the north.
One should worship Bhadrakālī, as well as Svasti, Svāhā, Śubhakārī, Gaurī, Lokadhātrī, and Vāgīśvarī. || 64 ||
(Now, the entry into the pavilion:
Having entered the interior of the pavilion, the practitioner should then first step with his left foot and behold the articles of worship with the root mantra. (65)
(Purification of the Flowers):
"In flower, in flower, in great flower, and also in 'strewn with flowers,' [with] 'svāhā'—one should purify the flower; this is approved by the Vārāhī Tantra. (66)
62. "Kāmarati" means desire and pleasure; "prītiṃ vasantaṃ" means dwelling with joy, that is, dwelling in joy.
65. "Maṇḍapāntar" means preceded by the left foot, that is, beginning with the right foot. Here...
The view of those who hold a contrary position has already been refuted (in the commentary on verse 5.28); therefore, everything regarding that should be understood from that very source.
Now, he states the mantra for purifying the flower (*puṣpaśodhana-mantra*) with the word "puṣpa": namely, "O Flower! O Flower! O Great Flower! O You Who Are Strewn with Flowers!
Svāhā!"—this is the mantra for purifying the flower in the context of the *Śrīvidyā*. As for what is stated in the second chapter of the *Kumārītantra*:
For the consecration of the flower, one should first extract the *praṇava*;
after that, the word "śatābhiṣeka" and then "śatābhi".
(This is the sprinkling preceded by the purification of the water.)

Having performed the purification of the water and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra upon the objects, one sprinkles them. Then, having rendered them nectar-like (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), etc., one performs the triple *tāla* gesture, the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), and the gazing (*īkṣaṇa*).
Then "ṣeka" is proclaimed, followed by "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Then the Praṇava, "puṣpaketu," and likewise "rājārhate," and having correctly said "śatāya samyak," one should indeed mutter "hūm."
"O Flower! O Flower! O Great Flower! O Beautiful Flower! O You who arise from flowers!
O You who are strewn with heaps of flowers! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Having purified the flower with this mantra, one should then fetch water as before.

Thus, the purification of flowers has been described; that pertains to subjects other than Śrīvidyā, because there is a specific injunction for Śrīvidyā. For this very reason, after stating the sequence of flower purification as taught in the aforementioned Kumārītantra in the Haratattvadīdhiti, [it is noted] regarding Śrīvidyā in the sixth chapter of the Vārāhītantra:
Reciting "Puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe puṣpāvakīrṇe svāhā," one should purify the flower; with that flower, one should perform worship.

Thus it has been stated. The essential point is that, even in the present context, the phrase "as approved by the Vārāhī Tantra" is specifically mentioned in order to demonstrate the sequence as accepted in the aforementioned Vārāhī Tantra.
67. Regarding the word "jala" (water): the mantra for purifying water has already been shown previously. Regarding the word "tataḥ" (thence):

After the recitation of the mantra for purifying the water, one should "render it nectar" (*amṛtīkṛtya*), meaning one should cause that water to attain the state of nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā* (the cow-seal).
Regarding the *dhenumudrā* and the consecration as nectar by means of it, the *Tantrasāra* states:
"The little fingers and ring fingers are again joined together, facing one another."
"Now, the *dhenumudrā* is proclaimed as being formed by the middle fingers and the index fingers;
by means of it, the best of practitioners should perform the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the offering] nectar).
The three *tālas* will be described further on. Regarding the phrase 'having veiled' (*avaguṇṭhya*), the *Tantrasāra* describes the *avaguṇṭhanamudrā*:"
"The fist formed with the left hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downward—this is considered the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā when it is rotated all around. Thus [it is said].
(Mandapa-pūjā)
One should worship the house with the mantra ending in "namas" addressed to the pavilion for the worship of Tripurā;
having performed the sprinkling with the Astra-mantra, one should draw a triangle there.
(Earth Worship) One should also worship the Earth there with this mantra: "Oṃ, the seed-syllable of Śakra, and obeisance to the Earth. (69)
(The offering of arghya with the earth as the recipient:
Alternatively, having taken up the arghya preceded by the root mantra—
(the mantra of prayer therein is as follows):
O Earth, you are the womb of gold, resting upon Śeṣa;
grant me a place for my worship, O Dharitrī, accept this water-offering from me.
(The mantra for the offering of arghya:
"Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, Dharaṇī, and to her who is called Dharaṇī;
O Supporter, svāhā!"—with this mantra, one should present the unsurpassed arghya. (71)

68. Regarding "Tripura": the ritual formula is *oṃ tripurārcanamaṇḍapāya namaḥ*. Although no specific instruction is given here, the mantra should be employed preceded by the syllable *oṃ*: "That which is joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and proclaimed with the word 'salutation' (*namaḥ*) at the end."
One's own name is called the mantra of all the gods.

By this [statement], since it prescribes that the name of the object of worship (sādhya-nāman), preceded by *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending in *namaḥ*, constitutes the mantra; and because it is clearly stated in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*: "Oṃ, obeisance to the sacrificial pavilion (*yāga-maṇḍapa*) of Tripurā. By the weapon-mantra (*astra*), namely *phaṭ*.
(69) Therein, he describes the worship of Earth within the triangle with the words beginning with *praṇava*: *praṇava* is *oṃ*; the seed-syllable of Śakra (*śakra-bīja*) is *laṃ*.

Then, "Salutation to the Earth" (*pṛthivyai namaḥ*). Thus, the mantra concludes as *oṃ laṃ pṛthivyai namaḥ*. (70) He states another ritual procedure for the worship of the Earth in the form of offering the *arghya* water, beginning with "Alternatively" (*athavā*). In this ritual, having taken the *arghya*, one should first recite the root mantra, and then the mantra: "O Vasudhā, you who have gold in your womb. Thereafter, *oṃ namo*...

One should offer the *arghya* with this mantra: "To the Blessed Earth, the Supporter of the World, Svāhā! By the phrase "or else" (*athavā*), it is indicated that while in previous kalpas there was merely worship, here, however, one offers the *arghya* intended for the Earth without performing worship.
(Purification of the Hands): One should perform the purification of the hands with scents and flowers using this mantra: || 72 ||
The pair of the first vowels with the crescent moon, followed by Manu and Bhṛgu with the visarga—
this is declared to be Manu (the expulsion of the elementals).
One should ward off beings that have already arisen. || 73 ||

72. Now, he describes the procedure for the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the words beginning "in the hand" (*kare*). The connection is that one should perform the purification of the hands with scents and flowers using this mantra which is about to be stated. Here, by the word "flowers," it should be understood that red flowers are intended.
This is clearly stated in the eighth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
Then the practitioner, having taken a red flower together with its fragrance,
should wipe the flower held in the palm of his hand with this very mantra,
using his left hand while [holding] the right hand [over it].
"Having smelled [the substance] with the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) and then with the *vāgbhava* syllable,
one should cast it toward the northeast with the remaining (*śeṣa*) or *śara* seed-syllable, O Pārvatī.
By this, the sequence for the purification of the hands is also explained.

73. It was stated in the previous verse that one should perform [the rite] "with this mantra of Manu"; he now states that mantra with the words beginning with *ādya* and ending with *ākhyāta*. *Ādyasvarayugam* means the pair of vowels *a* and *ā*. *Sendukhaṇḍam* means accompanied by the nasal dot (*anusvāra*). By this, *aṃ* and *āṃ* are obtained. Regarding *manuyuta*: *manu* is the fourteenth vowel, the diphthong *au*; joined with that is *bhṛgu*, which is the letter *sa*. And that [letter *sa*] is followed by the visarga (*sargī*).
Joined with the *visarga*, this yields *sauḥ*. Thus, the mantra for purifying the hands (*kara-śodhana*) results as *aṃ āṃ sauḥ*.
This same mantra for purifying the flowers (*puṣpa-śodhana*) is also stated in the eighth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra* as follows:
"Having extracted the first [syllable] of the *mātṛkā* and the second [syllable] along with the *bindu*..."
Joined with the letters beginning with *ka* at its peaceful end, and appended with the letter *ai* at its final end—
thus is this Great Vidyā considered to be that which effects the purification of the hands.
And thus, by reflecting upon the previously cited statement from the *Gandharva-tantra*, one should take a red flower together with its stalk in the right hand;
[the mantra for that occasion is as follows].
May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. 74.
(Dispelling terrestrial obstacles:
One should scatter durvā grass and unbroken rice grains in all directions while reciting the root mantra and the weapon mantra.
Then, the wise practitioner should [visualize] the Virgin Goddess (Kumārikā) accompanied by the sky, fire, and the letter of creation (S). 75.
Uttering the word "phaṭ" for the weapon-mantra (*astrāya*), while touching the ground with the *amṛtā* [finger],
one should strike the earth three times with the heel of the left foot.
(Dispelling divine obstacles:
One should ward off divine obstacles with the face turned upward. || 77 ||
(The Dispelling of Obstacles from the Atmosphere):
The maiden should give three claps in an ascending sequence, making a sound at the regions of the feet, the heart, and the head, respectively. (78)
(The Binding of the Directions and the Visualization of the Fire-Wall):
Having performed the binding of the ten directions with snaps of the fingers from both hands, the best of practitioners should meditate upon a wall of fire in all directions. (79)

The sequence for purifying the hands is understood as follows: having cleansed [the hands] with the seed-syllable of desire, *klīm*, using the left hand; having smelled [them] with the *vāgbhava* syllable, *ai*; and having cast [the impurities] toward the northeast with the weapon-seed-syllable, *phaṭ*. Regarding the fruit of this aforementioned purification of the hands, it is stated in that very same source: "The tips of the fingers become pure through the grasping of the flower."
Purity is attained by rubbing with the hands; by wiping, the back is cleansed.
By smelling [the water], the gods are satisfied and there is a gathering of sacred fords (tīrthas).
By casting it away, all obstacles are removed and a difficult position is avoided.
"Whatever defilement of the two hands arises from contact with foul-smelling excretions, all that, even if its form is unknown, shall be destroyed by this rite.
(79) Regarding "with snaps of the fingers": a snap of the fingers (*choṭikā*) is the sound produced by the index finger and the thumb.
(The Mantra for Binding the Directions):
"I bind the eastern direction with the discus; homage to the Discus, *ṭha* twice.
With this mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions, beginning with the east. (80)
(The Astra-mudrā is to be employed for the binding of the directions:
Having covered the directions with the index finger, its tip pressed against the tip of the thumb—this is declared to be the Astra-mudrā for binding the directions, beginning with the East. 81.

(The mantra for the fire-rampart: "Protect, protect the three worlds! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! This mantra, beginning with the syllable Tāra (Oṃ), is proclaimed as the one known by the name Agniprākāra (the Fire-Rampart). || 82 ||
(Astramudrā):
Having placed the two hands with the tips of the tridents facing outward, one should move them crossed over on both sides;
this is declared to be the Astramudrā, characterized by a wall of fire.
She pacifies the malice of others and removes the fear of serpents and thunderbolts. || 83 ||

80. It was previously stated that one should perform the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandhana*); regarding that, he states the mantra beginning with "aindrīm. Thus, the mantra for the binding of the directions is: "I bind [it] with the discus of Indra; obeisance to the Discus, svāhā! 81. He describes the weapon-gesture (*astramudrā*) to be employed during the aforementioned binding of the directions, beginning with the words "having covered" (*ācchādya*).

With the index finger (*tarjanī*)—which has its tip thundering at the forefront of the eldest (*jyeṣṭhāgra-stanita-agrayā*), meaning that whose tip (*agram*) thunders at the front (*agre*) of the eldest—one should perform the binding while covering the directions. This is the connection: this is known as the weapon-mudrā (*astramudrā*) for the binding of the directions, starting with the east.
Furthermore, regarding what was previously stated, "with the snapping of the two hands," the meaning there is also by means of snaps performed with this weapon-mudrā.
To be understood: 82. It was previously stated that one should meditate on the enclosure of fire; regarding that, he states the mantra beginning with "trailokya":
preceded by *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), meaning it begins with the *praṇava*. Thus: *oṃ trailokyaṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

The mantra for the fire-fortress (*agniprākāra*). The essential meaning is that one should contemplate the fire-fortress preceded by the recitation of this mantra. (83) To describe the nature of the fire-fortress, he speaks of the *astramudrā*: "With the trident... and so forth. Having made both hands such that their tips are like the points of a trident—that is, having formed the tips of the hands like a trident—by this [it is implied] the index, middle, and ring fingers of the two hands...
(Dispelling Obstacles to Recitation) The practitioner,
being self-restrained, should scatter water and unbroken grains of rice consecrated with the fire-seed syllable and the weapon-mantra, in order to remove obstacles to the recitation. (84)
(Worship of Brahmā and Vāstupuruṣa):
Then one should worship the Vāstupuruṣas and Brahmā in the southwest;
[this is] the triangular maṇḍala.
Having drawn a triangle on the ground, one should perform the worship of the foundational power (adhāraśakti) and the others.
(Regarding the placement of the seat: One should place there a seat that is charming, soft, and smooth.
One should strictly avoid a seat or an arghya vessel that is broken. 86.

(Regarding the placement of the seat [āsana-āropaṇa], the seer and so forth: Merupṛṣṭha is declared the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is said to be the meter (chandas), and Kūrma is declared the deity (devatā) therein for the placement of the seat. || 87 ||
The application has been stated;
having then held [the rosary], one should recite this prayer-mantra.
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Support me always and make this seat pure. (88)

It is said that one should extend [the hands] upwards like the point of a trident. Such hands, being crossed and reversed, should be brought together; the meaning is that one should insert the three aforementioned fingers of the second hand into the space between the three aforementioned fingers of the first hand. This is the *astra-mudrā*, characterized as a rampart of fire (*vahniprākāra*). Just as others, having crossed a rampart of fire, are unable to attack a city...

The meaning is that beings such as *bhūtas* and *hiṃsrās*, who are hostile toward the practitioner (*sādhaka*) whose nature is to form this mudrā, are not able to cause even the slightest harm to him; he forgives them in this way. He states this very point by way of describing the result, beginning with the word "para" (verse 84).
Regarding the phrase "with waters": it means consecrated with the seed-syllable of fire and the weapon-mantra, specifically with the mantra "raṃ phaṭ."
(The Mantra for Worshipping the Seat):
Having placed three *kūrca* grasses there, one should then utter the *māyābīja*.
At the end of the word "ādhāraśakti," one should draw the lotus seat (*kamalāsana*).
Having offered the word of salutation (namaḥ), one should worship one's own seat. || 89 ||
(Mantra-sipping of water):
Having sipped water according to the prescribed rite with the three *kūṭas* in accordance with the rule;
(ascending the seat and worship of the lineage of gurus).
Having ascended that seat, one should perform the worship of the Guru.

89. Regarding the word *kūrca*: the "three *kūrca*s" refers to the three blades of *kuśa* grass designated by the technical term *kūrca*, as described in the fifth chapter (verse 32). The placement of *kuśa* grass upon the seat is also mentioned in the *Svatantra-tantra* cited in the *Śyāmā-rahasya*, as follows:
Having held [the kuśa grass] thus, O Goddess of Devas, one should cause the kuśas to be placed right there.

Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should recite the Ādhāraśakti mantra. Having drawn the lotus-seat (kamalāsana), one should worship it with the mantra ending in "ṅe namo" (namo). Thus [it is said].

"Mayābījam" and so forth. Thus, the mantra for the worship of the seat culminates as: *hrīṃ ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*. However, the author of the *Tantrasāra* states this mantra preceded by the three seed-syllables: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. Regarding the fruit of the aforementioned purification of the seat, the *Gandharva Tantra*, in its seventh chapter, says:
"O Dear One, whatever defect there may be in another seat due to being poorly crafted and so forth,
it goes to destruction through the ritual procedure when its true form is unknown.
(90) By means of the three *kūṭas*— namely *ai*, *klīṃ*, and *sauḥ*— through these three *bālākūṭas*, with reference to the *Śrīvidyā*.
This is because of the statement found in the Bhairavatantra beginning with "having drunk with the three seed-syllables of the Child" (*bālābījaiḥ*):
"O Goddess, the first is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmarāja,
and the third is the Śakti-seed, which should always be joined with Śiva."
This is because the *Rudrayāmala*, in its statement regarding the *Haratattvadīdhiti*, declares that the aforementioned *Bālā* mantra consists of three *kūṭas*.
Furthermore, this sequence for sipping water (*ācamana*) has been clearly established in the commentary on the twenty-fifth verse of the fifth chapter.

Regarding the instruction "one should perform the worship of the Guru," here "worship" refers to the act of prostration, which will be described later. This is explicitly stated in the *Gandharvatantra*:
In the seventh chapter (p. 453):
"Then, one should worship Gaṇeśa in the region above the left ear, within a complete lunar disc, and in the upper portion of the right ear."
Then, one should meditate upon Goddess Durgā in the region above the head.

(Therein, the sequence of the practitioner’s attire and so forth: Anointed with red sandalwood, adorned with a red garland, his face colored with betel-juice, and resplendent in red garments. || 92 ||
His limbs were smeared with camphor powder, his mind was filled with the bliss of the ultimate cause, and he shone brilliantly with incense and lamps mixed with camphor. || 93 ||
Adorned with various red ornaments and situated in a house reddened by lac, or else impassioned by the mental resolve [of the deity], the practitioner remains with a steady mind. (94)

(Protection of the Self) O Tripurasundarī, the wise one [should perform self-protection] by means of the Bālā-mantra, or by its initial and concluding portions, according to the sequence that will be described hereafter. 95.
Placing his hand upon his heart and saying, "Protect yourself,
protect yourself," the practitioner performs self-protection (this is *karaśuddhi*).
One should perform the purification of the hands. || 96 ||
Having joined his palms in reverence with his lotus-like face bearing a gentle smile,
he should then bow to the Guru at the upper part above his left ear.
"A wise person should bow to Gaṇeśa on the upper part of the right ear;
one should bow to Durgā in front, and to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetranāyaka) behind.
(92–94). He explains what kind of practitioner should perform such acts as bowing to the Guru, etc., beginning with the words "raktā" and so forth.
95–96 | Now he describes the sequence for self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*) with the passage beginning with "the child" (*bālā*) and ending with "having performed the protection of oneself.
(p. 454) Or else, the wise one [should do so] by repeating the previously mentioned mantra twice;
then, after the three seed-syllables of Bālā, [one should worship] O Tripurasundarī! 97.

With the mantra "namaḥ" [at the beginning] and ending with "namaḥ," the name-mantras enriched with these syllables should be deposited starting from the thumb and the other fingers, extending in sequence to the palms and the backs of the hands. (98)

By the Bālā mantra, namely *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*; that is to say, by the "remainder of the beginning" (*ādyaśeṣa*) of that Bālā, which is the residual portion of the first, namely *klīṃ sauḥ*. And thus, having placed the hand upon the heart, one should recite *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*, followed immediately by *klīṃ sauḥ*, and then *tripurasundari ātmānaṃ rakṣa rakṣa* (O Tripurasundarī, protect me, protect me); this is the sequence for self-protection (*ātmarakṣākrama*). However, in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*:
The practical application is seen as: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripureśvari māṃ rakṣa rakṣa* (O Tripureśvarī, protect me, protect me).

[Verses 96–98] Now, he describes the sequence for purifying the hands with the words beginning "karaśuddhim" (purification of the hands). By means of the previously mentioned [mantra], namely *aṃ āṃ*, which is obtained from the statement: "The pair of initial vowels together with the crescent moon, joined with the Manu (the letter *ma*), and Bhṛgu (the letter *bha*) with the visarga—this is declared to be the Manu" (15.71). Thus, *aṃ āṃ*.

The connection is that one should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) by repeating the mantra *sauḥ* twice. Here, this should be noted: this purification of the hands consists of the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), because it is the occasion for it, because the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) will be described immediately after this, and because it is explained in that very way in the *Tantrasāra* and other such works. Herein [are the syllables] *aṃ* and *āṃ*.

Since the six syllables are obtained by repeating twice the mantra consisting of the three seed-syllables *saiṃ*, *auḥ*, and *rit*, the application of each individual seed-syllable to the thumbs and so forth, ending with the backs of the palms, has been taught. Accordingly, in this ritual manual (*kalpa*), it is stated: *aṃ tripurasundari aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ* (To Tripurasundarī, *aṃ*, salutation with both thumbs); *āṃ tripurasundari tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ* (To Tripurasundarī, *āṃ*, salutation with both index fingers); *sauḥ tripurasundari*... [salutation with both middle fingers].

"Salutation to the two middle fingers. Aṃ Tripurasundarī, salutation to the two ring fingers. Āṃ Tripurasundarī, salutation to the two little fingers. Sauḥ Tripurasundarī, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. Thus the ritual application concludes. He states the second method with the words "Alternatively," and so forth; here too, the phrase "by repeating twice" is to be connected.

This is because there is no subverting evidence, and it is also in accordance with the natural sense of the statement in the second chapter of the Gandharva Tantra, which will be cited later, beginning with "by repeating the root-vidyā twice," and so forth. Thus: *aiṃ* Tripurasundarī, salutation to the two thumbs;
*klīṃ* Tripurasundarī, salutation to the two index fingers; *sauḥ* Tripurasundarī, salutation to the two middle fingers; and then *aiṃ*.

The application should be performed in such a form as: "To Tripurasundarī, salutation with the two ring fingers" (*tripurasundaryai anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*), and so forth. However, in the *Tantrasāra*, within the section on the *Śrīvidyā*, this very first sequence is presented in a different manner, as follows:
"This seed-syllable, repeated twice, [is assigned] to the middle finger and the other fingers."
"One should perform the purification of the hand, the palms, and also the backs of the hands,

individually with mantras consisting of names joined with the fourth [case-ending] and the word 'ati'. By this, it is meant that first one purifies from the ring finger up to the back of the palm, and then from the thumb up to the middle finger.
He states the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*):
(The mantra of Bālā) is Speech (*vāk*), preceded by Śambhu [the letter *ka*], followed by Desire (*kāma*) [the letter *e*], and endowed with the vowel of Indra [the letter *i*] and the visarga.
(The ritual placement of the limbs):
By means of this young girl, the practitioner should perform the six-limbed rite. (99)
In this view, the mention of the term *Tripurasundarī* is not prescribed. Following these very authorities, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* have demonstrated the following sequence of application:
*aṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *āṃ tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ*, *sauḥ kaniṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *aṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*. This same [sequence] is also found in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*.

A sequence is observed; however, the distinction there is that the application of the ritual formulas disregards the ending with *namaḥ* (namas), as follows: *aṃ* with the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ* with the two ring fingers, *hūṃ* with the two little fingers, *sauḥ* with the two thumbs, and *aṃ namaḥ* with the two thumbs, and so forth. But in the ninth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
O Supreme Goddess, by repeating the root-vidyā twice, one should sequentially assign the six limbs upon all the surfaces of the fingers,
ending with the vocative case suffix "ṅe," using the six-limbed formula: *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*.
"Then, having placed [the mantras] on the two hands, one should likewise place them on the six limbs.

By this statement, an alternative method is seen, wherein—without accepting the previously mentioned rule of ending with "namaḥ" (namo'ntatva) in the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment)—it is stated that the mantras end with "namaḥ," "svāhā," "vauṣaṭ," and so forth. In this regard, there is the statement from the *Gandharvatantra*:
The intended meaning of the phrase "by repeating the root-vidyā twice" is as follows, from the second chapter of the *Viśvasāra-tantra* held by the radiance of the *Hara-tattva*:
"Whichever mantra the Guru should bestow upon whichever disciple according to the prescribed rite,
that should be known as the root-mantra (mūla-mantra), which is endowed with all the tantras."
Thus, the definition of the *mūlavidyā* has been established. Furthermore, regarding the statement in the previously cited *Gandharva Tantra*—
namely, "by repeating the *mūlavidyā* twice"— it is intended not merely the *bālābīja* as mentioned in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*,
but rather the inclusion of the respective mantras bestowed by one's own Guru from among all the previously mentioned *vidyās* consisting of three peaks (*trikūṭa*).

The object of awakening (*bodhya*)—the author himself will clarify this during the occasion of defining the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). Thus, since various differences of opinion are observed here, one should follow whichever sequence accords with the tradition of one's own guru; this is the general direction [of the argument].
(99) Now, it was previously stated that the hand-placement (*karanyāsa*) is performed with the *Bālā* mantra. But what about the limb-placement (*aṅganyāsa*)?
He will explain that [the mantra] is preceded by the *bālābīja*; therefore, he asks, "What is this so-called *bālābīja*? and answers: "Speech" (*vāk*).

"Speech" refers to the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava, *ai*. "Kāma" refers to the seed-syllable of Kāma, *klīṃ*. "Preceded by Śambhu": Śambhu is the letter *ha*, and what precedes it is the letter *sa*. That which is preceded by Śambhu possesses the vowel of Indra and the *visarga*; the vowel of Indra is the fourteenth vowel, *au*, and there is also the *visarga*.

The phrase "like the vowel of Śakra and the visarga" is an epithet for "preceded by Śambhu. Thus, it results that the *bālā-vidyā* is *ai klī sau*. By this—meaning, by the aforementioned *bālā-vidyā*—the practitioner of mantra, having uttered its three seed-syllables, [should worship] O Tripurasundarī! (p. 456)
The word "namas" and so forth should be stated first, and thereafter the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 100 ||
(In that regard, another sequence:

Or else, by repeating the root [mantra] twice according to the sequence to be described hereafter, one first [says] "To the heart, namaḥ," and then "To the head, vahnivallabhā" (the beloved of fire). 101.
"Vaṣaṭ" is declared for the crest (śikhā), "hūm" is uttered for the armor (kavaca), "vauṣaṭ" should be for the three eyes, and "phaṭ" is proclaimed for the weapon (astra). || 102 ||
(Regarding the rule for the fingers therein:
One who knows the mantra should place [the mudrā] with the three fingers—the index, middle, and ring fingers;
and then with the index and middle fingers, together with the thumb.

100. Here, while setting forth two sequences even for the ritual assignment of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), he first speaks with the words beginning "of this" (*asyā*). "Of this" means of this young girl (*bālā*). The "three seed-syllables" are *aiṃ*, *klīṃ*, and *sauḥ*. Then [comes] "Tripurasundarī". Then, before the word "namaḥ", one should employ the six limbs beginning with the heart; this is the ellipsis. And thus: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripurasundari hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *aiṃ klīṃ*...

"Sauḥ Tripurasundari, obeisance to the head"—in this manner, everywhere, this placement (nyāsa) begins with the *bālā* mantra and ends with "obeisance" (*namaḥ*). 101–102. He states another sequence with the words "to be described," etc. Alternatively (*athavā*) indicates another option.
"From the sequence to be described" means from the sequence beginning with "obeisance to the heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), etc. "Of the root" (*mūla*) refers to the root mantra that is to be worshipped.

By repeating this [mantra] twice, the number six is achieved through the doubling of the vidyās consisting of three peaks (kūṭas); thus, the application of the six [syllables] to the six limbs beginning with the heart becomes logically consistent. And so: first the Vāgbhava peak, then "Hṛdayāya namaḥ"; then after the Kāmarāja peak, "Tripurasundari Śirase svāhā"; then...

After the Śakti-kūṭa, [recite] *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; again, after the Vāgbhava [kūṭa], *kavacāya hūṃ*; again, after the Kāmarāja-kūṭa, *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*; again, after the Śakti-kūṭa, *karatalapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ phaṭ*—this is the sequence. *Vahnivallabhā* is *svāhā*.

103. Regarding this, he states the rule for the fingers with the words beginning "the index finger" (*tarjanī*) and so forth. This rule for the fingers is to be understood according to the previously mentioned sequence beginning with the heart. Thus, one should place [the mudrā] on the heart with the index, middle, and ring fingers; likewise, the index—
Then, with ten fingers, and subsequently with three and two [fingers] as before;
[this is] the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
For the sake of pleasing the deity, one should first make the resolve while facing either east or north. (103)
(Bhūtaśuddhiḥ) Then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). (The procedure therein:)
Having personally placed his own hands, palms upward, upon his own lap.

[One touches] the head with the two middle fingers and the topknot with the thumb; in this same sequence, [the others] are likewise [touched]. This is clearly stated in the ninth chapter of the Gandharva-tantra:
"The heart is said to be [touched] by the middle, ring, and index fingers; the head [by the thumbs]."
"With the middle and index fingers, O Dear One, the *śikhā* [mudrā] is formed with the thumb;

the *kavaca* is said to be with all ten fingers, and the *netra* is declared to be with three fingers; likewise, the *astra* is declared to be made with two fingers accompanied by sound. Thus it is said.
Regarding the fault in not performing the assignment of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), it is stated in that very same [text]:
"Even worship, austerity, adoration, and fire-offerings performed with perfected mantras will not yield fruits if they are devoid of the assignment of limbs."
104. Worship performed by one who is devoid of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is like a malevolent spell;
it yields a contrary result, just as worship performed without devotion does.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Agastya-saṃhitā* cited in the *Haratattvadīdhiti*:
"Without the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), all rites such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship—
even if performed with full illumination— remain entirely fruitless."
Indeed, for one who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship without the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
that web of placements is in vain and that worship shall become fruitless.

Therefore, by the statement in the second chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, "Hence the best of practitioners should perform the purification of the elements" (*bhūtaśuddhi*), which declares the obligatory nature of *bhūtaśuddhi*,

[the author] teaches the purification of the elements to be performed immediately thereafter, beginning with the words, "Then one should perform the purification of the elements. [The term] "with a steady mind" (*sthiracitta*)...
The meaning is that it is impossible for one with a restless mind to perform that practice. "In her own lap" means in the region of her own bosom.
(p. 458) [One should meditate on] Kulakuṇḍalinī, whose nature is the Root-Vidyā, in the Mūlādhāra;
she has the form of a sleeping serpent and is endowed with three and a half coils. || 105 ||
Thin like the awn of wild rice, she is the embodiment of all the gods;
resembling ten million flashes of lightning, she encircles the self-manifested liṅga.
Having meditated upon her with the Haṃsa-mantra, or with the Praṇava,
or with the Kūrca-bīja, the wise and learned one should firmly cause the Goddess to flee.
Having brought about the unification of those two— the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—
and having contemplated the supreme void, the earthly element dissolved into water.

105–106 | Regarding the term *mūlādhāra*: the nature of the *svayambhū-liṅga* and the *kuṇḍalinī* has already been explained in detail in the sixth chapter (verses 10–12); therefore, we do not take pleasure in repeating it here.
107 | Regarding the word *dhyātvā*: the meaning is "having meditated upon the *kuṇḍalinī* in the form described above," by means of the mantra *haṃsaḥ*.
With the syllable *praṇava* (Om) or with the seed-syllable of the *kūrca* (*hūṃ*), one should firmly cause that Goddess—who is coiled like a sleeping serpent—to move and awaken; this is the meaning.
By whichever path the stainless *brahmadvāra* is to be reached, [one should proceed].
Having covered that door with her mouth, the Supreme Goddess fell fast asleep.

Since her state of being "asleep" is designated by the statement in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, her awakening is taught by the phrase "one should cause [it] to dissolve. This is explicitly stated in the thirteenth chapter of the *Picchilātantra*:
"O Goddess, O Beloved, [one should awaken her] with the mantra of the Haṃsa or with the Kūrca-bīja."
"Having made her conscious, one should bring her together with the Earth.

(108) Then, he states what is to be done by means of the verse beginning with "ekībhāvam" (unification), etc. The meaning is: of those two well-known entities—the individual soul (*jīvātman*) abiding in the *anāhata* [cakra] and the Kuṇḍalinī who is of the nature of the Supreme Soul (*paramātman*)—there is a unification.

The meaning is: having made no distinction between these two and having reflected upon them; that is, having led the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which resides within the pericarp of the *anāhata* lotus, by means of the *haṃsa*-mantra into the *kuṇḍalinī*—which is the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and resides within the pericarp of the *mūlādhāra* lotus—and having reflected upon their unification.

This has been explained by us in the commentary on the fifty-first verse, beginning with "the Goddess by the syllable *hūṃ*," in the sixth chapter: "Having led the life-force (*jīva*) together with the mantra of half the heart-mantra into the lotus of the mouth, one should contemplate the water drawn up by the fire as being of the nature of light."
One should contemplate nirvāṇa as fire being carried away by the wind, and [thus] the form of the wind. || 109 ||
The wind, drawn in by space, indeed dissolves into space;
the mind, subject to the power of the ego, is drawn into the Great Principle (mahat) by the Great One.
And within Prakṛti, one should then contemplate the principle of Mahat—
eternal, consisting of light, and having the nature of the knowledge of Brahman.
(The movement of Kuṇḍalinī, together with her essential nature, into Paraśiva:
She is absolute, solitary, peaceful, devoid of qualities, and identical with the Supreme Self;
she indeed goes into the Supreme.
(The nature of Paramaśiva) is supreme and free from all affliction;
it is the supreme state, situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, whose form is emptiness. 112.

By these and other [statements]. Regarding the phrase "the earthly portion": here this should be noted—the five lotuses beginning with the *mūlādhāra* and ending with the *viśuddha* are, respectively, the locations of the five elements consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
The sixth, the *ājñā*-lotus, is the location of the mind. And therein, one should contemplate the aforementioned Kuṇḍalinī together with the earth.

Having led the earth into the *svādhiṣṭhāna* lotus, one should contemplate it dissolved into the water situated there; then, together with that water, one should lead the *kuṇḍalinī* into the lotus called *maṇipūra*, and having visualized that water dissolved into the fire situated there,
one should again raise the *kuṇḍalinī* along with that fire to the *anāhata* lotus, and having dissolved that fire into the wind located there, [one should proceed] again together with that wind.

Having raised Kuṇḍalinī to the lotus called Viśuddha, one should dissolve that wind into the space situated there. Then, having led her along with that space to the mind located at the Ājñā-cakra, one should contemplate that space as dissolved therein; together with her and the individual soul (jīvātman), one should dissolve the mind into the ego (ahaṅkāra), the ego into the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), and the Great Principle into primordial nature (prakṛti).
The process of dissolution culminates with the instruction "one should dissolve. However, the specific details should be consulted in the commentary on verses 51–53 of the sixth chapter.
Regarding the term *prakṛtim*: now, after the dissolution of the principle of *mahat* into *prakṛti*, one dissolves *prakṛti*, which is of the nature of light (*prakāśasvarūpām*).

One should contemplate her as eternal and consisting of the nature of the knowledge of Brahman; the sense is that this is because she is non-different in form from Kuṇḍalinī, who possesses a nature such as light and so forth.
(112) Now, he describes the elevation of Prakṛti, together with the individual soul and Kuṇḍalinī, into Paramaśiva.

(The nature of that as the supreme bindu: The Void (*śūnya*) is like the moon reflected [in water], a station subtler than the subtle, pervading all while consisting of darkness; yet, within the Void, it is known as the supreme light.

Having known that entire sphere of light, consisting of all things visible and invisible and beyond the reach of dispute, as being everywhere, the best of practitioners have cast off even Death himself from that state. || 113 ||
One should first contemplate the syllable YAṂ at the region of the navel as wind;
by that very [wind], one should dry up the liṅga and the principle (tattva) for sixteen measures.
By the words "kaivalya" and so forth: "saiṣā" means that aforementioned Kuṇḍalinī is this very Prakṛti.

By this, the non-differentiated nature of Kuṇḍalinī and Prakṛti is indicated. The meaning is that she goes into the Supreme Śiva, who resides within the triangle situated in the center of the lunar orb located in the interior of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head.

Now, he describes the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Paramaśiva with the words beginning "and supreme" (*paramaṃ ca*). "Free from affliction" (*nirāmaya*) means liberated from all sufferings such as birth, old age, and death; it refers to the state that is the supreme void-nature, the nature of the Supreme Bindu, and identical with the Supreme Brahman. As it is said in the Sixth Prakāśa: "That within is the void..."
By the passage beginning with "served by all the hosts of gods and exceedingly secret" (verse 42),

[the author] specifies the "void" (*śūnya*) as defined by etymology (*nirukta*). Since this has already been explained implicitly in the sixth chapter (*prakāśa*), it is not further commented upon here.

114. Having thus described the process up to the yoga of Kuṇḍalinī within the Supreme Self, the Supreme Śiva, he teaches breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the verse beginning "nābhau" and so forth. The meaning is that one should first contemplate the seed-syllable *yaṃ*—which is the wind—in the region of the navel. Here, the word "pūrvam" (first) is a form derived from the root *pṛ*, as stated in the rule "pūrva-parva-marva-pūraṇe."

The meaning of *pūrva* is "that which fills," as in *pūrayati* (it fills), hence *pūraka* (inhalation). Since *kumbhaka* (retention) and *recaka* (exhalation) will be explained hereafter, the word *pūrva* in this context has the meaning of *pūraka* alone. By that very [means], namely by the previously mentioned seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the wind, one should dry up the *liṅga*, which is the principle (*tattva*), the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*). Here, drying up and so forth [are to be performed].

It should be understood that this refers specifically to the *liṅga-śarīra* (subtle body) accompanied by the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) situated in the left side of the abdomen. In the second chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*,

following the description of the nature of the personification of sin— beginning with "the personification of sin situated in the left side of the abdomen, having the luster of collyrium," and so forth— it continues:
O Supreme Goddess, one should dry the body with the seed-syllable of Vāyu;
having thus made it dry along with its sin by that sequence,
O Śivā, it is then completely burnt by the seed-syllable of Agni together with the sin.
One whose nature is devoted to desire should perform sixty-four *kumbhakas*;
then, by means of thirty-two *mātrās*, one should indeed exhale through the right [nostril]. 115.
One should contemplate the red-colored seed-syllable of fire at the base of the genitals;
by means of that, one should burn the body, which consists of the subtle impressions (vāsanās), as a linga.
Following the sequence previously described, by means of the right nostril,
the preceptor should likewise perform the counting with his left hand.

This is because it has been explicitly stated in such passages, because it is seen accordingly in the *Tantrasāra* and other works, and because the author himself stated in the *Śyāmārahasya* that one should dry up the body together with the "person of sin" (*pāpapuruṣa*). As for what is said in the sixth chapter of the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
The sin situated in the left side of the belly is a man with the luster of collyrium;
for the purpose of its destruction,
O Maheśānī, the great Liṅga-body has been manifested— of that there is no doubt.
"By [this], the sinful body shall be burnt, but one's own body shall not be destroyed.

By such statements, it is taught that the sinful person (*pāpapuruṣa*) alone constitutes the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), and that its drying up and so forth are performed upon that very body; this should be understood as an alternative method. Regarding the phrase "by sixteen measures" (*ṣoḍaśamātrayā*), the definition of a measure (*mātrā*) is stated in the third chapter of the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"Having circumambulated the knees, neither too quickly nor too slowly, the snapping of the fingers is performed; that is proclaimed as a *mātrā*.
(115) Regarding "consisting of desire": one should dry up the *liṅga* which consists of desire, that is, which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as stated previously.

The connection [is as follows]: by this, it is indicated that through the drying up of the seed-syllable (*liṅga*) consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the latent impressions themselves are also eradicated.
"By sixty-four" means that one should perform the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) by reciting the aforementioned seed-syllable of the wind (*vāyu-bīja*) sixty-four times.
"Thirty-two" means that, having closed the left nostril, one should [exhale] through the right nostril by reciting the same seed-syllable of the wind thirty-two times.
The meaning is that one should exhale the breath.
(116) Having thus described the sequence of drying, he describes the sequence of burning with the words beginning "of red color" (*raktavarṇam*). By means of that seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*);
the rest is clear.

117. He describes the sequence of the seed-syllable recitation (*bījajapa*) with the words "previously," and so forth. Thus, one performs inhalation (*pūraka*) through the right nostril, retention (*kumbhaka*) through both, and exhalation (*recaka*) through the left. As for the count of the recitation, the meaning is that one should perform it using the fingers of the left hand.
Having visualized the white, watery syllable *vaṃ* at the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*).
Having thus produced the nectar from the thousand-petaled lotus, || 118 ||
Having performed the *pūraka* and other breath-control exercises, one should flood [the body] down to the soles of the feet;
then, having visualized the syllable *laṃ*, the seed-syllable of the earth, at the root of the anus.
By that very sequence of yoga, the wise one should, through the intellect,
bring about the supreme Śāmbhava body, which is entirely free from both sin and merit.
Thus, by means of the mantra, while yet living, I [received] that supreme goddess Kuṇḍalī, who was drenched in the highest nectar, from the presence of the Supreme Self.
The knower of mantras should place the five elements in their respective locations;
the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon himself as being the Great Śrī Tripurā. (This refers to the meditation on one's own nature as the form of the Goddess. 122.

118–120 | Regarding the syllable *vaṃ*: likewise, having visualized the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, *vaṃ*, which is white in color, at the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*), one should perform the inhalation (*pūraka*) and other breath-control exercises with that seed-syllable; having produced nectar by means of that very syllable, one should cause it to flood [the body] from the thousand-petaled lotus down to the soles of the feet—this is the meaning. Regarding the syllable *laṃ*: thereafter, according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should visualize the seed-syllable of Earth, *laṃ*, at the *mūlādhāra*.
Having meditated upon the supreme [Self] as distinct from the previous state and unpenetrated by sin or merit, one should "accomplish" the Śāmbhava body;

that is to say, one should fashion it. For this very reason, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* have also stated: "By reciting the seed-syllable of Varuṇa (*vaṃ*) sixty-four times, having fashioned the entire body with the nectar flowing from that moon on the forehead—consisting of the letters of the Mātṛkā."

121–122 | With the words "so 'ham" and so forth, he describes the re-establishment of those who were previously raised up by the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) back into their respective places by means of the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). Thus, from the Supreme Self, by means of the mantra "so 'ham," one brings the individual self (*jīvātman*) into the *anāhata* [cakra], which is drenched in the supreme nectar, satisfied by the tasting of the nectar of the state of identity with Paramaśiva.

One should cause Kuṇḍalinī and the five elements—beginning with space (vyoman) and ending with earth—to enter from Viśuddhi down to Mūlādhāra; this is precisely what is meant by the phrase "one should employ them each in their own respective places. By this, the mind, ego, and the principle of Mahat are also explained. Regarding the word "the Self" (ātmānam): one whose self has been purified by the aforementioned practice [should contemplate] the Self in the form of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevī).
The meaning is that one should meditate [upon her].
(The nature of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī:
She whose beautiful face is graced with slightly budding jasmine-like teeth, and who is illuminated by three eyes.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady, whose breasts are as lofty as the finest wine, who possesses the splendor of a radiant red lotus,
who is adorned with various ornaments, who wears a silken garment the color of the bandhūka flower,
and who holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and a multitude of arrows. (123)
(The Installation of the Life-Force): Placing the hand upon the heart, one should perform the installation of the life-force (*jīvanyāsa*). (The Mantra for the Consecration of Vitality):
One should extract the reversed life-force mantra (prāṇamantra), preceded by the noose (pāśa).

This mantra for the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) is proclaimed for all rites. Such a method was taught by Śiva himself in the Jñānārṇava [as the authoritative corroboration of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as explained in the Nirukta]. 125.
123. In the previous statement, it was said, "This is the Great Śrī Tripurā"; in order to explain the meditation upon her, he describes her essential nature with the words beginning with *īṣat*.
124–125. Having thus described the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), he shows the sequence for the placement of the living soul (*jīvanyāsa*) as taught in the *Jñānārṇava*.

By the words "in the heart" (*hṛdi*) and so forth, the meaning is that one should perform the *jīvanyāsa* (the ritual placement of the life-force) using the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra* which is about to be described.

He states the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*: "in reverse" (*viparītam*). The *prāṇa-mantra* is *haṃsaḥ*; its reversal is *so'ham*. That reversed *prāṇa-mantra* is preceded by the *pāśa* (noose), that is, the seed-syllable *āṃ*. By this, [the mantra becomes] *āṃ so'ham*.
The *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra concludes [as follows]: "In the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said in the second chapter:
'One should establish the life-force (*jīva*) in the body by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra;
having uttered the circle of the mouth (*mukhavṛtta*), one should utter the *haṃsa* in reverse order.'"
O Supreme Goddess, one should extract this; it is considered a three-syllabled Vidyā.
This mantra for the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) shall accomplish all rites.
By that very procedure, O Goddess, one should stabilize one's own body.
Thus [ends the section on] facial expression.
(p. 464) (There is another sequence for the purification of the elements:
Alternatively, one may perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in another manner.
By means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal, all that [is dissolved] into the Supreme Self.
Having joined the elements together with the seed-syllable of wind (Yam),
one should then dry them up by means of fire through the process of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thereafter, being composed, one should join those very [elements] together by means of *kumbhaka*;
one should then perform the immersion of that ash with the nectar of the water-seed (*jalabīja*). || 128 ||
By means of the practice of the sequence of exhalation (recaka) and the seed-syllable of the earth (bhū-bīja), the knower of mantras,
having made the body very firm, should perform the remainder as previously described.
(Another sequence for the purification of the elements:
Alternatively, having united the Goddess Kuṇḍalinī with the five elements and so forth within the Supreme Self, one should contemplate the identity of those two. 130.

126–129 | He describes the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) by means of another sequence, beginning with "Alternatively" (*athavā*) and ending with "one should perform as before" (*pūrvavad ācaret*). Regarding "the process of withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*): the order of withdrawal should be understood as follows: earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, and air into space. From this very self (*ātman*), space was produced; from space... [and so forth].

Because the Śruti states, "From wind, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth," and so forth, describing creation in the sequence beginning with space (ākāśa), [the author] says "by means of the order of dissolution" with the intention that this sequence of earth and the others is the order of dissolution. All of that—the entire range from earth up to space, obtained through the previously mentioned order—is [dissolved] into the Supreme Self residing in the thousand-petalled lotus (sahasrāra) in its causal form.

The meaning is "having joined. By this, the dissolution of the qualities of the elements such as smell and taste, as well as the nose and other sense organs, the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), should also be understood. Now he teaches *prāṇāyāma* with the words beginning "by the seed-syllable of air" (*vāyubījena*). Since the sequences of *kumbhaka* and *recaka* will be described hereafter, this should be known as the sequence of *pūraka*. [He dissolves] those endowed with sin.

The connection is as follows: one should dry up the *dhātus*—the bodily constituents—along with the "person of sin" (*pāpapuruṣa*) previously shown, by means of the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*) according to the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). The rest is clear.
(130) He shows another sequence for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) with the words "Alternatively," and so forth. In this sequence, [one should contemplate] Kuṇḍalinī...

Then, by means of the five elements beginning with earth—which reside within the pure cakras from the *mūlādhāra* up to the end—along with those included by the word "etcetera," one should contemplate "I am that" through the yoga of meditation with the mind. Having flooded [the body] at the base with the nectar of the moon, one should bring that [nectar] back together. || 131 ||

Having purified the elements and so forth in their own respective places by means of the stainless mass of their radiance, he meditates upon them with the realization of non-duality: "I am that, and she is I. (132)
(Prāṇāyāma:
One should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with either the root mantra or the syllable Om (praṇava);
or else, one may perform the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃyama) of Śrīvidyā by means of the Bālā mantra. 133.
(Another sequence for the purification of the elements):
Having meditated upon the Supreme Goddess in the form of pure consciousness at the *mūlādhāra*, one who is composed should raise her up by the utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ*. 134.

The meaning is that one should unite the qualities of the elements, such as smell and the rest, along with the organs of knowledge and action, within the Supreme Self residing in the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra), and then contemplate the identity (*aikya*) of those two—the Kuṇḍalinī and the Supreme Self.
(131) Thereafter, he instructs on what must be done, beginning with the word "dhyāna": "Then, having resorted to the yoga of meditation through the mind, [one realizes] 'I am He'..."

One should contemplate; that is to say, one should meditate upon the non-difference between the Nirukta Paramātman and the Jīvātman. Furthermore, he describes the bringing down of Kuṇḍalinī from the Sahasrāra to the Mūlādhāra: "With the nectar of the moon"—having flooded that Kuṇḍalinī with the stream of nectar dripping from the lunar orb situated at the Sahasrāra, [he brings her] to the root.
The meaning is that one should bring [the breath] upward above the self-manifested liṅga (svayambhūliṅga) situated within the mūlādhāra lotus.

(132) Regarding the phrase "the elements and so forth": the connection is that one should also bring back the elements and so forth—which were previously led to the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra) together with Kuṇḍalinī—to their respective locations in the manner previously described. "Stainless by the mass of light of those two" refers to those two...

The meaning is that one whose self has been purified by the masses of light from Kuṇḍalinī and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) should contemplate non-difference with the Supreme Self and with Kuṇḍalinī— thinking "I am He" and "She is I.
(133) Here, he demonstrates the three methods of breath control (prāṇāyāma) beginning with the words "by the root-mantra," etc.

134. He states another sequence for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) with the words "In the *mūlādhāra*. The phrase "having raised that" implies [it] up to the *sahasrāra*. The rest is clear.
(Prāṇāyāma)
One should fill the external air through the iḍā with sixteen mātrās;
perform the kumbhaka with sixty-four, and exhale with half of that [thirty-two]. 135.
And having held the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb,
one should thus perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) in both direct and reverse order.
(An etymological analysis of the term *prāṇāyāma*): The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are the winds within the body; *āyāma* is said to mean extension.
Thus, it is called *prāṇāyāma* by the sages, and it is the destroyer of sin. (137)
(One who does not perform breath control, purification of the elements, and the ritual placements prescribed by their own specific manual lacks the qualification for the worship of the deity):

"But without performing breath control, or likewise without the purification of the elements, or without performing the ritual placements according to rule, one has no qualification for worship. (138)
(An etymological analysis of the term *nyāsa*): It is called *nyāsa* because of the placement (*nyasana*) of the deities of the five elements and the limbs. || 139 ||
(An Exposition on the Purification of the Elements):
Since all elements whatsoever are specifically portions of Brahman, they are eternally supremely pure by virtue of the *mātṛkās*, the *kalās*, and so forth. 140.

In that regard, through the conceit of being a living soul (jīva) and indeed through the web of defects, or by the will of Brahmā, these defects are firmly attributed to one's own self; thus, the identification with the body and other such faults have been described. (141)

137 | "The vital breaths," and so forth; this is clear. He describes the sequence of *prāṇāyāma* in the second chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*: "The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index and middle fingers—is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*. Thus it is said.
Through the thorough knowledge of those [elements], having realized one's own state as Brahman, let it be understood that the abandonment of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is purity. (142)
(Ṛṣyādinyāsa): Now, the best of practitioners should perform the nyāsa of the ṛṣi and the other [components].
Dakṣiṇāmūrti shall be the ṛṣi, and Paṅkti is declared to be the metre. (143)
The deity is the auspicious Mahātripurasundarī in the form of Brahman;
her seed-syllable (bīja) is Vāgbhava, while Śakti is the peak-syllable (kūṭa) and the power (śaktikā).
The supreme practitioner, being wise, should place the *kīlaka*, which is Kāmarāja, upon the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet, in due order. (145)

143–145 | He teaches the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*). Therein, he explains the seer and other attributes of the mantra of the venerable Tripurasundarī, starting with the verse beginning "The seer shall be... Thus, its seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is *paṅkti*, the deity is the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable is the seed (*bīja*), the *śakti* peak-syllable is the power (*śakti*), and the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable is...
It should be known as the *kīlaka*. Its application (*viniyoga*), however, is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"The application is fully explained for the accomplishment of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

Regarding the term "head" (*śiras*): the connection is that one should sequentially assign the previously mentioned seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth to the head and the other limbs ending with the feet. And thus...

The application is as follows: "On the head—salutation to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti; on the face—salutation to the Paṅkti metre; in the heart—salutation to the deity Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; in the secret place—salutation to the seed-syllable Vāgbhava; at the feet—salutation to the power-kūṭa, the Śakti; in all limbs—salutation to Kāmarāja, the kīlaka."

Regarding the fault incurred when the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), and deity (*daivata*) is not performed, the *Gandharva Tantra*, in its eighth chapter, states: "When [a mantra] is recited without the placement of the seer, meter, and deity, even if it is accomplished, one shall not obtain its fruit therein."
(The instruction on the six-limbed placement and the necessity of performing the placement of the *mātṛkā*:
Having first performed the six limbs (*aṅga*), one should then carry out the placement of the *mātṛkā*.
(In that regard, the placement of the *ṛṣi* and so forth for the *mātṛkā*:)
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the mother is Mātṛkā. || 146 ||
The deities are considered to be the consonants, the seeds the powers, and the vowels;
the unmanifest is to be known as the pin (kīlaka). One should perform the placement (nyāsa) according to the stated sequence.
(The ritual placement of the hand on the Mātṛkā):
One should write the vowels, excluding the neuter ones and accompanied by the bindu (anusvāra), in their proper order;
and between each pair [of vowels], one should write the five groups of consonants, likewise accompanied by the bindu. 148.

146–147 | Here, he states that the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) must be performed, saying "the six limbs" (*aṅgaṣaṭkam*). This means having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Since the specific sequence for the placement of limbs regarding Tripurā has already been demonstrated previously, it is not shown again here.
Now, while explaining the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, he first teaches the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [components] with the words beginning "The seer" (*ṛṣiḥ*).

Thus, for this *mātṛkā-mantra*: Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Mātṛkā (Sarasvatī) is the deity (*devatā*), the consonants are the seeds (*bījāni*), the vowels are the powers (*śaktayaḥ*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the pin (*kīlaka*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the ritual placement of the letters (*lipinyāse*). Of this...

Nowadays, the practice is seen as being in the form of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa and its constituent mantras. In the *Tantrasāra*, the author, having introduced the topic with "Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa" and stated "of this Mātṛkā-mantra," etc., describes the Mātṛkā-nyāsa beginning with: "On the head, oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi)," and so forth. However, in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, the venerable Brahmānanda [states] regarding this Mātṛkā-mantra: "Brahmā..."

Without first stating [the details] such as "the seer is Ṛṣi, the metre is Gāyatrī," [the text] merely prescribes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the head and other limbs in this sequence: "Obeisance to Brahmā, the seer, on the head"; "Obeisance to Gāyatrī, the metre, on the mouth," and so forth.
Thus, when it is stated in the *Tantrasāra* and other works that "of this mantra... and so on, the ritual placement must be preceded by the knowledge of the seer, the metre, the deity, and the rest.

This is intended with the sense that [the mantra] is to be performed, and not with the intention that it must be uttered as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), for no authoritative evidence is found for such a status of this mantra in the reading beginning with "tathātvena asya mantrasya" and so forth. For this very reason, even in the present context, in the passage "The unmanifest (*avyakta*) should be known as the *kīlaka*;

one should perform the placement (*nyaset*) according to the stated sequence," the word "should be known" (*jñeya*) indicates precisely that the placement is to be carried out preceded by this knowledge; such is the direction.

148. He teaches the sequence for the placement of the *mātṛkā* on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) with the verse beginning "of the vowels" (*svarāṇām*), etc.: "And [one should place] the neuter [vowels] and the remaining letters in the intervals, and thereafter the *ya*-class [of consonants]. (This is the limb-placement.)
As before, the practitioner of mantra should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) of the Mātṛkā.
(Meditation on Mātṛkā):
She is as white as the full moon of autumn, composed of all the scripts, with three restless red eyes,
radiant with the luster of white ornaments, and blazing with a crown of moon-crested matted hair and a necklace.

The meaning is that one should write the five groups of consonants, along with the bindu (anusvāra), in their respective order between each pair of vowels—from *a* to *au*, excluding the short *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*—that is, within the space between every two letters. By this [mantra]: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ āṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*.

*iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *huṃ*; *oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ* to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*—thus the end is reached.

149. Regarding the word "śeṣa" (remainder): it means that one should write the group beginning with *ya*—that is, the letters from *ya* to *kṣa*—in the interval between the two letters *anusvāra* and *visarga*, which remain from the vowels previously mentioned. Thus: *aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ*.
*Haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ phaṭ* with both palms and backs of the hands—this is the *karanyāsa*. It is clearly stated in the second chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The *ka*-group is in the middle of *aṃ* and *āṃ*; the *ca*-group is in the middle of *iṃ* and *īṃ*."
"Uṃ ūṃ—in the middle of these is the *ṭa*-group; *eṃ aiṃ*—in the middle of these is the *ta*-group;
*oṃ auṃ*—in the middle of these is the *pa*-group, O Supreme Goddess, in due order.
At the end of the *anusvāra* and *visarga* are the *ya-* and *śa*-groups, together with their respective *lakṣas*. Thus it is said.

"According to the previous [method]" means that after the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment), one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* (limb-assignment) by the same sequence as the *karanyāsa*, just as before. Here, the word "limb" (*aṅga*) includes both the fingers, beginning with the thumb, and the body parts, beginning with the heart.

Thus, "according to the previous" means according to the previously mentioned hand and limb assignment of the root deity, following the sequence beginning with "Salutation to the two thumbs" (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*), and so forth.

"One should perform the placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa)," as indicated by the phrase "as before. Regarding the limbs suitable for placement in the *aṅganyāsa*, the *Jñānārṇava* states in its second chapter:
"O Goddess, the heart, the head, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and then the armor (*kavaca*)."
One should assign the Netra-weapon mantra ending in the dative case, followed by "namaḥ" and "svāhā," in due order.
"O Dear One, one should employ [the mantras] ending in *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
This six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) rite of the Mātṛkā is remembered as the remover of all sins. (p.
470) [She is] holding a rosary, a garland, a full water-pot, and the boon-granting gesture, adorned with pure silk garments.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon Vāgdevī, whose face is like a lotus and who is bent by the weight of her breasts. || 150 ||
(The Procedure for the Internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa):

Having meditated in this manner, one should first perform the nyāsa of the letters situated in the sequence of the six cakras, from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, according to their individual order. (151)
(External Mātṛkā Nyāsa):
Having meditated upon the internal mātṛkā in this manner, one should perform the external mātṛkā nyāsa. (In this regard, there is an option concerning whether it is preceded by seed-syllables.)
Or one may assign [the deities] alone upon the body; one may also assign [them] beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha.

151. Thus, immediately after the meditation, he describes the internal placement of the *mātṛkā* (the alphabet) with the words beginning "one should place" (*nyaset*). "Six" refers to the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, which are situated in the sequence of the cakras starting from Viśuddha down to Mūlādhāra. "One by one" means that one should place one letter upon each petal of the lotuses. He states this clearly:
In the eighth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra* and in the second chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"One should place the sixteen vowels upon the eight-petaled lotus at the throat;
one should place the twelve consonants beginning with 'ka' upon the twelve-petaled lotus of the heart."
One should place the ten letters beginning with *ḍa* upon the ten-petalled lotus at the navel;
and one should place the six letters beginning with *ba* upon the six-petalled lotus situated at the *liṅga*.
"One should place the four letters on the base and the vowels on the four petals;
O Dear One, one should place *ha* and *kṣa* on the two-petalled lotus located between the eyebrows.
Regarding the phrase "one should place, O Dear One," the reading in the *Gandharvatantra* is "one should contemplate. Previously, [the letters] were with the bindu (*m*).

By the statement "one should likewise write the five groups [of consonants] along with the bindu," since the letters of the Mātṛkā are taken with the bindu for both the hand-assignment (karanyāsa) and the limb-assignment (aṅganyāsa), there is no authority for abandoning that sequence; therefore, in the present case as well, the assignment must be performed using only the letters accompanied by the bindu. For this very reason, the authors of the Tantrasāra also [prescribe] the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a' as being with the bindu.

By the passage beginning with "one should place [the letters] on the sixteen-petaled lotus at the base of the throat," the placement (*nyāsa*) of the phonemes together with their *anusvāras* has been taught. (152) Having thus described the internal *mātṛkā*-placement, he now states the external *mātṛkā*-placement: "One should place [them] externally... (p. 471).
[This is] the instruction for the placement of each individual syllable upon every limb.
The best of practitioners, following the sequence according to the distinction of each individual syllable, [should perform the ritual]—
[this being the rule for the fingers according to the division of the limbs]—
with the middle and ring fingers upon the forehead and the circle of the face. 153.
Then, one should place [the mudrās] on the eyes with the middle, ring, and index fingers;
and at the base of the ears with the combination of the ring finger and the thumb, using the *vṛddhā* finger.
Then, by joining the little finger and the thumb, [one should touch] the two nostrils. || 155 ||

The practitioner of mantra should place [the mudrā] on both cheeks by joining the index, middle, and ring fingers; then, on the pair of upper and lower lips, he should place them sequentially with the middle finger. (156)
The most excellent practitioner should place [the mantra] upon the two rows of teeth with the ring finger, and he should place it on the region of the head with the middle finger. (157)
The wise practitioner should place the *anāmikā* on the face, the middle fingers on the hands and feet, and the three fingers beginning with the little finger on the joints and tips. 158.
On both sides, at the back, and in the region of the navel—that is the interval—one should place [the marks] with the middle, ring, and little fingers together with the thumbs. 159.
With all the fingers [he placed] the elements beginning with *yā* (the earth element) into his belly;
skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the [seven] elements (*dhātavaḥ*). 160.
One should then place the vital self (prāṇātman), the individual self (jīvātman), and the supreme self (paramātman) with the palm itself upon the heart, using all the fingers. || 161 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "the Mātṛkā" and so forth: "kevalām" means alone, without other seed-syllables (*bīja*) joined to it at the outset. The connection is that one should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the Mātṛkā preceded by Śrīkaṇṭha—that is, preceded by the seed-syllable *a*, which is the seed-syllable of Śrīkaṇṭha.
(153–162) Now, [it is explained] where, in each case, the deposition of the letters beginning with *a* is performed through the application of specific fingers.
One should place [the syllables] upon the shoulders and the back of the neck in successive order;
starting from the heart, one should indeed apply them with the palms of the hands to the feet, the belly, and the face. 162.

(There is an option between beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, and between having the nasal bindu and being devoid of it. In this very manner, the collection of fifty syllables [is formed], beginning and ending with *om*, or ending with *namaḥ*, either with the nasal bindu or devoid of the bindu. || 163 ||
(There is an option between that which possesses both the *visarga* and the *bindu*, and that which possesses neither.
That which possesses the *visarga* and that which possesses both [the *bindu* and the *visarga*] (is the result of possessing the *bindu* and so forth).
The secret is said to be the Tattva.
That which is joined with the Bindu bestows wealth; that which is devoid of the Bindu bestows knowledge;
that which has the Visarga bestows sons; and that which possesses both bestows worldly enjoyment. || 164 ||

(Regarding the option of beginning with the seed-syllables of Māyā and others in the ritual placement: The [mantra] beginning with the Vāgbhava syllable preceded by the seeds of Māyā and Lakṣmī, or else [the one] beginning with the three [syllables] in sequence, or that beginning with Ramā—these should be placed by the most excellent practitioners. 165.

He specifies all that which is to be performed in detail with the words beginning "each single" (*ekaika*): the meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the forehead and other locations according to the distinction of each individual syllable, from *a* up to *kṣa*. Thus, one should place *aṃ namaḥ* on the forehead with the middle and ring fingers; [one should place] *āṃ* on the circle of the face with the middle, ring, and index fingers.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the syllable *namaḥ*. In this manner, for the eyes and other [limbs] as well, the placement of the phonemes beginning with *i* (the letter *ikāra*, etc. should be performed according to the method stated in the root-text, by means of the respective application of fingers.
