Since it is stated that "one should install the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā in sequence," it should be understood that one should install each *pīṭha* preceded by each individual letter of the Mātṛkā. Here too, as before, there is the conjunction with the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Thus, for example:
(1) *hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ aṃ kāmarūpapīṭhāya namaḥ*—this is one sequence.
Beyond this, there is the great seat (*mahāpīṭha*) situated in front, both mobile and stationary;
then the great seat Pūrṇaśaila, and likewise another, Arvuda.
The sacred seat of Āmrātakeśvara, and likewise another, Ekāmra;
then the stainless Trisrotas-pīṭha, and after that Kāmakoṭṭa.
Kailāsa, Bhṛgupīṭha, Kedāra, Candrapīṭhaka, Śrīpīṭha, and likewise Oṃkāra; after that, Jālandhara. (283)
Mālana, likewise Pīṭha, Kulānta, Devikoṭṭaka, the great Pīṭha known as Gokarṇa, and Māruteśvara; || 284 ||
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājagṛha, Mahāpatha, the seat named Kollagiri, and beyond that, Elāpura. (285)
Kāmeśvara is a great seat (mahāpīṭha), and Jayantikā is a great seat;
likewise Ujjayinī is a seat, as is the wonderful one named Kṣīrikā. (286)
The seat of Hastināpura, the one called Uḍḍīśa, Prayāgaka, Kānyakubja as a great seat (mahāpīṭha), Māyāpura, and Jaleśvara; 287.
(2) *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ* to the seat of Kāmarūpa, obeisance—this is the second.
(3) *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ* to the seat of Kāmarūpa, obeisance *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*—this is the third.
(4) *Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aṃ* to the seat of Kāmarūpa, obeisance—this is the fourth.

In the same way, for the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) such as Vārāṇasī and the others, one should first apply the conjunction of any one of the seed-syllables *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, or *śrīṃ* according to this very sequence, and then perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the locations of the *mātṛkā*s, preceded by each individual *mātṛkā* letter with its nasal bindu (*sabindu*), in the following order: *āṃ vārāṇasīpīṭhāya namaḥ*, *iṃ nepālapīṭhāya namaḥ*, and so forth. As it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
In the fourteenth chapter:
"One should always perform the placement of the fifty seats (pīṭhas) according to the Mātṛkā [alphabet].
Regarding this, there is a mutual discrepancy among the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, *Jñānārṇava*, *Gandharva*, and other tantras in their description of the names of the seats.
A discrepancy is observed, which should be understood from their respective sources:
"Malaya, the great seat (mahāpīṭha), and that very one called Śrīśaila; the seat named Merugiri, and then the seat Girivara. (p. 503) || 288 ||
Mahendra, Vāmana-pīṭha, Hiraṇyapura, Mahālakṣmīpura, and the supreme pīṭha known as Uḍḍiyāna. (289)
One should sequentially place the shadow-umbrella and the fifty syllables of the Mothers.
(This is the conclusion of the Sixfold Placement.
By performing this sixfold placement, the practitioner of mantra becomes manifest as Śiva himself. 290.
(The Praise of the Installation of the Seats) In this world, there is no person—be it father, mother, or anyone else—to be worshipped by him.
Thus, those who have installed [the deities] within their bodies are to be worshipped by all yogis. (291)
(The Fault of Not Performing the Pīṭha-nyāsa):
If a practitioner performs prostration devoid of the sixfold nyāsa, he shall meet death before long and fall into hell. || 292 ||
(Now, the placement of the arrow and the desire:
Next, I shall describe the placement of desire (*kāma-nyāsa*), which causes the agitation of the three worlds. || 293 ||

290. "Fifty" means that one should install the fifty seats (*pīṭha*) which have the nature of the fifty letters of the *mātṛkā*. And thus, because the *mātṛkā* letters themselves constitute the nature of those respective seats beginning with Kāmarūpa, their union (*yoga*) is taught in various places. Also, in the third chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, which explains the conventions of worship:
Immediately after the description of the seats (*pīṭha*) such as Kāmarūpa, Ādicchāyā, Chatra, Anta, and Pīṭha, [the text states]:
"These seats have been fully described; they abide in the form of the *mātṛkā*.
By this, the fact that the seats are of the nature of the *mātṛkā* is clearly stated. By this [it is implied that] Gaṇeśa and the others should be employed first.
The *mātṛkās* have also been explained. Regarding "sixfold" (*ṣoḍhā*): the connection is that if one were to perform this placement (*nyāsa*), then one would become Śiva directly.

The *mātṛkās* have also been explained as "sixfold"; the connection is that if one were to perform this placement, then one would become Śiva directly. (292) If the practitioner (*sādhaka*), who is a master of the sixfold placement, should bow down, then [he is superior to] one who is devoid of the sixfold placement.
The connection is that he attains death before long.

(Verses 293–296). Having thus described the sixteen-fold ritual placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), [the author] begins to state the ritual placement for the fulfillment of desires (*kāmanyāsa*).
(On this, the meditation on Kāma:)
Desires, which have the appearance of pomegranate flowers and a deluding form, are adorned with flower-arrows, bows, and quivers, and are joined with their respective powers (śaktis). || 294 ||
(Contemplation of the Powers of Desire):
One should contemplate the Śaktis, adorned with all ornaments, resembling saffron in color, holding blue lotuses in their hands, and capable of attracting the three worlds. (295)
(First, the application of seed-syllables:
One should place the seed-syllables of Kāma, Māyā, and Ramā, along with the letters of the Mātṛkā, upon the body. || 296 ||
(The names of the deities to be assigned: Kāmayukta, Rati, Kāma, Prīti, and Kāntaka; together with Kāminī, Bhrānta, and then accompanied by Mohinī. || 297 ||
Kāmadhuk is joined with Kamalā; Kāmacāra is with Vilāsinī;
Karṇakalpalatā likewise; and Komala is accompanied by Śyāmalā. || 298 ||
The sentiment (rasa) is Śucismitā joined with Kāma, known as Kāmavardhana;
it is accompanied by Vismaya and joined with Viśālākṣī. || 299 ||
[The author] proceeds with the words *kramate-kāmetyādinā*. Therein, first of all, he states a praise (*praśasti*) for the purpose of attracting the practitioners (*sādhaka*s): *trailokyeti*.

He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*) of the desires (*kāma*) to be deposited during the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites, with the passage beginning *dāḍimī* and ending with *śaktisaṃyutān*.
He also describes the visualization of the powers (*śakti*), such as Rati and others, with the passage beginning *sarva*. By this [means], according to the sequence to be described hereafter—
It is indicated that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) must be performed for the *kāmas* (desires) together with their respective *śaktis* (powers). Regarding the word "kāma":

the connection is that one should place upon the body the aforementioned *kāmas* and their *śaktis*, characterized by their respective qualifiers, using the seed-syllables of *Kāma*, *Māyā*, and *Ramā*, as well as the letters of the *Mātṛkā*. In this context, *Kāma* is *klīṃ*, *Māyā* is *hrīṃ*, and *Ramā* is *śrīṃ*; [the placement is] by means of these.
The meaning is that they have been previously joined with the *mātṛkā* letters, from *a* to *kṣa*.
(297–310) He explains the names of the Kāmas and their Śaktis, which are to be deposited according to the aforementioned sequence: (p.
505) Vimala is joined with Lohitā, Ratinātha with Digambarā.
Ratipriyā, Rāmā, Rātrināyakā, and Kubjikā. (300)
The beloved is accompanied by Smara; the lover is joined with Nityā;
the night-stalker is with Kalyāṇī; and the son is joined with Bhoginī. || 301 ||
Nandīśa joined with Kāmadā, Madana with Sulocanā, and likewise the one named Ānandayitṛ with Sulāvaṇyā. || 302 ||
Niśācara with Mardinī, Ratihaṃsa with his subsequent [consort], Kalaha joined with Priyā, and Puṣpadhanvan with Kāṅkṣiṇī. (303)
Mahādhanus with Sumukhī, Grāmaṇī with Nalinī, Bhīma with Jaṭinī, and Bhrāmaṇa with Pālinī. || 304 ||
Then follows *bhramaṇa* joined with *śikhinī*, then *śyāmadugdha*;
thereafter *bhrāmaṇa* joined with *ramā*, and *bhṛgu* well-concealed by *bhūmi*. (305)
The intellect is deluded, restless, prone to wandering, and fickle; it is alluring, long-tongued, and joined with darkness. || 306 ||

By the words "joined with desire" (*kāmayuktā*) and so forth, it follows that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this sequence: *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ*—salutation to Kāma and Rati; *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ*—salutation to Kāma and Prīti; *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ iṃ*—salutation to Kānta and Kāminī. This ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed in the same locations as those for the Mātṛkās, as previously described. Thus it has been stated.
In the fourteenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess, O sinless one, one should always perform the nyāsa with the letters of the Mātṛkā, just like the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
The rest is clear.
The Secret One is accompanied by Lolākṣī; Bhṛṅgiṇī increases delusion; Mohaka is with Capeṭā; and Manmatha is joined with Nāthā. || 307 ||
Mātaṅga is joined with Mālinī; Bhṛṅgin with Kalahaṃsinī;
Gāyaka is likewise joined with Viśvatomukhī. (308)
Then follows Gīta joined with Gajanandikā;
then Nartaka with Rañjinī, and Lekha endowed with Kānti. (309)
Unmatta, Kalakaṇṭhī, Kanaka, Vṛkodara, Megha accompanied by Śyāmā, and Vimala together with Śrī. (310)
(Conclusion of this ritual placement: By means of this application of the ritual placement, one becomes a shaker of the three worlds. || 311 ||
(Now follows the instruction for the placement of the nine sources:
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the nine sources by repeating the three seed-syllables of Bālā:
in the two ears, the chin, the two temples, the mouth, and the two eyes. (312)

312. Now, he describes the *navayoninyāsa* (the deposition of the nine wombs) with the words beginning "Bālā," etc. Here, it means that one should perform the deposition by repeating three times—i.e., thrice—the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Bālā, characterized as *ai*, *klīṃ*, and *sauḥ*, across twenty-seven locations from the ears to the throat; or alternatively, it means repeating the triad of Bālā’s seed-syllables three times. One should thus deposit the nine wombs.
The connection [is as follows]. By this it is meant: the nine locations of the womb, beginning with the ear and ending with the throat, have been described;
they number twenty-seven. Furthermore, when the three *bāla*-seeds are repeated three times, there are twenty-seven seeds.
One should place each seed in turn upon each of the aforementioned locations. Thus, on the right ear: *ai* / *namaḥ*.
*klīṃ* namaḥ on the left ear; *sauḥ* namaḥ on the chin. Again, *aiṃ* namaḥ on the right cheek; *klīṃ* namaḥ on the left cheek;

*sauḥ* namaḥ on the mouth. Thus, it follows that one should place each seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the other locations as well, according to this sequence. Nor should it be argued that by the phrase "by repeating the three seed-syllables of Bālā," the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three syllables upon each individual limb is being taught.
One should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) consisting of the nine wombs (*navayoni*) with the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence:
on the nose, the pair of shoulders, the heart, the two elbows, the abdomen, the pair of knees, the base of the genitals, and the pair of feet. (313)
The best of practitioners should place [the seed-syllables] known as the nine yonis in the secret place, on both sides, on the chest, on the pair of breasts, and on the throat. (314)

Having visualized a square by means of the three seed-syllables of the Child (Bāla), one should contemplate the Śrīcakra through the application of the deposition of the spheres (golaka-nyāsa). || 315 ||
Having mentally resolved upon nine locations— the six cakras, the forehead, the hairline, and the cavity of that head— the best of practitioners should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).

In the *Tantra-vacana* cited in the *Nibandha* on the *Tantrasāra*, by the word "in sequence" (*kramāt*), the application of each seed-syllable (*bīja*) individually is stated. For this very reason, the author of the *Tantrasāra* also clearly declares the application of each individual seed-syllable, stating: "The first seed-syllable on the right ear, the second seed-syllable on the left ear, the third seed-syllable on the chin," and so forth. The same is the case in the *Tripurārcana-rahasya*. [The fourth and fifth are] on the two temples and the two cheeks.
This is the meaning.

[Verses 315–316] Next, he states what is to be done: "The child" (bālā), etc. The connection is as follows: having thus performed the placement of the nine sources (navayoninyāsa) and having visualized the Śrīcakra as a square by means of the three seed-syllables of Bālā, one should again contemplate the Śrīcakra as a sphere (golaka) by means of Bālā alone.
For this very reason, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* also state, after introducing the passage:

"One should install the nine-yoni [maṇḍala] with the young [goddess] Tripureśī," and then declaring, "The practical application (prayoga), however, has been stated in the section on Bhairavī": [They proceed to quote the relevant verses.]
Again, having recited Bālā, one should place [the seed-syllable] in the form of a sphere;
again, having recited Bālā, one should contemplate a square.

By this, it is stated that the contemplation of the *nirukta-caturasra* (the etymological square) and so forth constitutes a constituent part of the *navayoninyāsa* (the deposition of the nine wombs). Regarding the phrase "the six wheels":

it should be understood that immediately after performing the sequence previously mentioned, one should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) upon the *mūlādhāra* and the other centers using the three "child-seeds" (*bālabīja*).
Thus, at the *mūlādhāra*: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ namaḥ*. Again, at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ namaḥ*. In this same order...
The result is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the four wheels beginning with Maṇipūra, as well as on the forehead, the hairline, and the crown of the head.
(The *Śrīvidyā-nyāsa*):
One should place the *Śrīvidyā* in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), then successively on the back and the private parts.
Thereafter, one should place the syllables of the mantra according to the sequence of each individual part. || 317 ||
On the head, in the secret place, in the heart, and also in the three eyes;
on the two ears, in the mouth, on the two hands, and thereafter on the back;
on the two knees, in the region of the navel, and completely in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 318 ||
(The Assignment of the Lunar Day Deities):
Thereafter, the practitioner of steady mind should assign the lunar day deities (*tithinityā*) conjoined with the vowels of the Mātṛkā, in accordance with their sequential order. (319)

317–318 | Regarding the phrase "the Śrīvidyā": the meaning is that one should install the fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā—beginning with *ka e ī la hrīm*—at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the back, and the secret place (*guhya*). Regarding the phrase "the letters of the mantra": the meaning is that one should install each individual syllable of the aforementioned fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā in the fifteen locations starting from the head and ending at the navel. And thus...
The sequence of application is as follows: *namaḥ* on the head (*mastaka*), *eṃ namaḥ* on the secret place (*guhya*), *īṃ namaḥ* on the heart (*hṛd*), and so forth.
Regarding the term "complete" (*saṃpūrṇam*): the meaning is that one should place the aforementioned fifteen-syllable mantra in its entirety upon the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
(319) Now, he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sixteen *Nityās* with the words beginning "the lunar-day *Nityās*" (*tithinityāśca*). And the lunar-day *Nityās* are—
The first is the eternal Sundarī, Mahātripurasundarī;
she is likewise known as Kāmeśvarī and Bhagamālinī.

Those whose characteristics have been described above—such as Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and so forth—are these Nityās. Because they are to be worshipped sequentially on the lunar days (tithis) beginning with the first (pratipad) and ending with the fifteenth, they possess the status of "Tithinityās" (Lunar-day Nityās). As for what is stated in the *Tantrasāra* and other works regarding the "installation of the sixteen Nityās," that refers to the one who is to be installed at the end of the aforementioned fifteen Nityās, corresponding to the sixteenth lunar day.
It should be understood that this is by means of the internal insertion of the Śrīvidyā. And the author himself will state:
"One should place the Śrīvidyā upon the head, extending through the fifteen lunar days (tithis). For this very reason, it is said in the seventh chapter of the Tantrarāja:
"Of the sixteen Nityās, [one should worship] each one in sequence upon the lunar days."
On each respective lunar day, one should perform that specific worship through recitation, fire-offerings, ritual adoration, and so forth.
Ghee, sugar, milk, cake, plantain fruit, honey, jaggery, coconut, fruit, parched grain, sesame, and curd.
(Therein is the placement of Kāmeśvarī. (1)
And therein, the first is the eternal Kāmeśvarī Vaśaṅkarī;
[one should place] Bālā at the edge of the circular heart, and then the word "Kāmeśvarī."
In the region at the end of *icchākāmaphala*, one should write the word *sarva*; then, having uttered the word *sattvavaśaṅkari*, [one writes] the word *sarvajagat*. (321)
At the end of the *kṣobha* [mantra], one should utter the three *kūrca* seed-syllables; having written the five arrows in reverse order, one writes the *kumārikā*.
One should offer flattened rice (pṛthuka), chickpea flour (caṇaka), mung beans (mudga), and milk-rice (pāyasa) in succession,
starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) through all fifteen days.
All these [mantras] are always prescribed for the first goddess, Lalitā, as well as for all the other Śaktis, beginning with Kāmeśvarī.

By such statements as these, the fact that there are sixteen Nityās is explicitly stated through the instruction on performing worship by means of offerings such as ghee for Kāmeśvarī and the others on their respective lunar days (tithis), while for Lalitā, it is prescribed on all lunar days. Regarding the phrase "one by one" (*ekaika*):
the meaning is that it is done in conjunction with the sequence of each individual letter of the Mātṛkā, from *A* up to the Visarga.
320. Therein, he explains the first *nityā* with the words beginning "Kāmeśvarī. The term "Vaśaṅkarī" is an epithet of Kāmeśvarī. As it is stated in the fifteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇavatantra*:
"Kāmeśvarī is the Great Vidyā who brings all the worlds under her control."

He states the extraction of the mantra for the purpose of this ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the words beginning "Therein" (*tatra*), etc. The three seed-syllables (*bīja*) are *ai*, *klīṃ*, and *saur*.

The "round one" (*vartula*) is the *praṇava* (oṃ). The three "darts" (*kūrca*) are *huṃ huṃ huṃ*. Regarding "the five arrows": the mantra of the five arrows—*drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*—will be explained by the author himself later on. By the phrase "in reverse order" (*vilomena*), [it means] *sauḥ klīṃ ai*.

This has been established. The rest is clear. And thus, the result is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the big toe with the mantra: *aṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ oṃ namaḥ kāmeśvari icchākāmaphalaprade sarvasattvavaśaṅkari sarvajagatkṣobhakari huṃ huṃ huṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ kāmeśvarīnityākalāyai namaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "on every footstep" (*pratipad*): it means on each step.
"One should arrange [the deities] ending with the fifteenth day"—this is connected with what precedes.
One should arrange this Nityā Kāmeśvarī on the big toe, beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the conclusion of the full moon (*pūrṇā*). (323)
(The Bhagamālānyāsa [2]) One should place the goddess Bhagamālā, the Mistress of the Yoni, on the right ankle.
After the syllable Vāgbhava and the word *bhaga*, one should write *bhage bhaginī*. 324.
O you whose limbs are the vulva, O garland of vulvas, O bringer of vulvas!
O you who are in the secret place of the vulva, at the edge of the vulva, O you who cause the vulva to fall! || 325 ||
In *sarvabhage*, at the end of *bhagavatiśaṅkari*, there is the word *bhaga*; in *rūpe*, at the end of the word *nitya*, there is the word *klinne*, and after that, the word *bhaga*. (326)
At the end of all the words of the essential form (*svarūpa*), one should utter *bhagāni*;
then, at the end of the essential form, one should write *me hyānaya varade*. (327)
Then one should say "rete" for semen and "surete" for the moistened vulva;
at the end of that, one should say "klinnadrave," followed by "kledaya" and "drāvaya. (328)
One should utter "Amoghe bhagavicche," "kṣubha kṣobhaya sarvataḥ," "sattvān bhageśvari," and also "vāgbhavaṃ blūṃ jaṃ. (329)

324. He speaks of the second [deity], Bhagamālinī, with the words beginning with "dakṣa" and so forth; the meaning is that one should place Bhagamālā on the right ankle. He describes the nature of the placement (*nyāsa*) with the words "vāgbhavam" and so forth. And thus: *Āṃ Aiṃ bhaga-bhage bhagini bhagodari bhagāṅge bhagamāle bhagāvahe bhagaguhye bhagayoni bhaganipātini sarvabhage bhagavaśaṅkari*.

O you whose form is the vulva, eternally moist; O you whose very nature is the vulva, bring all vulvas to me! O giver of boons, O excellent seed, O you who are moist with the vulva, O you who are the liquid of moisture, make [them] wet, cause them to flow! O infallible one, O you who cut through the vulva, agitate, shake all sentient beings! O Mistress of the Vulva! Ai Blūṃ Jaṃ Blūṃ Bheṃ Moṃ Blūṃ Heṃ Blūṃ Ai Blūṃ! O moist one, bring all vulvas under my control!

The mantra *strīṃ blūṃ hrīṃ bhagamālinīnityākalāyai namaḥ* is established according to the cited authorities. Regarding the phrase *bhagāṅge*, if the reading were *bhagānte*, it would become *bhagabhagamāle*. The variations in the sequence of this mantra, however, should be investigated in works such as the *Jñānārṇava* and the *Tantrasāra*.
Blūṃ bheṃ moṃ blūṃ at the end of Svarūpā; blūṃ heṃ blūṃ is Vāgbhava; and at the end of the word *klinne*, [there are] all the *bhagas*. 330.
"Bring her under my control!"—at the end of this word is the syllable *strīṃ* and *blūṃ*, the Mistress of the World (*bhuvaneśvarī*).
She is Bhagamālā, the Great Vidyā who causes women to melt with passion. || 331 ||
(3) The Nityaklinnānyāsa: Tāra, Māyā, and Vāgbhava, followed by "nityaklinne madadrave," and ending with the wife of fire (svāhā)—this is declared to be the mantra of Nityaklinnā. 332.
Having reached the third lunar day, one who is composed should place [the syllables] upon the body.
One should write the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and the two goads (*aṅkuśa*) in the middle, and inscribe the syllable *bhraṃ*. (Bheruṇḍā 4) || 334 ||
One should write separately the letters ending with the final of the *ca*-group (the letter *ma*), excluding the last one (*na*), joined with the fire-syllable (*ra*).
This is endowed with the fourteenth vowel (*au*) and accompanied by the *nāda* and *bindu*.
Conjoined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), this mantra of Bheruṇḍā has been revealed. (335)

332. Now, he states the third [mantra], Nityaklinnā, beginning with "Tāra" and so forth. Thus, the mantra results as follows: *Haṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Aiṃ Nityaklinne Madadrave Svāhā Nityaklinnānityākalāyai Namaḥ*. Having uttered the seed-syllable of Parā, [one says]: *Nityaklinne Madadrave*.
The mantra joined with the wife of Agni (Svāhā) is declared to be this Nityaklinnā.

According to the statement in the fifteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, however, the mantra is: *iṃ hrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā*. It should be understood that this [mantra] has these two forms. (333) He states the time and place for the aforementioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "The third," and so forth.
334–336 | He describes the fourth [mantra], Bheruṇḍā, beginning with "the Praṇava" and so forth. First, one should write the Praṇava (oṃ).
Then, between the two goads—the two seed-syllables *kroṃ* and *krom*—one should write the syllable *bhroṃ*, that is, the seed-syllable *bhroṃ*.
(p. 512) "The best of practitioners should place it in the womb-section of the fourth [mantra]. 336.
Having extracted Bhuvaneśī and Vahnivāsinī joined with the [instrumental] case-ending *ṅe*,
the foremost of teachers should place them ending with the heart-mantra at the navel in the fifth [stage].
(Mahānityeśvarī) [is formed by] the Praṇava, the consort of Śambhu, the syllable *pha* with *re*, and the imperishable letter;
followed by the Moon with the Visarga, then *nityaklinne madadrave*.
One should place Agnijāyā Mahānityeśvarī on the sixth day upon the breast.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should say "Salutation to Śivadūtī";
on the seventh [day], one should personally install this Śivadūtī within one's own heart. (339)

First, there is the conjunction with the fourth vowel; by this, [the mantra] ending in *īṃ oṃ kroṃ bhroṃ krom* is obtained. Then, the *ca*-group (cavarga) minus the final [consonant], which means excluding the letter *ña*; that [group] joined with fire (*vahni*), meaning conjoined with the letter *ra*; likewise, endowed with the fourteenth vowel, the letter *au*; and further, accompanied by *nāda* and *bindu*—*nāda* and *bindu* being well-known terms—it is endowed with those two. *Vahnijāyā* is *svāhā*.

The rest is as before. Thus, the mantra concludes as follows: *īṃ oṃ kroṃ bhroṃ kroṃ crauṃ chrauṃ jrauṃ jhrauṃ svāhā bheruṇḍānityākalāyai namaḥ*. (337) He speaks of the fifth [Nityā], Vahnivāsinī, beginning with the words "Bhuvaneśī," etc. *Bhuvaneśī* is *hrīṃ*. And thus...
The result is that one should place [the mantra] at the navel with the words: *uṃ hrīṃ vahnivāsinyai namaḥ* and *vahnivāsinīnityākalāyai namaḥ*.

(338) He speaks of the sixth, the Great Mistress of Eternity (*mahānityeśvarī*), beginning with the word "praṇava": here first is the *praṇava* (oṃ), then *śambhuvanitā* which is *hrīṃ*, then the seed-syllable consisting of *pharema*, namely *phreṃ*, and then the letter *sa* joined with the *visarga*.

Then, regarding "nityaklinna" and so forth: at the very beginning, there is the conjunction with the sixth vowel (*ū*). Thus, the resulting formulation is: *ūṃ oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ saḥ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā mahānityeśvarī-nityākalāyai namaḥ*. One should place this on the breast. Here, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* maintain that [the deity is] Mahāvajreśvarī. However, in the fifteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, it says:
By the statement, "The eternal Mahāvidyeśvarī has been described by me in this context," it is seen that the name *Mahāvidyeśvarī* is assigned to the *Nityā* by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
(339) Now, he describes the seventh *Nityā*, Śivadūtī, beginning with the words "the seed-syllable of Māyā" (*māyābīja*) and so forth. Here, first—
One should quickly write the syllable *parāṅ* [as] the armor (*kavaca*) and the syllable *ble* in the sky (*khe*), followed by the word *kṣaḥ*.
Having written the seed-syllable consisting of *strīṃ* and *hūṃ*, one should write the weapon (*astra*) seed-syllable *kṣepara*.
On the eighth day, one should place the twelve-syllable Tvaritā mantra on the throat.
Kulasundarī (9), who consists of all lion-thrones, is like a young girl;
one should place her around the throat on the ninth day of the bright fortnight. 341.
One should place the five arrows and Mahānityā upon the lower lip on the tenth day. (10) Mahānityā. 342.

The seventh vowel is then the *māyābīja*, *hrīṃ*. Thus, the result is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the heart with the mantra: *ṛṃ hrīṃ śivadūtyai namaḥ śivadūtinityākalāyai namaḥ*.
(340) Now, he describes the eighth [deity], Tvaritā, beginning with the words "the *tāra*" and so forth. Here—

"First the eighth vowel, then the *tāra*," and so forth. And thus, it results that one should place [the mantra] on the region of the throat on the eighth day with: *ṛṃ oṃ hrīṃ huṃ khe ca ble (che? kṣaḥ strīṃ huṃ kṣe hrīṃ phaṭ tvaritānityākalāyai namaḥ*. However, in the fifteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
Having uttered the seed-syllable *oṃ*, one should write the supreme armor (*kavaca*);
having written *khe*, *cche*, and *kṣaḥ*, one should also write the female seed-syllable (*strībīja*). Then *huṃ*, *kṣe*, and the supreme weapon (*astra*)—this is the twelve-syllabled vidyā.

Because of the inclusion of "khe ca cche kṣa" in this statement, and because it is likewise seen in the *Tantrasāra*, the reading "khe ca ble kṣa" mentioned in the root text is to be considered doubtful.
(341) Now, he describes the ninth [deity], Kulasundarī, with the words beginning with "sarva... and so forth. And thus: ḷṃ ai/ klīṃ sauḥ.
The result is that on the ninth day of the bright fortnight (śuklanavamyāṃ), one should place [the mantra] "kulasundarīnityākalāyai namaḥ" on the throat.

(342) Now, he describes the tenth Mahānityā with the verse beginning "pañcabāṇam," etc. Here too, first as heard in the text is the syllable *ḷ*, then the five seed-syllables of Pañcabāṇa, and then "mahānityākalāyai namaḥ."
(The mantra of the Five Arrows: The two letters at the end of the fifth group [pa], joined with the letter *ra* and endowed with the two preceding long vowels,
further joined with the *nāda*, the *bindu*, and the *kalā*, constitute Kāma, whose nature is *ba-la-ūm*.
The moon with the visarga following it is declared to be the five arrows. || 343 ||
(11) [The mantra] *nīlapatākinī* is circular; it consists of the syllable *bhuvaneśānī*, the seed-syllable *phaḥ*, the *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), the hook (*aṅkuśa*),
the eternal *madadrava* (*huṃ*), and the hook (*aṅkuśa*).
On the eleventh day, one should install the Vidyā Nīlapatākinī upon the staff.
143. Now, in response to the inquiry as to what this so-called "five-arrow mantra" is, he says: "The two at the end of 'tha'" (thāntadvayam).

This means two *da* sounds; furthermore, these are joined with the letter *ra*, and likewise endowed with the first two long vowels—meaning they are joined with the second and fourth vowels—and likewise endowed with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*. By this, *drāṃ* and *drīṃ* are obtained.

*Kāma* refers to *klīm*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kāma. Likewise, *blūm* consists of the letters *ba*, *la*, and *ū*. Then, *saḥ* with the visarga is the Moon, the seed-syllable of the Moon, which is the letter *sa*. Thus, the mantra of the five arrows is: *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*.
This is also stated in the fifteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
Having drawn two vertical lines situated in the fire [triangle] in sequence,
it is adorned on the left by a circular mouth and an eye.
These two arrows have been declared: the Mādana [arrow] situated on the earth (the letter *la*), enriched by the fourth vowel and the bindu, O fair-faced one, in the form of resonance (*nāda*).
The letter *pha* joined with the sequence [of *u*], adorned with the left ear [the letter *r*],
joined with *bindu* and *nāda*, and possessing the visarga— this, O Dear One, is the Moon.

O Maheśānī, listen also to the names of the five arrows: O Goddess, they are Kṣobhaṇa (the agitator), Drāvaṇa (the liquefier), and that which is named Ākarṣaṇa (the attractor), followed by Vaśya (the subjugator) and Unmāda (the maddener), O Supreme Goddess, in due order.

Thus, it results that: *ḷṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ mahānityānityākalāyai namaḥ*. (344) Now, he describes the eleventh Nityā, Nīlapatākinī, beginning with the words "vartulam" and so forth. Here, first of all, there is the application of the eleven vowels according to the method previously stated. *Vartulam* refers to the Praṇava (*oṃ*). *Bhuvaneśānī* refers to *hrīṃ*. After that—
(12) Vijayā:
The wise man should place this Vijayā on the twelfth day and at the time of the Śruti, having joined the beginning of Kāla with Kāla itself, well-united within the remaining staff. 345.
(13) [Sarvamaṅgalā]:
Having uttered "Salutation to Maṅgalā," one should place the Moon conjoined with Vāruṇa and the seed-syllable *tāra* everywhere upon the eyes as Sarvamaṅgalā. 346.
*Phreṃ*. Here, although *phreṃ* should have been said, it is stated as *phareṃ* for the sake of metrical conformity (*chandaḥ*). It is exactly the same in the *Jñānārṇava*.
*Śruṃ*. In the fifteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The Praṇava, Bhuvaneśvarī, and the syllable consisting of *phareṃ*..."

In the statement explaining the extraction of the *Nīlapatākā* mantra— namely, "The second [syllable] consists of *blūṃ*, and then the goad (*aṅkuśa*) of Bhuvaneśī"— the two seed-syllables *blūṃ* and *āṃ* are obtained by the phrase "the second [syllable] consisting of *blūṃ*" following *phreṃ*. The author of the *Tantrasāra* has likewise followed this same sequence for the extraction of the mantra.

It has been shown [that this is so]. Regarding the reading *śruṅmāyā* at its root, since such an extraction of a mantra is impossible, it appears that the reading *blvāṃ māyā* has been corrupted by a scribe’s error and has thus taken on the form *śruṅmāyā*. However, if the reading is *blvāṃ māyā*, then because the two seed-syllables *blūṃ* and *āṃ* are easily established, any contradiction with the *Jñānārṇava*, the *Tantrasāra*, and other works would be entirely avoided.

And thus, the fifteen-syllable mantra results as follows: *evaṃ ca eṃ oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ blūṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ nityamadadrave huṃ kroṃ nīlapatākinīnityākalāyai namaḥ*. This is stated in the fifteenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:

"Having uttered the word *nitya* and [the name] *madadravā* with the vocative case-ending, [one recites] the armor (*kavaca*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and [the mantra of] Nīlapatākinī with fifteen [syllables].
(345) Now, he describes the twelfth [vow], Vijayā, beginning with the words "Kālādya," etc. First, [the first...]*
The conjunction with the twelve vowels: Then there is the letter *bha*, preceded by *kāla* (which is the letter *ma*); that is conjoined with it. The remainder is the letter *ra*;
the staff is the vowel *au*. Thus, the application is: *aiṃ bhūmarauṃ vijayānityākalāyai namaḥ*. This is stated in the Jñānārṇava as cited in the Tantrasāra:

"O Goddess, the syllable *ra*, joined with the letter *ba* and the time-syllable (*kāla*), endowed with the vowel of Indra (*śakra*), and marked with the *bindu* and *nāda*, is the Vidyā known as Vijayā.
(346) He describes the thirteenth Nityā, Sarvamaṅgalā, beginning with the words "the moon," and so forth. Here, first—

The yoga of the thirteen vowels: then the moon is the letter *sa*; that [is] joined with the water [element], i.e., joined with the letter *va*; and the seed-syllable of the Tāra, which is the *praṇava* (OM). (Jvālāmālinī, verse 14)
*Tāram* at the beginning, followed by *hṛd*, then *bhagavati*; then *jvālāmālini devi*;
and *devi* at the end of every word, followed by *sarvapadānte ca bhūtasaṃhārakārike*. (347)
At the end of the word *jātavedasi*, one should write the pair of words *jvalanti*;
then *jvala*, the pair *prajvalat*, and three *huṃ* syllables. || 348 ||
The mantra consisting of the three seed-syllables of fire (Raṃ), followed by Huṃ and Phaṭ-Svāhā, should be employed;
one should then project a garland of flames upon the skull in the southern portion.
(15) Vicitrā:
Ending with the *ka*-group and ending with the vowels, adorned by Indra, the self-sound (*svara*), and the moon;
this is the Vidyā named Vicitrā—one should place it in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). 350.

The connection is that one should say this. Then, at the end of every word in all directions, one should say "namaḥ sarvamaṅgalāyai. Thus, one should place [the mantra] on the eyes: *oṃ svoḥ namaḥ sarvamaṅgalāyai*. This is clearly stated in the fifteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"One should write the seed-syllable of Tāra (oṃ) joined with the Moon (u) and Varuṇa (va)."
"Then, O Goddess, on the fourth [petal], one should write Sarvamaṅgalā.
This mantra, ending with the *hṛdaya* (heart-mantra), O Goddess, is this eternal Sarvamaṅgalā.
(347–349). Now, he describes Jvālāmālinī, the fourteenth [deity], beginning with the words "Tāram" and so forth. Here, first—

The conjunction of the fourteen vowels: then the high-pitched *praṇava* (Oṃ), then *hṛt* (Namaḥ), then *bhagavati*, then *jvālāmālini devi*, and then *devi*. The rest is clear. And thus: Oṃ Oṃ Namaḥ Bhagavati Jvālāmālini Devi Devi, O you who cause the destruction of all beings, O Jātavedas, blaze, blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up! Huṃ Huṃ Huṃ Raṃ Raṃ.
"Raṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā, obeisance to the digit (kalā) of the eternal Jvālāmālinī"—thus it is established that one should place [this mantra] on the southern part of the skull.
(350) Now, he describes the fifteenth eternal goddess, Vicitrā, beginning with the words "the end of the *ka*-group," and so forth. Here, first—
The conjunction of the fifteenth vowel [ṃ], then the letter *ca* at the end of the *ka*-group, the letter *ka* at the end of the vowels, and the vowel of Śakra, which is the diphthong *au*.
Thus, it results that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) with the mantra: *aṃ ckauṃ vicitrānityākalāyai namaḥ*.
(The specific detail regarding this aforementioned placement.)
The wise practitioner should place [the mantras] on the right during the bright fortnight and on the left during the dark fortnight, in due order.
(Śrīvidyā [16]) One should place the Śrīvidyā upon the head, extending through fifteen lunar days.
(The Deposition of Stability):

Thereafter, one should perform the deposition of stability (*sthitinyāsa*) using the sixteen syllables of the Śrīvidyā mantra, [placing them] on the five fingers of both hands, at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the mouth, and the heart. (353)
From the navel down to the feet, from the throat up to the navel, and another from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) down to the throat;
thereafter, on the two feet, and subsequently on the fingers, according to the division of each individual syllable. || 354 ||
(The Sṛṣṭinyāsa):
One should perform the Sṛṣṭinyāsa with the sixteen syllables of the Śrīvidyā:
in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), the hair-tuft, the eyes, the ears, the nose, and the shoulders. (355)
351 | Regarding the specific distinction in the placement (*nyāsa*) according to the different views, he says: "Śukla... and so forth.

352 | Now, he describes the sixteenth *nityā*, the Śrīvidyā, beginning with the word "Śrī. By the phrase "going through the three, five, and fifteen [days]," it is stated that this placement must be performed on all lunar days (*tithis*), from the first day (*pratipad*) up to the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*). Here, first—

The conjunction with the sixteen vowels: Then the root mantra, and then "Obeisance to the eternal digit (kalā) of the venerable Mahātripurasundarī," one should place upon the head. Thus ends the placement of the sixteen Nityās.
(353-354) Now he describes the placement of stability (sthitinyāsa) with the words beginning "the placement of stability" and so forth, using the sixteen syllables of the Śrīvidyā.

The connection [of the sentence] is that one should perform the *sthitinyāsa* (placement of stability) by means of the differentiation of each individual syllable in the sixteen locations beginning with the fingers of the hand.

"In the two feet" and then "in the fingers" means in the toes of the feet. Thus, there are eight [locations]: five in the fingers of the hands and three in the [apertures] beginning with the *brahmarandhra*; one [placement] extends from the navel down to the feet, and one extends from the throat down to the navel.

From the *brahmarandhra* to the throat there is one [syllable], making eleven; with five on the toes of the feet, this is the sequence for the sixteen-syllable placement (*nyāsa*). (355–356) Now he describes the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* with the words beginning "Śrīvidyā" and so forth. Here too, according to the distinction of each individual syllable:
[the syllables are placed] on the two teeth, the two lips, the tongue, and the pit of the throat. (p. 518)
On the back, all the limbs, the heart, the breasts, the belly, and the penis. || 356 ||
(Withdrawal Deposition): One should perform the withdrawal deposition by means of the sixteen syllables of the Śrīvidyā. (357)
On the feet, the calves, the knees, the hips, the navel, the back, on both sides, as well as on the two breasts and the shoulders. (358)
One should place a *bindu* on the two ears, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the mouth;
thereafter, one should place them on the regions of the ears and the hands in that same sequence.

(The distinction between the qualified practitioners for the three etymological assignments [nirukta-nyāsa]): The assignment known as "origination" (utpatti-nyāsa) is for those dwelling in the first stage of life;
the "subsistence" assignment (sthiti-nyāsa) is for householders; and that called "dissolution" (saṃhāra-nyāsa) belongs to the ascetic. 360.

Thus it is connected. And so, the meaning is that one should place each individual syllable of the previously mentioned sixteen-syllabled Vidyā in the sixteen locations, beginning with the *brahmarandhra*.
(Verses 357–359) Now, he describes the placement for withdrawal (*saṃhāranyāsa*) with the words "the Śrīvidyā," etc.; likewise, [it is performed] from the feet up to the backs of the hands.

The meaning is that one should place the sixteen syllables of the previously mentioned Śrīvidyā upon the sixteen locations. "Andhu" refers to the location of the anus. Here, the reading "karṇayoḥ" (on the two ears) appears to be erroneous;
rather, [the locations are] the two hands, the two shanks, the two knees, the waist, and the back of the fingers.
O Pārvatī, [one should place them] at the navel, on both sides, as well as on the breasts,
the shoulders, the two hands, the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), the face, and the eyebrows; thereafter, in sequence, in the region of the ears and around the wrists.

Thus, it should be understood that because the *Tantrasāra* cites the phrase "of the two hands" (*karayoḥ*), there would otherwise be the fault of redundancy with the term "ear-region" (*karṇapradeśa*) which is to be mentioned later.
(The placement of the Mistress of the Wheel, *Cakreśvarī-nyāsa*)
Then the best of practitioners should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Cakreśvarī. (In that regard, the determination of the locations:
[It is performed] in the regions of the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, and the navel. (361)
One should likewise place [the mantra] at the base of the linga, at the foundation, and on all limbs. (The sequence of placement:
Then, having recited the Tripura-vidyā which effects the purification of the hands... (362)
The wise knower of mantras should place Tripureśī with the three seed-syllables of Bālā alone,
and the Śrīmat Tripurasundarī with the root mantra.
The knower of mantras should place Tripurāvāsinī with the very same mantra mentioned previously; then he should place Tripurāśrī and Tripurāmālinī.
And likewise, having uttered the Bālā mantra, one should then [worship] Tripurāsiddhā, then Tripurātmikā, and then Tripurabhairavī.

361–362. Next, he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Cakreśvarī with the words beginning "atha" and so forth. Therein, he first identifies the locations suitable for the placement with the words beginning "śiras" and so forth. He then states the sequence of the placement with the words beginning "kara" and so forth.

The *vidyā* that effects the purification of the hands consists of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) "aṃ," "āṃ," and "sauḥ," as was already demonstrated previously (verse 70, chapter 15). At the outset...

The connection is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Tripurā after reciting the *vidyā* known as Karaśuddhikarī. Thus, it results in the following: "Aṃ Āṃ Sauḥ, salutation to Tripurā"—this is how one should place [the mantra] on the head.

(363) He now describes the second *nyāsa*, the placement of the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*), beginning with the words "Bālā" and so forth. Thus, [one should place]: "Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, salutation to Tripureśvarī."
It concludes that one should place "namaḥ" on the forehead. Regarding the third, the placement of the Cakreśvarīs, he says: "with the root mantra.
Thus, it concludes that having uttered the root mantra, one should place "namaḥ to the illustrious Tripurasundarī" between the eyebrows.
(364-365) Now, [he describes] the five Cakreśvarīs beginning with Tripurāvāsinī and ending with Tripurātmikā—

He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the passage beginning with "by the previously mentioned" and ending with "consisting of Tripurā. By "previously mentioned," he means the root mantra, because that alone was stated immediately prior; and since no specific [mantra] is mentioned, it applies to all [deities] from Tripurāśrī onwards up to those consisting of Tripurā, even when they are positioned in front.
The seed-syllable of Śiva, Soma, and Vahni, joined with Vāgbhava, and ending in *māyā*—possessing the moon, the sky, desire, Indra, and fire, along with the nasal drop (*bindu*). (366)
The Vidyā of Tripurabhairavī consists of space (a), moon (i), and fire (ra), adorned by the sound of Śakra (e), joined with the visarga and the moon (i). 367.

(The Deposition of the Seats) Next, I shall describe the deposition of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*) according to the sequence of the *Tattvavimarṣiṇī*: having uttered the root *vāgbhava* [bīja], one should then recite the word "in the fire-wheel" (*agnicakre*). (368)
The root-yoga is to be understood as follows: having thus uttered the root-mantra, one should conclude by performing the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Salutation to Tripurāvāsinī" at the throat;

"Salutation to Tripurāśrī" at the heart; "Salutation to Tripurāmālinī" at the navel; "Salutation to Tripurāsiddhā" at the base of the genitals; and "Salutation to Tripurātmikā" at the *mūlādhāra*. This is the final result.

365–367 | Now, he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Mistress of the Ninth Wheel (*navamacakreśvarī*) with the words beginning "Bālā" and so forth. The meaning is that first one should utter the *bālā* mantra—namely, *aiḥ klīṃ sauḥ*—and thereafter one should utter the *tripurabhairavī* mantra.

He explains the *tripurabhairavī* mantra, which consists of three peaks (*trikūṭa*), with the words beginning "Śiva" and so forth. *Śiva* is the letter *ha*; *Soma* is the letter *sa*; and the seed-syllable of Fire (*vahnibīja*) is the letter *ra*.

By "Vāgbhava" is meant the letter *ai*. Thus, *hasaraiṃ* is obtained as the Vāgbhava-kūṭa. Regarding "Viyat": Viyat is the letter *ha*, Indu is the letter *sa*, Kāma is the letter *ka*, Śakra is the letter *la*, Vahni is the letter *ra*, and Bindu is the anusvāra (*m*). By this, *hasakalarīṃ* is obtained as the Kāmarāja-kūṭa. Regarding "Ākāśa": Ākāśa is the letter *ha*, Candra is the letter *sa*, and Vahni...

The letter *ra*, the vowel *au* (the sound of Śakra), and the *visarga* and *bindu* are well known. Thus, the mantra of Tripurabhairavī is *hasaraiṃ*, *hasaka larīṃ*, and *hasarauḥ*. This is clearly stated in the twelfth chapter of the Sāradā-tantra:
"The ether [letter *ha*] situated in the earth [la], the moon [sa], and fire [ra], followed by the element [ka] and topped with the *bindu*."
The mantra consists of the letter situated in the northeast (Vaiśvānara) among the vowels starting with *vi* (i.e., *e*), marked by the dot of the left eye (*i*);
followed by the letter situated in the sky (*a*), *Bhṛgu* (*b*), and fire (*r*), possessing the crescent moon of creation (*visarga*).
Thus, it follows that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on all the limbs with the mantra: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ hasaraiṃ ha sa ka la roṃ ha sa rauḥ tripurabhairavyai namaḥ*.
[Verses 368–376] Now, he promises to describe the placement of the sacred seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*) with the words beginning with "the seat" (*pīṭham*), starting from the root-mantra (*mūla*).
In the abode of Kāmagiri, within the form of the feet of Mitreśanātha, the Goddess [is present] at the end of the word "Kāmeśvarī," as the power whose essence is Rudra. (369)
Having recited the *pādukā* mantra, one should place it in the *mūlādhāra*;
then, having recited the second part of the root mantra, one should place the foot upon the solar wheel (*sūryacakra*).
From the seat of Jālandhara, the pada belongs to Ṣaṣṭhīnātha;
following the word "Vaktreśvarī," the goddess [arises] from the power whose essence is Viṣṇu.
The wise practitioner should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the heart with the mantra known as Pādukā;
having uttered the seed-syllable of Śakti, he should then utter the word "pada" in the lunar wheel (somacakra).
At the end of the word *pūrṇagiri*, one should extract the word *gahvara*.
From the sound whose essence is Uḍḍīśanātha, [arises] Mālinī preceded by *bhaga*. (373)
Reciting the mantra of the Śrī-pādukā of the Goddess, the power of the self of Brahman,
one should place it between the eyebrows after first uttering the seed-syllable of the fourth state (turya).
From the Brahma-wheel, having flown up from the Uḍḍiyāna seat,
one should thereafter [worship] Mahātripurasundarī, who is of the nature of Caryānātha.

Then, from the station of the Supreme Brahman, one should utter the station of the Power of the Self (ātma-śakti); having recited the mantra of the sandals (pādukā-manu), one should install it in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 376 ||

The mantras of the illustrious Tripurasundarī, consisting of the three peaks (*kūṭas*) in the form of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti, have been previously demonstrated. Here, by the term "root-Vāgbhava," the first peak of the aforementioned mantras composed of those peaks is to be understood. Thus, having uttered the Vāgbhava-peak of one's chosen mantra—such as *ī e ka la hrīm* or any other—first, [one should proceed].

The conclusion is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) at the *mūlādhāra* with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Śrīpādukā of the Goddess Kāmeśvarī, who is Rudrātmaśakti, whose essence is Mitrīśanātha, and who resides in the abode of Kāmagiri within the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*). This is stated in the tenth chapter of the *Gandharva Tantra* (p.
522) regarding the *tattvanyāsa*:
Now I shall describe the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), which cuts away all sins.

At the end of the *vāgbhava* [syllable], one should then place the word "to her who pervades the *ātmatattva*," followed by "salutation to Mahātripurasundarī"; thus one should perform the placement with this mantra. (378)
Having uttered the Root-Vāgbhava [syllable], then the word for the Fire-wheel (agnicakra),
and thereafter the abode of Kāmagiri, one should extract the word for Mitrīśa.
After the word *nāthātmake*, one should then place the word *kāmeśvarī*. Following that, from the word *rudrātmaśakti*, one should assign the mantra "Obeisance to the Śrī-pādukā.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, [one should do so] in the Ādhāra and in the heart. Thus it is said.

Regarding the phrase "with the root as the second": thus, having uttered one of the *kāmarāja* syllable-combinations (kūṭa) beginning with *ha sa ka ha la hrīm*, it is concluded that one should place [the mantra] in the heart, saying: "Obeisance to the Śrī-pādukā of the goddess Vajreśvarī, who is the essence of Viṣṇu and whose power is the sixth Lord (*Ṣaṣṭhīnātha*), within the Sūryacakra at the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Jālandhara."

Regarding the phrase "the seed-syllable of power" (*śaktibīja*): thus, having uttered any one of the power-fragments (*śaktikūṭa*) of one's chosen mantra, such as *sa ka la hrīṃ*, one should finally conclude by placing [it] between the eyebrows with the formula: "Obeisance to the Śrī-pādukā of the Goddess Bhagamālinī, who is the Brahman-natured Power and identical with Uḍḍīśanātha in the cave of Pūrṇagiri within the lunar wheel. This is the final result.

Regarding the term *turyā*: because the collective utterance (*samaṣṭyā*) of the three *kūṭas* following their individual utterances constitutes the fourth state (*turya*), the mantra consisting of the three *kūṭas* is designated by the term "seed of the fourth" (*turyabīja*). Thus, having uttered any one of the mantras such as *ī e ka la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, or *sa ka la hrīṃ*, [one should worship] at the Wheel of Brahman (*brahmacakra*) in the sacred seat of Oḍḍiyāna, which is the nature of Caryānātha.

The meaning is that one should perform the placement (nyāsa) at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Śrīpādukā, who is the supreme Brahman, the self-power (ātmaśakti), of the goddess Mahātripurasundarī.
This is clearly stated in the *Kulāmṛta* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"The state of the Supreme Brahman is the Cakra; thereafter is the state of Uḍḍīyāna."
Having joined the word *pīṭha* with the word *pada*, then the word *caryānāthātmake pada*; then, after the word *mahātripura*, the word *sundarī*;
then, after the end of the words *devībrahmapadātmā*, [join] *śaktiśrīpādukām*. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the *pīṭhanyāsa* (377–382).
Having thus described the *pīṭhanyāsa*, he promises to explain the *tattvanyāsa*:
"The *tattva* [is placed] from the base up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and from that point up to the creeper of the eyebrows."
Having uttered Kāmarāja, one should [place] Vidyātattva and so forth as before. || 379 ||

Having uttered the seed-syllable of Śakti from the navel up to the creeper-like eyebrows, and likewise from that starting point down to the heart, one should similarly [utter] the Śiva-tattva and the others.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) from the base to the heart, starting from the root of that liṅga, ending with the fourth seed-syllable and including all the principles (tattvas). || 381 ||
To Vyāpikā, ending with "namas," belongs Mahātripurasundarī;
one should then place that mantra, beginning with the first word, from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 382 ||
(The Weapon-Placement): Then one should perform the weapon-placement (*astranyāsa*), which brings pleasure to the Goddess, in due order.
Having uttered the five arrows, one should utter the arrow of Kāmeśī. (383)

By the words "the nyāsa," etc., he shows the sequence for the nyāsa of the *tattvas*. Regarding the phrase "ending with the *vāgbhava*": here too, as before, there is the application of the three *kūṭas* both individually and collectively. Thus, having uttered the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* of the root mantra, one says: "Obeisance to Mahātripurasundarī, who pervades the *ātmatattva*," [extending] from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*.

One should place [the mantra] from the *brahmarandhra* down to the eyebrows. Regarding "the Kāmarāja": having uttered the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, one should place it from the region of the navel up to the eyebrows with the formula, "Salutation to Mahātripurasundarī, the pervader of the Vidyā-tattva.
From the eyebrows up to the heart, one should place "the Śakti-seed," which means the *śakti-kūṭa*. And so it is said:

Having uttered the *śaktikūṭa* as before, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) from the *mūlādhāra* to the heart with the mantra: "Obeisance to Mahātripurasundarī, the pervader of the *śiva-tattva*";

and from the heart to the base of the *liṅga* with the following: "By this [mantra]... which means that, as before, one should utter the mantra consisting of the three *kūṭas* at the end of the fourth seed-syllable (*turyabīja*), followed by: "Obeisance to Mahātripurasundarī, the pervader of all *tattvas*."

The sequence for the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) culminates as follows: one should deposit [the mantras] from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, and again from the *brahmarandhra* down to the feet.
(383) Now, he teaches the deposition of the weapon (*astranyāsa*) with the words beginning "the deposition of the weapon," etc. Regarding "the five arrows": *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ*.

The mantra of the five arrows, *blūṃ saḥ*, has already been taught by the authors of this work. Thus, having uttered the five arrows, one should utter the five arrows of Kāmeśvarī; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, the wise practitioner should write the five syllables of the skin and so forth in their proper sequence.
It is joined with Ananta and endowed with the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā. || 384 ||
The five arrows of Kāmeśvarī are said to be the bestowers of desire. || 385 ||
(The sequence of ritual placement; therein, the placement of the arrows:
Then, one should draw the arrow through the gem-opening from the Jambhalas.
[One should place] "Kāmeśvara" from the arrows upon one's own heart and the lower right hand. (386)
One should write the seed-syllables *yā*, *dī*, *drā*, and so forth for the Jambhalas;
and for the arrows, one should write "Kāmeśvarī" followed by the word "namas. || 387 ||
The best of practitioners should place the flowery arrows of the Goddess; [this is] the placement of the bow.
Then, one should place the syllables beginning with *drā* and *dyā*, ending with *dhaṃ* and *ṅe*, followed by the word "enchanter" (*saṃmohana*). (388)

384. He describes the five arrows of Kāmeśvarī with the verse beginning "tvagādi" (skin, etc.). It should be understood from the *Śrīkaṇṭhanyāsa* and other sources that the five syllables *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *śa* correspond respectively to skin, blood, flesh, fat, and bone. In the root text, by the phrase "the five syllables beginning with skin," the aforementioned group of five syllables starting with *ya* is indicated; and that [group] is [conjoined] with the infinite *ā* (ākāra).

It is likewise endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. By this, it is stated that *yāṃ*, *rāṃ*, *lāṃ*, *vāṃ*, and *śāṃ* constitute the five arrows of Kāmeśvarī. This is clearly stated in the *Guptārṇava* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Drāṃ, drīṃ, klīṃ, blūṃ, and sa—these are proclaimed as the arrows of Kāma."
"Yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ—this is the five arrows of Kāmeśvarī.
By this [verse], he describes the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the passage beginning with "maṇi" and ending with "sādhakasattama. And likewise:
*drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ jaṃ*—to the Jambhalas, the arrows of Kāmeśvara.

The formula is "namaḥ" (salutation). He states the locations for the placement [of the mantras] as "the heart," etc., and "beginning with ya," etc. Thus, the formula is: *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ jaṃ jambhalebhyaḥ kāmeśvarībāṇebhyo namaḥ*.
The locations for the placement, however, are as before.
388–389 | Now he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the bow of Kāmeśvara-mohinī, beginning with *drāṃ*:

"Thus, one should perform the placement ending in *ṅ* [i.e., *drāṃ*] and ending in *namaḥ* for the bow of Kāmeśvara. With this mantra, the practitioner of mantras should place it on his own left lower hand."
Then follows the "word of delusion" beginning with *yā* and ending with *thaṃ ṅe*. || 389 ||
The practitioner should place the sugarcane bow in the left hand of Vāmadevī by means of the mantra ending in "namas," beginning with "Kāmeśvarīdhanuṅ. || 390 ||
(The placement of the noose:
The seed-syllables beginning with *drā* and *yā*, together with the circle of the mouth (*o*) and the nasal bindu, are for the purpose of subjugation; thereafter follows the word *Kāmeśvara*. (391)
One should place [the mantra] "pāśāya namaḥ" on the upper left hand;
then [the letters] beginning with 'ya' and ending with 'dra', followed by the sky (ha), fire (ra), māyā (ī), and the moon-point (bindu).
Then, for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should place the word "Kāmeśvarī" followed by "pāśāya namaḥ" upon the upper-left [hand] of the Goddess. (393)
(The placement of the goad:
*Aṅkuśanyāsa*) The seed-syllables beginning with *drā*, followed by *kroṃ* and ending with *ṅe*, then *stambhana*;
at the end of *kāmeśvarāṅkuśāya*, [one says] *namaḥ* for the upper left hand. (394)

The practical application is as follows: *drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ dhaṃ sammohanāya kāmeśvaradhanuṣe namaḥ*. Regarding the locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) performed with this aforementioned mantra, he states "with this" and so forth. Next, he describes the ritual placement of the Enchanting Bow of Kāmeśvarī, beginning with "yādi" and so forth. And thus: *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ*.

The application is as follows: *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ thaṃ sammohanāya kāmeśvarīdhanuṣe namaḥ* (Salutation to the bow of Kāmeśvarī for the purpose of enchantment). 391–392. Now, he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the noose (*pāśa*), beginning with *drāṃ* and so forth. Thus, the application is: *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ āṃ vaśīkaraṇāya kāmeśvarapāśāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the noose of Kāmeśvara for the purpose of subjugation).
"Yādi," etc. And thus, the application is as follows: *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ hrīṃ vaśīkaraṇāya kāmeśvarīpāśāya namaḥ*.
(394) Now, he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the goads (*aṅkuśa*) for these two with the words beginning "drādi. And so: *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ*.
The practical application culminates as follows: *saḥ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ kroṃ stambhanāya kāmeśvarāṅkuśāya namaḥ*.
The seed-syllables beginning with *yāṃ* and ending with *drāṃ*, followed by *kroṃ*, the word *stambhanaṃ* (paralysis), and the word ending in the dative case (*ṅe*).
One should place Kāmeśvarī and Aṅkuśā at the end, on the upper right side of the Goddess. || 395 ||
(The deposition of the syllables in code): Thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform the deposition of the syllables in code in sequence:
on the roots, middles, and tips of the hands; and at the root, the heart, and between the two eyebrows. (396)
One should place [the mantras] in these locations by encircling them with three segments of the root-mantra;
and in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should place the fourth [mantra] as the all-pervading [layer] by means of that very same [root-mantra].
(The Tripurānyāsa): One should then perform the fifty-fold Tripurānyāsa with the phonemes of the Mātṛkā.
[395] "Beginning with *yā*," and so forth. And thus: *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ*.
The practical application culminates in: *saḥ kroṃ stambhanāya kāmeśvaryaṅkuśāya namaḥ*. This concludes the assignment of the weapons (*astranyāsa*).
According to the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, this assignment should be performed with the *tattvamudrā* (396–397).
Having thus described the assignment of the weapons, he now states the assignment of the syllable-clusters (*kūṭanyāsa*): "Then, the *kūṭanyāsa*..."

By the words "one should perform" (*kuryāt*) and so forth, the connection here is as follows: one should sequentially place [the mantras] by repeating the three root-sections (*mūlakhaṇḍa*) upon the base, middle, and tips of the two hands, and likewise in these locations: the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, and the space between the eyebrows.
In this regard, it should be noted that [this refers to] the previously mentioned triad of peaks (*kūṭa*), which consist of the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti [bījas].

Having uttered the *vāgbhava* syllable-group (*kūṭa*) of one’s own chosen mantras, one should place it at the base of the right hand; having uttered the *kāmarāja* syllable-group, one should place it in the middle; and having uttered the *śakti* syllable-group, one should place it at the tip. Then, the placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed on the base, middle, and tip of the left hand in this same manner. Thereafter, having again uttered the *vāgbhava* syllable-group, [one should place it] at the *mūlādhāra*; having uttered the *kāmarāja* syllable-group...

It should be understood that after uttering the *śaktikūṭa* in the heart, one should place it between the eyebrows. Regarding "in the aperture of Brahmā" (*brahmarandhre*), this refers to the fourth seed-syllable (*bīja*), which is the mantra consisting of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three *kūṭas*. It should be understood that its status as the "fourth" (*turīya*) is in relation to the mantra employed through three repetitions.

And thus, one should place [the mantras]: *evaṃ e ī ka la hrīṃ namaḥ* at the base of the right hand; *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ namaḥ* in the middle; and *sa ka la hrīṃ namaḥ* at the tip. This should be understood for the other specified limbs as well. "By that very same" means by the fourth [syllable], which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three peak-syllables (*kūṭa*).
(Therein is the determination of the fifty-three cities:
On earth, there are those named Kāminī, Modinī, and Madanonmādinī. (398)
Then there is Khecarī, named Kāminī, followed by Ghaṇṭikā and Kledinī;
then Śivadūtī, Subhagā, Bhagā, and Vidyeśvarī. (399)
Mahālakṣmī is Kaulinī, and Kāmeśī is Kulamālinī;
another is named Vyāpinī, and thereafter is the one called Bhagāvahā.
Vāgīśvarī by name, Kāmā, Piṅgalā, and Bhagasarpiṇī; then there is she named Sundarī, and Nīlapūrvā Patākinī. (401)
Siddheśvarī, Amoghā, and Moghā, who wears a garland of their blood;
Maṅgalā, Bhagamālinī, Raudrī, and Yogeśvarī. || 402 ||
Ambikā is Aṭṭahāsā; from Vyoma comes the station of Vyāpinī;
Vajreśvarī is Kṣobhiṇī, and likewise Śāmbhavī is Aṇimā. (403)
Lokeśvarī is named Raktā; Sūkṣmā is white, as is Aparājitā; Sambartā, Vimalā, and Moghā; and Bhairavī is known as Ghorā. || 404 ||
Then these are remembered as Sarvākarṣiṇī and Tripurāntā.
(This is the instruction for the placement [nyāsa] in the locations of the Mātṛkās:
One should place these just like the Mātṛkās for the sake of pleasing Tripurā. (405)
398–405 | Now, he describes the *nyāsa* of Tripurā with the passage beginning with "pañcāśat" and ending with "tripurāprītihetave.
The fifty Tripurās are those beginning with Kāminī and ending with Sarvākarṣiṇī.
These Tripurās, which end with the word "Tripurā," are to be installed by means of the letters of the Mātṛkā—the phonemes of the Mātṛkā from *a* to *kṣ*.

The Connection: Here, because it is stated that "one should perform the placement of these [syllables] like the Mātṛkās," it should be understood that this placement is to be performed in the locations of the Mātṛkās, beginning with the forehead; and thus: *aṃ* to Kāminī (p. 528).
(The placement of the wheels; therein, the promise to explain the placement along with its praise.)
I shall now describe the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa), which is most excellent and bestows auspiciousness;
it constantly purifies the body, grants spiritual accomplishments, and destroys sins. (406)
(The sequence of ritual placement; therein, the placement for the first enclosure:

The best of practitioners, having preceded [the mantra] with the *māyā* and *śrī* seed-syllables, should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) at the end of the phrase "obeisance to the first line of the square" (*caturasrādyarekhāyai namaḥ*). (407)
On the right shoulder, the back, the fingertips, the buttocks, and the toes of the feet;
and on the toes of the left foot, the hip, the fingertips, the back, and the shoulder. (408)
In these very ten locations, one should assign the ten powers beginning with *aṇimā*;
then, one should again draw the central line of the square as before.

One should place "namaḥ" on the forehead and "āṃ modinyai namaḥ" on the perimeter of the mouth. In this same manner, it should be understood that the placement (nyāsa) of Madanā and the others, ending with Sarvākarṣiṇī, must be performed upon the other limbs as prescribed in the sequence for the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. The rest is clear.
406. Now, he promises to describe the placement of the *cakras* (*cakranyāsa*) preceded by a demonstration of its fruits, beginning with the words "In the *cakra*" (*cakretyādi*).

407. Therein, he shows the sequence of the placement (*nyāsaparipāṭī*) beginning with the words "In the four-cornered [figure]" (*caturasretyādi*). The phrase "preceded by the *māyā* and *śrībīja*" is connected respectively with "in the four-cornered [figure]" (*caturasretyādi*) and "the powers such as *aṇimā*" (*aṇimādyā ityādi*). The same applies to the phrase beginning with "on the right shoulder" (*dakṣāṃsetyādi*). Likewise...

Amṛtānandanātha also stated in his *Yoginīhṛdaya-ṭīkā* that one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) at the ten locations starting from the right shoulder blade and ending at the back of the crown, using the mantra "Oṃ caturasrādyarekhāyai namaḥ. Thus, the meaning is that one should perform the pervasive placement at the ten locations beginning with the right shoulder using the mantra "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ caturasrādyarekhāyai namaḥ."

409. Now, he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis] upon the right shoulder and so forth as previously defined: "Right here" (*atraiva*). The connection is that one should place the ten [powers] beginning with *aṇimā* upon these very ten locations, consisting of the right shoulder and the rest. As for those beginning with *aṇimā*: *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, *prākāmya*, *bhukti-icchā*, *prāpti*...

The names of all the *kāmās* are to be understood from the *Tripurārcanarahasya* and other such texts. Now, one might object: in the preceding passage beginning with "on the back of the right shoulder," there are mentioned the back of the right shoulder, the tip of the right hand, the right buttock, and the toes of the right foot.

Since one obtains only eight locations—namely, the toes of the left foot, the left hip, the tip of the left hand, and the back of the left shoulder—how is it justified that there are ten locations in this very context? It is said [in response]:
in the third chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
Then, on the right shoulder, the back, the palms, the buttocks, and the toes of the feet;
then on the toes of the left foot, the buttock, the palm, and the shoulder and back.
O beautiful one, one should install the powers beginning with *aṇimā* within these very ten locations by means of pervasiveness throughout the roots, bases, and backs of the fingers and toes.

By the inclusion of the front and back parts of the head through the phrase "on the crest, the root, and the back" within this statement, the number of locations as ten is established. This same sequence for defining the ten locations is also observed in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*. Therefore, [the discrepancy] is surely due to the negligence of a scribe.

It appears that the portion indicating the front and back parts of the head has slipped from its original place. Let wise practitioners examine with earnestness whether this reconstruction is correct or not. Now, let us return to the subject at hand: thus, "hrīṃ śrīṃ aṇimāsiddhyai namaḥ" on the back of the right shoulder; "hrīṃ śrīṃ laghimāsiddhyai namaḥ" [on the left].

On the tip of the right hand. In this same manner, it should be inferred accordingly for the other limbs as they have been explained. Having thus described the placement of the first line of the square consisting of three external lines, he describes the placement of the middle line with the words "of the square" (*caturasra*). "As before" means by way of pervasion (*vyāpakatvena*). And thus: *hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

It should be understood that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by saying "Salutation to the central line of the square," placing it upon the eight locations beginning with the big toes of the feet as pervading the body;
then, upon those very same locations, one should sequentially place the eight powers (*śaktis*) beginning with Brahmāṇī. These eight, beginning with Brahmāṇī, are:
Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī.

And thus, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this sequence: *hrīṃ śrīṃ brahmāṇyai namaḥ* on the big toe of the right foot, and *hrīṃ śrīṃ māheśvaryai namaḥ* on the big toe of the left foot; in this same manner, the placement of Kaumārī and the others should also be performed on the sides and so forth.
In this regard, the procedure for the placement on the final line of the square (*caturasra*) is not seen even in the three manuscripts we rely upon. This [is as follows]:

Thinking that this may be an error due to the scribe's negligence, this procedure is demonstrated according to the respective authorities through a comparison with the *Yoginīhṛdaya* and the *Tripurārcanarahasya*. As stated in the third chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"The lines of the square should be consecrated with the mantra 'Obeisance to the final line' (*caturasrāntyarekhāyai namaḥ*)."
One should perform the placement [of the mantras] pervasively throughout the body as previously described up to its end;
then, one should place the ten mudrās in her ten locations,
and subsequently, one should place eight of them within the eight locations beginning with Brahmāṇī.
"One should place the remaining two [syllables] at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta) and on the big toe.

Thus, the meaning is that *hrīṃ śrīṃ caturasrāntyarekhāyai namaḥ* should be deposited within the aforementioned previously mentioned sites of Brahmāṇī and the others by means of pervasion (*vyāpakatvena*). Regarding "of that" (*tasyāḥ*): of that...

The wise one should place the Brahmāṇīs and the other goddesses on the two big toes at the end of the four corners according to their etymological derivation, on the two sides, on the two knees, on the two outer shoulders, and finally behind. 410.
One should place the remaining two at the end of the twelve and on the big toe;
may all these yoginīs protect the entire surface of the earth. || 411 ||
The wise practitioner should place the eight [syllables] of those [goddesses] in the positions of the eight Brahmāṇīs;
having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with this, he should then install the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī).
Upon the support [of the body] is the goddess Tripurā, the supreme mistress of the Śrīcakra;
likewise, there is the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā and the Buddhist philosophy. 413.
The meaning is that one should install the ten mudrās, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, in the ten locations along the line.

These [ten] beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī are as follows: eight are Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, Sarvavidrāviṇī, Sarvākarṣaṇī, Sarvavaśaṅkarī, Sarvonmādinī, Sarvamahāṅkuśā, Sarvakhecarī, and the one called Sarvabījā; and two are Sarvayoni and Sarvatrikhaṇḍā.
"Making ten in total," as stated in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*. He explains their locus of placement (*nyāsasthāna*) with the words beginning "Brahmā" and so forth. The connection is as follows:

one should place the eight [mudrās] beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Sarvabījā at the locations of the eight [Śaktis] beginning with Brahmāṇī, starting from the right shoulder and so on. Regarding the word "the remaining two": these are the two previously mentioned remnants, Sarvayoni and Sarvatrikhaṇḍā, which are to be placed respectively at the *dvādaśānta* (the end of the twelve).

The meaning is that one should thus place [the mantras] on the region above the forehead and on both big toes. And so: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī Mudrā" on the right big toe; "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the Sarvavidrāviṇī Mudrā" on the left big toe. Having placed the remaining six in this sequence up to the left shoulder:

It results that one should place [the mantra] "Obeisance to Sarvayonimudrā" above the forehead, and "Obeisance to Sarvatrikhaṇḍāmudrā" on both big toes. However, in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, a different sequence is observed when combined with the seed-syllables (*bīja*) from the front.
By the term "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*) found in the aforementioned statement of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, the region above the forehead is to be understood. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīsvacchandasaṃgraha* as cited in its commentary:
"That which is known as the 'End of the Sixteen' (*ṣoḍaśānta*) is the lunar orb situated in the space [of consciousness].
Below that location is the solar disc, possessing twelve powers."
"It is known as the *dvādaśānta*, situated in the region of space.
(412–413) Now, he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel, beginning with the words "the Mistress of the Wheel" (*cakreśīm*):
"Then, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) ending with 'salutation to the sixteen-petaled [lotus]' (*namaḥ ṣoḍaśapatrāya*)."
And the practitioner should place Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others in these [locations]. || 414 ||
In the right ear, on the right back, at the elbow, on the back of the hand, and then successively on the right thigh, knee, ankle, and the sole of the foot. (415)
One should arrange [the letters] in reverse order in these regions and on the left,
within the sixteen-petaled wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra) that fulfills all desires.

And likewise, one should place [the mantras] at the *mūlādhāra*: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Tripurācakreśvarī; obeisance to the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī Mudrā; obeisance to the Buddhist system (bauddhadarśana).
(414–416) Now, regarding the sequence: he describes the placement (*nyāsa*) in the sixteen-petaled lotus, the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*), which fulfills all desires. Thereafter—

By such statements as these, the meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) by way of pervasion upon the right ear and other locations with the mantra: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ṣoḍaśadalapadmāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the sixteen-petaled lotus). Regarding "Kāmākarṣiṇikā and the others": since it is stated that these are to be applied in reverse order to the eight limbs beginning from the right ear and ending at the soles of the feet, they are to be placed on the locations starting from the soles of the feet and ending at the left ear.

The phrase "and in the eight limbs" means that the sixteen secret Yoginīs, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī, are to be installed within the sixteen limbs in the form of a sixteen-petalled lotus. This is explicitly stated in the third chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"Within that, [one should recite] 'Salutation to the sixteen-petalled lotus'."
Having performed the placement upon those petals, one should place Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others;
[the locations are] the right ear, the back, the shoulder, the elbow, the back of the hand,
as well as the thigh, the knee, the ankle, and the sole of the foot.
"Thus, this same group of eight is considered to begin with the sole of the left foot.
As for Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others: Kāmākarṣiṇī, Buddhyākarṣiṇī, Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī, Śabdākarṣiṇī, Sparśākarṣiṇī, Rūpākarṣiṇī, Rasākarṣiṇī, Gandhākarṣiṇī, Cittākarṣiṇī, and Dhairyākarṣiṇī.
The sixteen [powers] are Smṛtyākarṣiṇī, Nāmākarṣiṇī, Bījākarṣiṇī, Ātmākarṣiṇī, Amṛtākarṣiṇī, and Śarīrākarṣiṇī.

These, along with their measures and so forth, will be explained in the eighteenth chapter, in the section on worship (*pūjāprakaraṇa*). And therein, the two seed-syllables (*bīja*), the vowels, and so forth, ending with Ākarṣiṇī, follow in sequence.
Then, one should worship in sequence with the seven-syllable mantra, "nityākalā."
